CRP maintained that the Rainbow Coalition would remain focused on its political objectives despite the alleged meetings.

“Let it be known, the Rainbow Coalition has come to stay. These meetings and backdoor politics will not stop the will of the people,”

It added, “Also let us quickly send a reminder to Nunieh that she must be in a hurry to have forgotten so soon how she was saved from the pangs of (enemies) while in office.

CRP urged Nunieh to reflect on her previous political experiences, saying it was concerned that she may have forgotten.

World.title: AAAN Flags Of 21st Edition of LAIF Awards
World.content:
Raheem Akingbolu

The Association of Advertising Agencies of Nigeria (AAAN), the umbrella body for advertising professionals in Nigeria, has announced the kick-off of the 21st edition of the Lagos Advertising and Ideas Festival (LAIF). This announcement was made by the newly re-elected President of AAAN, Lanre Adisa, at a press conference in Lagos.

Also, a new leadership was unveiled for the Lagos Advertising and Ideas Festival Management Board. The newly appointed board members include: Funke Adekola, President; Jumoke Akinyele, Vice President; Victor Oyaroro; Tobi Williams; Rotimi Ade-Onajobi; Toheeb Balogun; Anne Obaseki; Dr. Meksley Nwagboh; Segun Akinyemiju; Sandra Amachree; Israel Obatunde; Olabisi Olusanya; and Jonathan Oyovwevotu.

Speaking at the press conference, Adisa described this year’s LAIF theme, “From Glitch to Great,” as not just a slogan but a powerful reminder that the path to greatness is rarely perfect.

“Every great idea faces obstacles. Every creative breakthrough is preceded by moments of doubt, disruption, experimentation, and even glitches. What distinguishes great creators is not the absence of challenges but the courage and resilience to learn, adapt, and keep creating. In many ways, it is the natural progression from grit through the inevitable glitches to greatness. That is the story of LAIF, and indeed, the story of creativity itself,” he said.

He noted that the AAAN remains committed to elevating LAIF from West Africa’s leading celebration of creativity to a globally respected benchmark for creative excellence, comparable to international award bodies such as Loeries, African Cristal, and Pitchers.

“That journey from glitch to great, from local acclaim to global relevance, will demand more from all of us: more originality, more craft, more innovation, and more courage to create ideas that can stand shoulder to shoulder with the very best in the world,” he said.

In her remarks, the newly elected President of LAIF Management Board, Funke Adekola, stated that the new board is committed to building on the previous board’s key learnings and structural momentum and to creating a festival that truly reflects where the industry has moved, as well as a governance structure that mirrors the modern creative economy.

Adekola stated that the new leadership will drive LAIF not only to establish itself as the champion of creative advertising but also as the ultimate benchmark for total business and cultural impact. She explained that the team is determined to position LAIF as the launchpad for the next operating system for African creativity, not just celebrating excellence but catalysing the future.

“As we step into a brand-new cycle today, we are not here merely to announce an award show. We are here to announce an evolution. This board stands on the shoulders of two decades of remarkable progress, and we are stepping into this season with a commitment to honour our past while fearlessly defining our future,” she said.

World.title: Group Backs Agbese on Nigeria’s Exit from International Criminal Court
World.content:
* Says Hague-based court has become a tool for caging African states

A Pan-African youth advocacy organisation, the Pan-African Youth Development Network (PAYDN), has thrown its weight behind the call by the member representing Ado/Okpokwu/Ogbadibo Federal Constituency in the House of Representatives, Hon. Philip Agbese, urging Nigeria to consider withdrawing from the International Criminal Court (ICC).

The group described the Labour Party lawmaker’s position, expressed last week during a television interview as “timely, courageous and reflective of the growing frustrations of many African nations over the selective application of international justice”.

In a statement issued on Monday and signed by its Country Director, Dr. Charles Okolo, the organisation argued that the ICC, rather than serving as a truly impartial institution, has increasingly been perceived as an instrument deployed against African countries, while powerful nations accused of similar or worse violations remain beyond its reach.

According to the group, the pattern of prosecutions and investigations undertaken by the Hague-based court over the years has reinforced the widespread belief that Africa has become the primary target of the institution.

“The concerns raised by Hon. Philip Agbese resonate with millions of young Africans who have watched with dismay as the International Criminal Court appears to reserve its prosecutorial zeal almost exclusively for African leaders and conflicts, while allegations involving influential global powers receive little or no meaningful attention,” the statement read.

PAYDN noted that justice must be universal and impartial, insisting that no international judicial institution can command legitimacy if it is perceived to operate on the basis of political convenience rather than the principles of fairness and equality.

The organisation maintained that Africa possesses the intellectual capacity and institutional potential to strengthen regional mechanisms capable of addressing crimes against humanity, war crimes and genocide without excessive dependence on external institutions that many perceive as politically influenced.

It added that the African Union (AU) should intensify efforts towards empowering continental judicial frameworks that reflect Africa’s realities while upholding international standards of justice and accountability.

The group stressed that Nigeria, as Africa’s largest democracy and one of the continent’s leading voices in international diplomacy, has a responsibility to champion reforms that promote fairness within the global justice architecture.

“Hon. Agbese’s intervention should not be dismissed as a rejection of accountability. Rather, it is a call for a more balanced international legal order where justice is blind to geography, race and political influence,” Okolo stated.

PAYDN further urged African governments to collectively review their engagement with the ICC and demand comprehensive reforms that would restore confidence in the institution.

The organisation said any international court that genuinely seeks global legitimacy must demonstrate equal commitment to investigating and prosecuting alleged crimes regardless of the nationality or geopolitical influence of those involved.

While reaffirming its commitment to the fight against impunity, the group maintained that justice must never become an instrument of geopolitical domination.

It therefore called on Nigerian policymakers, civil society organisations and stakeholders across Africa to initiate constructive conversations on strengthening African judicial institutions while engaging the international community on the need for a more equitable global justice system.

“We call on our leaders, especially those in National Assembly to make this a national call. At the African level, our organization shall work closely with Nigeria’s delegation for the next extraordinary session, to cause a formal motion to be submitted and moved on this subject matter at the Pan African Parliament in South Africa,” the statement concluded.

World.title: Minimum Wage Cannot Sustain Nigerian Workers, Retiring Pension Chief Warns
World.content:
• Etukudoh demands living wage, better working conditions for civil servants

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja

A retiring senior pension officer in the Federal Civil Service, Mrs. Maria Nkereuwem Etukudoh, has warned that the current minimum wage is inadequate to sustain Nigerian workers amid rising costs of living, calling on the Federal Government to urgently introduce a living wage that reflects prevailing economic realities.

Etukudoh, who retired after 25 years in the Federal Civil Service, including her tenure as Head of the Pension Unit at the Federal Ministry of Finance, said soaring costs of fuel, transportation, food, housing and other essential commodities had significantly eroded the purchasing power of civil servants.

Speaking at a retirement reception held in her honour in Abuja Sunday, she said the gap between workers’ earnings and the cost of living had become so wide that even her salary could barely meet basic transportation needs.

“My salary cannot even fill my car with fuel for two weeks. We need a living wage, not just a minimum wage that loses value before workers receive it,” she said.

Etukudoh said the removal of fuel subsidy and the resulting increase in transportation costs had compounded the economic difficulties confronting workers, particularly civil servants who commute considerable distances to their places of work.

“To go to work became burdensome. Buying fuel, paying transport fares, feeding the family and paying rent became very difficult,” she said.

The retiring pension administrator warned that inadequate remuneration was not merely a welfare issue but one capable of undermining workers’ morale, commitment and productivity.

She urged the government to make workers’ welfare a priority, arguing that a motivated workforce remained critical to efficient public administration and effective service delivery.

“Government should continue improving workers’ welfare because the current minimum wage cannot take anybody anywhere,” she said.

According to her, adequately compensated workers would be more motivated to contribute meaningfully to national development.

“When workers are properly compensated, they will give their very best to public service,” she added.

Etukudoh, who spent a significant part of her career dealing with pension administration, also used the occasion to draw attention to the difficulties confronting retired workers across the country.

She said her experience had exposed her to the hardship faced by Nigerians who devoted their productive years to public service but were sometimes subjected to prolonged delays before receiving their retirement benefits.

According to her, “There are many challenges because I am retiring as a pension officer.

“You see retirees who have worked all their lives for this country, and when it is time for them to receive their reward, in most cases they don’t get that reward. Is that not terrible?”

She disclosed that some pensioners were compelled to remain around government offices for extended periods while waiting for their entitlements, with some allegedly sleeping outside offices.

She said: “Sometimes you see them crying. Some of them even want to sleep in the office. In some offices, they actually sleep outside because they are waiting for their entitlements.

“It saddens my heart that after giving all their youthful years, strength, resources and time to the nation, they are not adequately compensated.”

Etukudoh therefore called for comprehensive reforms in pension administration at the federal and state levels to ensure prompt payment of pensions and other retirement benefits.

She also urged pension administrators to treat retirees with dignity and compassion, rather than subjecting them to unnecessary bureaucratic delays.

“When pensioners come to you, don’t push them aside.

“When they cry, wipe away their tears. If you can assist them with transport fare, do so.

“Support them emotionally, physically and spiritually. Pray with them and for them because one day every worker will become a pensioner,” she stated.

The retiring pension chief, however, acknowledged efforts by the present administration to address some outstanding pension liabilities, expressing hope that such initiatives would be sustained and expanded.

“There is hope. In this present administration, efforts have been made to pay some outstanding pensioners.

“There are also plans to improve contribution rates and strengthen exit benefit schemes.

“Government is trying, and we pray they will do even more because when workers are properly compensated, they will give their very best to public service,” she said.

Etukudoh also lamented the poor working conditions in some government offices, saying inadequate facilities and obsolete equipment could further undermine workers’ productivity.

“In many offices we don’t have laptops, computers, printers, chairs or even decent office facilities.

” Sometimes the environment does not dignify workers. When people work under such conditions, service delivery suffers,” she stated.

She called on the government to provide basic working tools and decent office environments as part of broader efforts to improve efficiency and productivity in the public sector.

Reflecting on her career, Etukudoh expressed appreciation to her husband, children, colleagues, relatives and members of her faith community for their support throughout her years in public service.

She particularly acknowledged her husband for encouraging her to join the civil service when she was initially reluctant.

“My husband persuaded me to join the civil service when I was reluctant. Today, I am grateful to Jehovah God, my children, my colleagues and everyone who supported me throughout this journey,” she said.

Her husband, Professor Nkereuwem Etukudoh, Provost of the Federal College of Medical Laboratory Science and Technology, described her retirement as the culmination of decades of sacrifice, commitment to public service and dedication to the family.

“I encouraged her to join the civil service in 2001, and from that time till now we have not suffered any loss.

She has worked, kept the home, remained faithful, and today she is retiring in glory. I thank God for her,” he said.

Professor Etukudoh, who disclosed that the couple had been married since December 31, 1988, said his wife’s retirement would not mark the end of her contribution to society.

“She is retiring, but she is not tired. She will continue to contribute to society, support the family and remain active in promoting the work of Jehovah,” he added.

The professor also called for greater national investment in medical laboratory infrastructure, local production of diagnostic equipment and reagents, as well as stronger professional training.

“There cannot be a healthy society without functional medical laboratories. Medical laboratory scientists are central to disease diagnosis and patient management, yet this critical sector has not received the attention it deserves,” he said.

He disclosed that the Federal College, under his leadership since 2018, had intensified efforts towards equipment fabrication and local production of laboratory reagents, stressing the need for Nigeria to reduce its dependence on imported diagnostic materials.

“These are two strategic areas that have largely been neglected in Nigeria.

“We are repositioning the institution to begin equipment fabrication and reagent production, in line with our statutory mandate.

“This will strengthen healthcare delivery, reduce dependence on imports and improve professional standards,” he said.

He commended the Federal Government for investments in education infrastructure, expressing optimism that sustained reforms would reposition medical laboratory education and contribute to improved healthcare delivery.

The retirement reception attracted family members, friends, colleagues and well-wishers, who celebrated Etukudoh’s career and described her as a compassionate public servant whose commitment to pensioners and the civil service had left a lasting legacy.

World.title: EFCC Under Olukoyede: Enforcement, Politics and Fight for Credibility
World.content:
Recent move by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission to freeze Osun state government’s account reignites debate over timing, independence and results of the country’s anti-graft war. Iyobosa Uwugiaren writes.

Baarely days before the Osun State governorship election, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) found itself at the centre of another political storm.

Reports emerged that the commission had frozen a bank account belonging to the Osun State Government. Governor Ademola Adeleke and his supporters immediately accused the EFCC of political interference, warning that the action was capable of crippling government activities on the eve of a crucial election.

The controversy dominated headlines and social media, apparently forcing President Bola Tinubu to publicly distance himself from the commission’s action. While critics have questioned the timing and alleged political motives, others have argued that anti-corruption agencies should not suspend investigations simply because elections are approaching.

As the debate intensified, attention once again shifted to the man leading Nigeria’s foremost anti-graft agency — Ola Olukoyede, the Executive Chairman of the EFCC — whose three years in office have become one of the most closely scrutinised in the commission’s history.

The Osun incident is only the latest example of how the EFCC’s work inevitably places it at the intersection of law, politics and public opinion. The criticism that trailed the Osun account freeze is hardly surprising. In Nigeria, every major anti-corruption drive has generated controversy, especially when investigations touch politically exposed persons, state governments, or strategic sectors.

For the EFCC Chairman, the political headwinds are part of the job description. The agency’s mandate — to investigate, prosecute and prevent economic and financial crimes — inevitably puts it on a collision course with powerful interests.

Yet beyond the partisan noise and daily headlines lies a more fundamental question: has the current leadership of the EFCC remained faithful to its constitutional mandate of fighting corruption without fear or favour?

To answer the question, it is necessary to look beyond the controversies and examine what the commission has done, how it has done it, and the constraints within which it operates.

Available evidence suggests that despite enormous political pressure, legal battles and relentless public scrutiny, the commission has intensified its enforcement activities under Olukoyede. The approach has been three-pronged: pursue high-profile cases, prioritise asset recovery, and expand the fight into new frontiers like cybercrime while strengthening institutional capacity.

One of the most remarkable examples of this commitment is the ongoing investigation into the alleged diversion of funds allocated for the rehabilitation of Nigeria’s state-owned refineries.

The probe is regarded as one of the largest corruption investigations in the country’s oil and gas sector in recent years. It touches on billions of public funds approved over several years for projects that Nigerians are yet to feel the impact of. The EFCC has so far recovered over N9.4 billion, US$21.2 million, and several landed properties allegedly linked to individuals under investigation in connection with the programme.

Beyond the impressive figures, the exercise demonstrates the commission’s determination to follow financial trails, recover proceeds of crime and ensure accountability in one of the country’s most strategic and opaque sectors.

For many observers, pursuing such a case illustrates the chairman’s willingness to confront corruption in areas traditionally regarded as politically sensitive. The petroleum industry has long been associated with enormous public expenditure and allegations of financial misconduct. Investigating it inevitably attracts resistance from influential interests. Nevertheless, the commission has pressed ahead, reinforcing the principle that no institution or individual should be beyond the reach of the law.

Also, asset recovery has become one of the defining hallmarks of the current EFCC leadership. The commission has disclosed that under Olukoyede, it has recovered over N566 billion in the last three years, alongside millions of dollars, pounds, euros, luxury vehicles, landed properties and other assets linked to proceeds of crime. Rather than focusing exclusively on arrests and media parades, the commission has prioritised tracing, confiscating and recovering illicit assets.

These recoveries do two things. First, they return stolen wealth to the public treasury. Second, they send a powerful message that corruption carries tangible consequences. “Crime does not pay” has ceased to be a slogan and becomes a financial reality for offenders.

Another significant indicator of the chairman’s commitment is the consistency with which the EFCC has pursued high-profile investigations and prosecutions. The commission has continued to investigate politically exposed persons, public office holders, contractors, and individuals suspected of financial crimes irrespective of their political affiliations. Former governors, ministers, heads of agencies and private sector actors have all featured in EFCC investigations in the last three years.

While the outcome of every investigation ultimately depends on judicial processes, the willingness of the EFCC to initiate inquiries into influential individuals has demonstrated institutional courage in an environment where political interference often poses substantial obstacles. Such investigations have reinforced the perception that no individual should be above the law, even if convictions remain slow in coming.

The EFCC has also intensified its prosecution of cybercrime, which has become one of the fastest-growing forms of financial crime in Nigeria. Internet fraud, identity theft, cryptocurrency scams, and business email compromise schemes have not only defrauded victims but have also negatively affected Nigeria’s international image and undermined confidence in legitimate digital businesses.

Recognizing the growing threat, the commission has increased intelligence gathering, surveillance operations, arrests, and prosecutions involving internet fraud syndicates. There have been several high-profile arrests and convictions, including mass operations in cybercrime hubs across the country. The chairman has repeatedly emphasized that combating cybercrime is necessary not only to protect victims but also to preserve Nigeria’s reputation within the global digital economy.

In addition to enforcement, the chairman has promoted preventive strategies designed to reduce corruption before it occurs. The EFCC has expanded public enlightenment campaigns targeting schools, universities, professional associations, religious organisations, and community groups. Anti-corruption clubs in educational institutions reflect an understanding that sustainable change requires shaping attitudes among younger generations.

The commission has equally strengthened collaboration with domestic and international partners. Financial crimes increasingly involve cross-border transactions and money laundering networks. Consequently, the EFCC has worked more closely with foreign law enforcement agencies, financial intelligence units and international organizations to trace illicit financial flows and recover stolen assets.

Institutional capacity building has also been a priority. The EFCC has invested in specialised training, modern investigative techniques, digital forensic laboratories, and intelligence-driven operations to deal with crimes involving technology, cryptocurrency, and complex international transactions. The chairman has also advocated stronger compliance with anti-money laundering regulations by financial institutions and improved inter-agency cooperation with police, customs, taxation and intelligence agencies.

Despite these achievements, a critical analysis must acknowledge the significant challenges confronting the chairman and the EFCC.

Perhaps the most persistent criticism concerns allegations of selective prosecution. Critics have continued to argue that anti-corruption efforts appear more vigorous against certain political actors than others, especially those in opposition. But the EFCC has consistently maintained that investigations are based on petitions, intelligence and available evidence rather than political considerations.

However, in anti-corruption work, public confidence is strengthened not only by actual impartiality but also by the perception that justice is administered fairly and consistently. The Osun account freeze, coming days to an election, fed directly into that perception problem.

The commission also has faced significant legal and judicial constraints. Many corruption cases remain in court for several years because of procedural delays, interlocutory appeals, and congested court dockets. Consequently, successful investigations do not always translate into timely convictions. These delays create public frustration and reduce the deterrent effect of anti-corruption enforcement. The chairman has repeatedly emphasized the importance of judicial reforms, including the creation of special courts, that would accelerate corruption trials while safeguarding defendants’ constitutional rights.

Anti-corruption agencies frequently investigate individuals possessing substantial political influence, financial resources, and legal expertise. Such circumstances inevitably expose the commission’s leadership to criticism, lobbying, media campaigns, and legal challenges.

Maintaining institutional independence under these conditions requires strong administrative leadership and strict adherence to legal procedures. The chairman’s ability to sustain investigations despite these pressures has been viewed by supporters as evidence of resilience. Critics, however, see every major action through a political lens, as the Osun case demonstrated.

Human rights concerns have occasionally emerged regarding some EFCC operations, particularly during mass arrests targeting cybercrime suspects in hotels, universities and cybercafes. Civil society organisations and legal practitioners have called for greater adherence to due process, respect for fundamental rights, and improved investigative standards. Addressing these concerns remains important because effective anti-corruption enforcement should always operate within constitutional and legal safeguards. Public confidence is strengthened when investigations are both effective and lawful.

The chairman has acknowledged a fundamental truth: the EFCC alone cannot eliminate corruption. Corruption in Nigeria is fueled by structural factors such as poverty, unemployment, weak institutions, inadequate public sector accountability, and political patronage. Consequently, law enforcement must be complemented by reforms in procurement systems, judicial efficiency, public financial management, transparency, and political accountability.

This is why the commission has leaned into prevention and public enlightenment. The establishment of anti-corruption clubs and partnerships with professional bodies are attempts to change the culture that enables corruption. The fight against corruption, the chairman has argued, requires a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach.

Looking ahead, experts have argued that sustaining the momentum of Nigeria’s anti-corruption campaign will require several things: continued investment in technology and intelligence-led investigations to match the sophistication of financial criminals; deeper international cooperation to trace and recover assets hidden abroad; judicial reforms to ensure that cases are concluded in reasonable time; greater transparency in the management of recovered assets to assure Nigerians that recovered funds are properly accounted for and deployed, and stronger witness protection and whistleblower mechanisms to encourage reporting.

Equally important is the need for consistent political support that respects the operational independence of anti-corruption institutions while ensuring appropriate oversight and accountability.

Notwithstanding the controversies, the Executive Chairman of the EFCC has demonstrated a visible commitment to advancing Nigeria’s fight against corruption despite operating within a highly complex political and institutional environment.

His leadership has been associated with intensified investigations, increased asset recovery, expanded prosecution of financial and cyber crimes, stronger public enlightenment initiatives, improved international cooperation, and enhanced institutional capacity.

Ultimately, Olukoyede’s legacy will be assessed not only by the number of arrests or the billions recovered during his tenure but also by the extent to which his leadership contributes to building stronger institutions, promoting the rule of law, and fostering a lasting culture of transparency and accountability in Nigeria.

The fight against corruption is a long-term national project. In the current dispensation, the EFCC under Olukoyede has remained a significant, and sometimes controversial, actor in that continuing effort. Whether Nigerians remember this period for the recoveries made or for the political battles fought will depend largely on what happens next — in the courts, in government, and in the daily lives of citizens.

World.title: GMH and the Cost of Keeping its Promises
World.content:
As it marks its eleventh anniversary, Vanessa Obioha looks at how the real estate company has navigated rising construction costs while maintaining customer confidence

When the naira began to lose significant value in 2023, Nigeria’s real estate developers faced a problem that went beyond rising construction costs. For developers selling properties off-plan, the bigger question was what to do about homes that had already been sold at prices agreed before the currency depreciation.

GodMade Homes Limited, popularly known as GMH Luxury, found itself facing that dilemma across eight developments.

Construction materials had become more expensive, particularly those linked to the foreign exchange rate. Labour and other project costs also rose. Yet customers who had committed to the properties had done so based on earlier prices.

GMH had a choice: pass the additional costs to customers, reduce project specifications, or absorb the difference.

According to the company, it chose the third option.

Between 2023 and 2025, GMH says it refunded more than N4 billion to customers who decided not to continue with their payment plans. Rather than revise the terms for customers who had already committed to their properties, the company says it allowed those who could no longer continue to withdraw and receive their money back.

The decision came at a cost. GMH says it also borrowed money during the period to meet its obligations, while continuing construction on the eight affected developments.

For the company, however, there was another consideration: maintaining the quality of the homes already sold.

As construction costs rose, project timelines inevitably came under pressure. GMH says it decided that if a compromise had to be made, it would be on delivery timelines rather than specifications. That meant taking longer to complete some projects rather than substituting materials or lowering the standards promised to customers.

“It’s in the moment that you face your deepest weakness that you receive the chance to forge your greatest strength,” says Ayoolanrewaju J. Kuyebi, the company’s Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer.

The episode highlights a wider problem confronting Nigeria’s off-plan property market: the difficulty of fixing a price for a project that may take years to complete in an economy where the cost of construction can change dramatically within months. For developers, absorbing such increases can threaten cash flow and profitability. For buyers, accepting revised prices after committing to a property can make the investment unaffordable. GMH’s approach was to absorb the immediate pressure rather than transfer it to customers who had entered the agreements under different economic conditions. The company says the strategy allowed all eight developments to remain active, although some timelines were extended. Two of its projects, in Lekki and Ikoyi, are now scheduled for delivery.

The episode also appears to have shaped how GMH views one of the less tangible assets of a property company: customer confidence. In a market where buyers are increasingly cautious about committing money to properties that may take years to complete, the ability to honour an agreement can be as important as the building itself. For GMH, the currency crisis therefore became more than a financial challenge. It became a test of how much it was prepared to absorb in order to preserve the terms on which customers had bought their homes in its eleventh year of existence.

The company’s eleventh anniversary provides the occasion to reflect on that period. But the more interesting story is what happened when the economics changed—and the decision the company made when its original promises became considerably more expensive to keep.

World.title: Osun Poll: NSCDC Deploys 10,210 Personnel, Tactical Units
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

The Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) has deployed 10,210 personnel and specialised tactical units to Osun State ahead of the governorship election, as security agencies intensify preparations to ensure a peaceful, free and credible poll.

The Commandant General of the NSCDC, Prof. Ahmed Audi, ordered the deployment of 10,000 personnel drawn from 10 neighbouring State Commands, alongside specialised formations of the Corps, to reinforce security operations across the state.

The deployment, which commenced Monday, is aimed at protecting voters, electoral officials, election materials, observers, journalists and residents from threats, intimidation and other forms of electoral violence.

According to a statement signed by the Assistant Commandant of Corps and National Public Relations Officer of the NSCDC, Babawale Afolabi, about 1,000 personnel each from the Oyo, Ondo, Ekiti, Ogun, Lagos, Kwara, Edo, Kogi, Delta and Federal Capital Territory Commands would reinforce the Osun State Command.

The personnel, comprising uniformed and undercover operatives, would operate alongside other security agencies under the established inter-agency security framework.

Audi also ordered the deployment of specialised formations, including the CG’s Special Intelligence Squad, Special Weapons and Tactics (SWAT) Unit, Specialised Female Squad, Mining Marshals, Special Strike Force, Crack Squad and K9 Unit.

The specialised teams, the Corps said, would strengthen intelligence gathering, crime prevention and detection, protection of critical assets, crowd control and other election-related security operations.

To ensure effective coordination and supervision, the Deputy Commandant General in charge of Operations, DCG Ayuba Phillip, alongside designated Assistant Commandants General and other senior officers, would relocate to Osun State to oversee the Corps’ election security operations.

The NSCDC boss assured residents that the Corps would remain professional, impartial and respectful of citizens’ rights throughout the electoral process.

Audi charged NSCDC personnel to work in synergy with other security agencies, stressing that the safety of electoral officials, election materials and voters remained critical to the success of the exercise.

“Our personnel have been properly briefed on the need to be professional, neutral and respectful in the discharge of their duties,” he said.

He warned political thugs and other criminal elements against attempting to disrupt the election, saying security agencies would not tolerate activities capable of jeopardising the electoral process.

“In collaboration with other security agencies on election duty, [the NSCDC] will not tolerate any activity intended to jeopardise the election process; criminal-minded persons and political thugs willing to disrupt the peaceful conduct of the election would face the wrath of the law as prescribed in the Electoral Act,” Audi warned.

The Corps appealed to political parties, candidates, supporters and residents to conduct themselves peacefully and allow the democratic process to take its course.

It also urged residents to remain calm, vigilant and cooperative with security personnel, while encouraging members of the public to promptly report suspicious activities and security concerns to the appropriate authorities.

The NSCDC said its operations would cover all 30 Local Government Areas of Osun State, in coordination with the Nigeria Police Force, the military and other sister security agencies.

The deployment comes as security preparations intensify for the Osun governorship election, with authorities seeking to prevent violence, intimidation and other disruptions that could undermine the credibility of the electoral process.

World.title: Who is the oldest living Springbok?
World.content:
Frik du Preez has the honour of being the oldest living Springbok according to the history books. Here's how old he is. Image: Blue Bulls

Following the news of the passing of former Springbok hooker Jacobus Frederick Beatrix “Piston” van Wyk, we got thinking: ‘Who is the oldest living Springbok?’

The answer?

A true legend of South African rugby: Frik du Preez.



At 90 years and 255 days, Du Preez is currently the oldest living Springbok, a little over 16 months older than Avril Malan.

Rugby great

Frederick Christoffel Hendrik “Frik” du Preez was more than a rugby great.

The former Springbok lock and flank was a player whose skill, personality and influence transcended provincial rivalries, earning him an enduring place in South African sporting history.

Despite retiring from international rugby in 1971, Du Preez was named South Africa’s Rugby Player of the 20th Century, an extraordinary recognition of the impact he had made during his career.

His popularity stretched far beyond his Northern Transvaal roots. At a time when provincial rivalries dominated South African rugby, Du Preez was admired from Pretoria to Cape Town and by supporters around the world.

A player ahead of his time

Du Preez possessed an extraordinary range of skills, particularly considering his size.



He was a powerful presence in the lineout, had pace and impressive running ability, and was one of the most accomplished kickers of his generation.

His versatility was perhaps best illustrated by his ability to punt, drop-kick and place-kick with equal confidence.

One of his most famous moments came against the British Lions in 1968.

After peeling around the front of a lineout, Du Preez collected the ball near the touchline and accelerated towards the try line. He then produced a perfectly executed sidestep before diving over to complete a spectacular try from around 40 metres.

It was the type of moment that captured the imagination of rugby supporters and helped cement his legendary status.

More than just a rugby player

Du Preez’s influence extended beyond what he achieved on the field.

Former Springbok great and administrator Danie Craven regarded him as one of the personalities who helped shape South African rugby.

Craven described Du Preez as one of the great players and personalities who had provided direction to generations of South African rugby supporters.

That admiration was reflected decades later when Du Preez was honoured as the country’s Rugby Player of the Century.

Former Springbok coach André Markgraaff also highlighted Du Preez’s character, suggesting that the legendary player would have been an ideal fit for the professional era because he could have demonstrated to modern players the value of humility.

A decade in the green and gold

Du Preez made his Springbok debut against England in January 1961 and remained an international player for more than a decade.

His final appearance for South Africa came against Australia in August 1971.

During that period, he became one of the country’s most capped players, sharing the Springbok record of 38 Test appearances with another legendary Northern Transvaal figure, loose forward Jan Ellis.

His overall record was even more remarkable when his non-Test appearances are taken into account. Du Preez played 87 matches for South Africa and scored 87 points.

That longevity was particularly impressive given the far smaller international calendar of the era.

Unlike today’s professional game, southern hemisphere nations did not have an annual Rugby Championship-style competition and international teams played considerably fewer Tests.

A place among rugby’s immortals

Du Preez’s legacy is not confined to South Africa.

When the Rugby Hall of Fame was established in 1997, he was one of only two South Africans inducted in its inaugural class, alongside Craven.

The company he joined underlined his standing in world rugby.

That group included some of the game’s greatest names, among them Gareth Edwards, Colin Meads, Hugo Porta, JPR Williams, Mike Gibson and Willie John McBride.

For a player whose international career had ended more than two decades earlier, his inclusion was a powerful acknowledgement of his contribution to the sport.

A legacy that endures

Du Preez’s election as South Africa’s rugby player of the 20th century ultimately reflected more than statistics.

It recognised a player who combined strength, skill and versatility with an unmistakable personality.

He could dominate a lineout, sprint 40 metres to score a try and then produce a match-winning kick.

But perhaps most importantly, he became a figure admired across the traditional boundaries of South African rugby.

Decades after his retirement, Frik du Preez remains one of the enduring symbols of Springbok rugby – a player whose influence continues to be felt long after his final appearance in the green and gold.

Factfile: Frik du Preez

Full names: Frederick Christoffel Hendrik du Preez Date of birth: 28 November 1935 Place of birth: Rustenburg School: Parys Springbok #375 Physical: 1.88m, 96.2kg Current age: 90

World.title: Camps Bay for retirees? Suburb with luxury coastal homes for 75% less
World.content:
Camps Bay is the crown jewel of Cape Town’s coast.

Being the jewel comes at a cost: R20 million to be exact.

Retirees who want a luxury coastal home have an alternative.



One Cape Town suburb has the lifestyle, amenities, view, and safety but not the price tag.

Suburb where Retirees can get Luxury Coastal Homes

Kommetjie is the newest suburb for wealthy retirees looking for value and space on the Atlantic Ocean.

According to Property24.com, homes in the area start at R4.9 million. But buyers could get on the property ladder for less.



As recently as July 2026, homes in Kommetjie have sold for R3 million.

Contrast this with Camps Bay.

According to Property24, the most affordable home sold in the last 30 days was R16 million.



This could be why shrewd retirees are selling their homes further afield and settling in Kommetjie.

Prices in this luxury coastal suburb are reminiscent of Camps Bay circa 2009.

Property Size Camps Bay Price Kommetjie Price Average R20 million R5.7 million < 200 sqm R7.5 million – R15 million R5.9 million – R6.1 million 201 – 500 sqm R11 million – R25 million R5.3 million – R10.5 million 501 – 800 sqm R15 million – R30 million R6.7 million – R13.5 million 801 sqm < R19.9 million – R65 million R4.9 million – R24 million

Beyond reasonable luxury homes, Kommetjie has cost-effective rates.



Rates and taxes in Camps Bay start at R2 000 for a modest 200-square-metre home.

For more space, rates skyrocket to R12 000.

Kommetjie rates start at R1 200 and typically max out at R2 500.



What to Do in Kommetjie

The suburb has the potential to become the next Camps Bay, but without the crowds.

Originally a quaint fishing town, Kommetjie has left that moniker in the dust and now has gorgeous sprawling properties within walking distance of the beach.

The suburb is lively but peaceful. There aren’t any large chain restaurants on the oceanside.



But that doesn’t mean retirees will have to say goodbye to an active lifestyle.

Long Beach offers roughly 8 kilometres of uninterrupted, powdery beaches, perfect for a morning walk or evening stroll.

On the beachfront, you have options like Espresso Coffee and Good Riddance Coffee Co.



Within a short drive, retirees can shop at Long Beach Mall, where there’s a Woolworths, Pick ‘n Pay Hypermarket, Food Lover’s Market, and an arts and crafts market on the first and last Saturday of the month.

Retail therapy doesn’t start and end at the mall.

There’s also Imhoff Farm, which offers experiential retail and restaurants.



Much like Camps Bay, Kommetjie has the most pleasant sunsets. The sky turns a gorgeous deep pink at sunset, with sunrise offering a diffuse orange and deep blue skyline.

Destination Driving Distance Long Beach 2 minutes Long Beach Mall 11 minutes Clovelly Country Club 21 minutes Mediclinic Constantiaberg 30 minutes Camps Bay 50 minutes

Kommetjie’s Property Prices are Rising

If you’re thinking of picking up property in Kommetjie, now might be the last time you can do so affordably.

According to Property24, prices in the area have been steadily increasing for years.



In 2025, the average property price was R3.795 million.

So far this year, the average price among the 66 sales in the area is R5.7 million.

Retirees aren’t the only group finding value in Kommetjie. Buyers aged 36 to 49 make up 41.2% of sales.



The suburb is benefitting from ever-increasing demand for affordable coastal living within the city limits.

This demand means it could become Cape Town’s new vibrant coastal community.

World.title: Fernando Da Cruz refuses to blame Brandon Petersen for goalkeeping howler
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs coach Fernando Da Cruz has refused to pin the club’s MTN8 quarter-final exit on goalkeeper Brandon Petersen. Image: Facebook @KaizerChiefs

Kaizer Chiefs coach Fernando Da Cruz has refused to pin the club’s MTN8 quarter-final exit on goalkeeper Brandon Petersen after Amakhosi suffered a 1-0 defeat to Golden Arrows at FNB Stadium on Sunday.

The Soweto giants returned to the MTN8 after a two-year absence, but their campaign came to an abrupt end as Golden Arrows secured their place in the semi-finals.



Caught off his line

The decisive moment arrived in the 53rd minute when Khulekani Shezi caught Petersen off his line with a cross-cum-shot from the right.

Shezi picked up the ball out wide before noticing Petersen’s advanced position and sent the ball towards the Kaizer Chiefs goal.

The effort beat the 31-year-old Amakhosi goalkeeper at his near post to give Arrows the lead.



However, Da Cruz was adamant that the defeat could not be blamed on one individual.

“I don’t want to say we lost because of one player,” the new Kaizer Chiefs coach told SuperSport TV.

Da Cruz said he would review the goal before making a definitive assessment, while suggesting Shezi may have intended to deliver a cross rather than attempt a direct shot.



“I will look at the goal because I will watch the game, but I think the player missed his cross and we lost it.”

Kaizer Chiefs failed to take their chances

For Da Cruz, the bigger frustration was Kaizer Chiefs’ inability to convert their opportunities after falling behind.

Amakhosi pushed for an equaliser but could not find the finishing touch needed to force the match towards extra time.



“The score is unfortunately the only one goal changed in the half and after that we tried to come back, but we had a lack of efficiency there.”

The result ends Kaizer Chiefs’ hopes of lifting the MTN8 trophy this season, while Arrows progress to the two-legged semi-finals.

For Amakhosi, there is little time to dwell on the disappointment.



Kaizer Chiefs return to FNB Stadium on Wednesday, 12 August when they face Sekhukhune United in their first home Betway Premiership fixture of the 2026/27 campaign.

Kick-off is at 19:30.

Da Cruz will now look for an immediate response from his side as Kaizer Chiefs turn their attention from cup disappointment to their league campaign.



Was Brandon Petersen to blame for the goal against Golden Arrows?

Let us know by clicking on the comment banner below …

World.title: Snow turns KwaZulu-Natal into a winter wonderland
World.content:
Heavy snowfall has disrupted road travel across parts of KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape, with several major mountain passes closed. Image: Facebook @rsatrucker

Heavy snowfall has disrupted road travel across parts of KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape, with several major mountain passes closed or hazardous and authorities urging motorists to postpone non-essential journeys.

The conditions are particularly concerning for truck drivers, with snow and ice creating dangerous conditions on high-altitude routes and reports of heavy vehicles becoming stranded.

READ | Snow chase: Sutherland, here I come …



R617 closed as KwaZulu-Natal activates snowfall response plan

In KwaZulu-Natal, the Road Traffic Inspectorate (RTI) has activated the province’s Snowfall Response Plan.

The R617 has been closed in the Kokstad, Kingscote and Underberg areas, with traffic being redirected onto the R56.

The RTI also reported that a truck was stuck on the R617 at Kingscote.

The KwaZulu-Natal Department of Transport has urged motorists to delay their journeys where possible and encouraged members of the public to remain indoors.

The R56 between Kokstad and Matatiele is being used as an alternative route, although motorists have been warned that conditions remain hazardous in places.

N3 affected by snow

The important N3 Toll Route between Johannesburg and Durban has also been affected by the winter weather.



At 09:00 on Monday, 10 August, the N3 Toll Concession reported light snowfall between Balgowan and Nottingham Road in the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands.

Wet road surfaces and reduced visibility are adding to the risks, particularly for heavy vehicles travelling between Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal.

Conditions can change rapidly along the Midlands section of the N3, particularly as temperatures fall later in the day.

Eastern Cape mountain passes closed

Several high-altitude routes in the Eastern Cape are also experiencing significant disruption.

The N9 between Graaff-Reinet and Middelburg is closed over Lootsberg Pass because of snow.

The R61 towards Nxuba (Adelaide) has been affected by snow-related closures around Wapadsberg Pass.

The R58 remains a major concern around the Lady Grey, Barkly East and Elliot corridor, with Barkly Pass closed because of heavy snow.

The N6 over Penhoek Pass, between Komani and Jamestown, has also been temporarily closed.

Motorists are being warned not to assume that a pass which was open earlier in the day will remain safe. Snow and ice can accumulate quickly, particularly overnight and during the early morning.

Why truck drivers face greater danger

According to the SA Trucker website, snow and ice present a heightened risk to heavy vehicles because their weight and momentum make braking and steering more difficult when tyre grip is reduced.

Drivers have been urged to:

Slow down significantly in snowy or icy conditions

Increase following distances

Avoid harsh braking and sudden steering

Carry sufficient fuel, food and water

Keep warm clothing and emergency supplies in the vehicle

Ensure mobile phones are fully charged

Monitor road and weather updates before and during a journey

Never drive around a road closure or attempt to cross a closed mountain pass

A longer journey is preferable to becoming stranded on an icy mountain road.

Other Eastern Cape disruptions

Snow is not the only problem affecting roads in the Eastern Cape.

The R102 between Gqeberha and Jeffreys Bay has been closed following rockfalls, while the R332 through the Baviaanskloof has been affected by flooding.

Freight operators therefore need to consider multiple weather-related disruptions when planning routes through the province.

Authorities working to clear roads

KwaZulu-Natal’s snowfall response includes the deployment of graders to clear accumulated snow and help prevent motorists from becoming trapped.

The provincial authorities have also warned that freezing temperatures can worsen existing damage to roads as water enters cracks, freezes and expands.

For motorists and truckers already on the road, authorities’ message is clear: do not treat the snowfall as simply an inconvenience.

With conditions changing rapidly across the affected provinces, drivers should check the latest road status before setting out and be prepared to delay their journey if necessary.

Major routes affected

KwaZulu-Natal

R617: Closed around Kokstad, Kingscote and Underberg

Closed around Kokstad, Kingscote and Underberg R56: Diversion for R617 traffic; hazardous conditions reported

Diversion for R617 traffic; hazardous conditions reported N3: Snow, wet roads and reduced visibility around Balgowan and Nottingham Road

Snow, wet roads and reduced visibility around Balgowan and Nottingham Road Underberg/highlands: Snow and icy conditions affecting travel

Eastern Cape

N9: Lootsberg Pass closed due to snow

Lootsberg Pass closed due to snow R61: Wapadsberg Pass affected by snow

Wapadsberg Pass affected by snow R58: Barkly Pass closed amid heavy snow

Barkly Pass closed amid heavy snow N6: Penhoek Pass temporarily closed

Penhoek Pass temporarily closed R56: Hazardous conditions around the Matatiele/Mount Fletcher corridor

Hazardous conditions around the Matatiele/Mount Fletcher corridor R102: Closed because of rockfalls

Closed because of rockfalls R332: Baviaanskloof affected by flooding

For truckers, the priority is simple: don’t chase a delivery schedule at the expense of safety. If a mountain pass is closed, stay off it.

World.title: ‘Being driven by the President’: Wicknell Chivayo shares light moment with President Ruto
World.content:
Zimbabwean business tycoon and philanthropist Wicknell Chivayo is making headlines after sharing a priceless moment with Kenyan President William Ruto.

In a now-viral video that has attracted thousands of comments and reactions, the businessman was seen being chauffeured by President Ruto.

The gesture appeared to warm the hearts of many, with some Zimbabweans jokingly raising concerns over whether Nairobi was trying to “snatch” Wicknell, who has wowed many with his philanthropic work back home.



Wicknell Chivayo attends Charlene Ruto’s ceremony

The publication has since established that the warm moment took place during the wedding of President Ruto’s daughter, Charlene Ruto.

Chivayo and his wife were among the distinguished guests who attended Charlene’s wedding ceremony.

In the now-viral video, Chivayo revealed just how much the gesture had moved him, describing the short journey as one of the most memorable experiences of his life.



“Those three kilometres alone will forever remain one of the most priceless journeys of my life,” Chivayo wrote.

He said he was overwhelmed by the gesture, asking: “God, what kind of grace is this?”

Zimbabweans react to Chivayo’s priceless moment

Chivayo’s post quickly sparked reactions from his followers, with many celebrating the encounter and describing it as a sign of grace and success.



Some praised his philanthropic work, while others joked about his growing connections with powerful figures across Africa.

One follower wrote that it was “pure grace” to be driven by great people, while another said: “It’s not easy to sit at tables where kings eat. You don’t get there by luck.”

Others viewed the moment as a source of national pride, with one commenter describing it as “BIG for Zimbabwe” and saying Chivayo was showing that Zimbabwean ambition could travel beyond the country’s borders.



Some reactions were more playful, with followers joking about money, billionaire ambitions and Chivayo’s continued rise.

Of late, the Zimbabwean businessman has made Kenya something of a playground, frequently travelling to the East African country for both business and leisure.

From holidays to business deals, Chivayo has increasingly been seen spending time in Kenya, where he has built relationships with influential figures.



African presidents’ favourite?

This is not the first time Chivayo has made headlines over his close ties with heads of state.

Back home, he has maintained close ties with Zimbabwe’s presidium and has openly supported the government’s efforts to transform the country’s economy under the Second Republic.

In recent years, Chivayo has also attracted attention for his relationships with several African leaders, partly through his philanthropic work and his investments in renewable energy.



A few months ago, he made headlines after reportedly being granted a diplomatic passport by Eswatini’s King Mswati III in recognition of his charitable contributions in Africa and his reported R3 billion renewable energy investment in the kingdom.

Chivayo has also rubbed shoulders with several other heads of state, including South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

World.title: Snow chase: Sutherland, here I come …
World.content:
This weekend's snow event stretched from the Eastern Cape Highlands to Sutherland's Roggeveld range: Image Facebook Vet Services Waipukrau

I have spent this entire weekend refreshing forecasts and calling people in the mountains just to get the timing right. Tomorrow, I finally chase the snow myself.

My snow chase to Sutherland starts tomorrow, but I have been watching this one build for days already.

Every SAWS update this week kept nudging the same story forward: a cold front, a cut-off low, and a wide stretch of South Africa’s mountains about to turn white.



By the time it actually arrived this weekend, I was already glued to every warning update like it was a scoreboard.

And then it happened …

Snow settled across the Eastern Cape Highlands, into Lesotho, over the southern Drakensberg, and across the Western Cape’s high ground, Matroosberg, the Cederberg, and further into the Karoo’s Roggeveld range near Sutherland.



Five of the best-loved snow spots in the country, all catching flakes within days of each other.

My snow chase to Sutherland: Watching the forecast become real

There is a particular kind of excitement that builds when you have been tracking a system for a full week and it finally delivers.

I read every update SAWS put out, cross-checked timing against what people on the ground were telling me, and watched the warnings shift from “possible” to “confirmed” one province at a time.



By the time the snow actually started falling, it did not feel like a surprise. It felt like watching something I had been promised finally show up.

Why I chose Sutherland, and why tomorrow

I am heading to Sutherland tomorrow morning, and I will not pretend the decision was purely emotional.

Sutherland sits roughly five hours from me, so getting the timing right matters more than almost anywhere else on that list.



Arrive too early and you are standing in the cold for nothing. Arrive too late and the snow has already started melting off.

I spent the past few days doing exactly what a proper snow chaser does: calling people who actually live near the Roggeveld range, asking what they were seeing outside their own windows, and lining that up against what the forecasts were saying.

Snow that continues into Monday and Tuesday gave me the window I needed to plan a trip that actually has a shot at catching it well.



The chase itself

There is something almost ridiculous about driving five hours on a hunch built from weather warnings and phone calls to strangers near a mountain range, and I would not have it any other way.

This is the part of winter I genuinely look forward to every single year, the anticipation, the phone calls, the slightly obsessive checking of forecasts, and then finally, the drive itself.

I will be sharing how the snow chase to Sutherland goes once I am back.



Have you ever planned an entire trip around a weather forecast, snow chasing or otherwise?

Let us know in the comments below, Mzansi …

Is it snowing in your area? If so, please send your photos to info@thesouthafrican.com.

World.title: RIP: Former Springbok hooker passes away
World.content:
SA Rugby president Mark Alexander has paid tribute to former Springbok hooker Jacobus Frederick Beatrix “Piston” van Wyk – who made 15 Test appearances between 1970 and 1976 – after he sadly passed away.

Van Wyk, who played for the erstwhile Northern Transvaal and Natal – now the Bulls and Sharks – started and ended his 15-cap Springbok career with Tests against the All Blacks.

Tribute to former Springbok forward

A versatile and aggressive hooker, Van Wyk also toured Australia in 1971 and faced the touring British & Irish Lions in 1974.



“It is with profound sadness that we mourn the passing of Piston van Wyk, a former Springbok whose legacy is etched into the proud history of South African rugby,” said Mr Alexander.

“Piston’s career was marked by his formidable scrummaging strength, his unwavering commitment to the team and his memorable performances against some of the world’s toughest opponents.

“From his debut in the green and gold to his standout contributions in numerous Test victories, Piston embodied the resilience and pride of the Springbok jersey. His presence on the field was a source of inspiration and his dedication to the game reflected the values of discipline, humility and sportsmanship.”



Special memories

Alexander added that Piston carried himself with dignity and integrity on and off the field.

“Leaving behind a legacy that extends far beyond the scoreboard. His name will forever be remembered among those who helped shape the path for future generations of players.

“We extend our deepest condolences to his family and loved ones. May they find comfort in knowing that his contribution to our sport and our nation will never be forgotten. Piston van Wyk’s memory will live on in the hearts of all who cherish the game of rugby and the values it represents.”

World.title: SASSA announces ALL payment dates for September 2026
World.content:
The Older Person’s SASSA Grant will be paid first on 2 September 2026, followed by the Disability Grant on 3 September 2026, and the Children’s Grants, including the Child Support Grant and Foster Child Grant, on 4 September 2026.

Unlike some months where dates are pushed later to avoid weekends, public holidays, or Mondays, September’s schedule follows SASSA’s standard early-month pattern, paying out grants on the 2nd, 3rd and 4th respectively.

How the schedule is decided

SASSA has reiterated that payment dates are set according to a consistent set of principles applied across the financial year. Grants are paid as early in the month as possible, staggered over three separate days to reduce strain on the National Payment System and retail points. Payments are never scheduled for the 1st of the month or a Monday, and any date that would otherwise fall on a weekend or the day after a public holiday is shifted to the next available working day.



Higher grant amounts remain in effect

Beneficiaries will continue receiving the increased grant amounts announced by the Minister of Finance earlier this year. The Older Persons Grant, Disability Grant and Care Dependency Grant now sit at R2 400 following an R80 increase, while the War Veterans Grant rose by the same amount to R2 420. The Foster Child Grant increased by R40 to R1 290, and the Child Support Grant and Grant-In-Aid both rose by R20 to R580.

Win R2 000 in the South African SASSA grant survey

If you receive a SASSA grant and want to share your story, we want to hear from you.

Take part in our survey and stand a chance to win R2 000. Your responses help us tell the stories that matter.

World.title: MEC Maile calls on communities to help protect Gauteng schools
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Gauteng Education MEC Lebogang Maile has said protecting schools is a shared responsibility.

Maile briefed the media on plans to curb issues affecting Gauteng schools.

He said issues around bullying, gender-based violence and gangsterism have been of great concern.

The department has embarked on a campaign called - it takes a village to raise a child.

“Violence, gangsterism, bullying, substance abuse, gender-based violence, vandalism and criminal activity around schools were repeatedly raised. The program of action strengthened Safe Schools intervention and cooperation with SAPs, community policing forums, NGOs and communities.

“Work is also being driven on anti-bullying interventions and misconduct measures while school safety matters are being assigned to the responsible education support and curriculum functions.

“The purpose is to move from responding only after incidents occur to prevention, early intervention, clear escalation and coordinated action around high-risk schools. Communities themselves remain essential to the solution. Protecting a school cannot be left entirely to government.

“The communities must help identify criminal activity, protect public infrastructure, support learner discipline and refuse to normalize drug dealing, vandalism and violence around schools."

World.title: MP Fadiel Adams expected to face tough questions at Madlanga Commission
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Member of Parliament and National Coloured Congress leader Fadiel Adams is set to testify under subpoena before the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry on Tuesday.

He is expected to face tough questioning about the unauthorised disclosure of classified state documents and his allegations of systemic corruption in South Africa’s criminal justice system.

In just a few hours, Member of Parliament Fadiel Adams will take the hot seat at the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry. This is exactly what Adams has demanded on social media: a chance to clear his name.

Adams is facing serious charges of fraud and defeating the administration of justice.

He’s also at the centre of IDAC scandals, including allegations that authorities used questionable information from Adams to pursue investigations against senior police officers.

IDAC State Advocate Drushantha Ramsamy testified that Adams ought to have been charged for being in possession of Crime Intelligence information.

Evidence before the commission revealed that Adams’s original complaint did not legally fall within IDAC’s mandate or trigger a valid investigation.

World.title: Holidaymakers stuck in Eastern Cape snow
World.content:
RHODES – What was meant to be a short time away from home for an East London family has resulted in an extended stay at snow-capped mountains in the hamlet of Rhodes.

Ainsley Sumner and his family had planned a little getaway at Tiffindell, but roads have been closed because of the snow.

“We will be stranded here for another day or two. It is nice and cold.

“We will have to wait it out. We will stay overnight to assess again before hitting the road back to East London where we are from.

“There is no point in trying to drive now as it will get dangerous,” Sumner said.

World.title: Police recover firearms linked to Reiger Park shooting
World.content:
GERMISTON – Police have recovered firearms linked to the Reiger Park murders on Friday night.

Two Anti-Gang Unit officers and two civilians were killed.

The firearms were recovered in Duka Thole, near Germiston.

On Sunday, Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said the state would deploy all necessary resources to solve the crime.

This is a developing story.

World.title: Power cuts put oxygen-dependent residents at risk
World.content:
KUGOMPO CITY - Ongoing power cuts are putting the lives of vulnerable Padkamp residents at risk.

Ester Gerber's husband relies on an oxygen machine that needs electricity, while another resident had to move in with her son because she also needs oxygen.

The Buffalo City Metro has cut off electricity for the people living in this government housing community because Public Works owes the municipality.

Gerber said her sick husband needs electricity.

“As you can see, he's very, very sick. We are depending on electricity for his oxygen. Our doctor did apply to vital air for to get oxygen without being able to use electricity. But since up to now, we haven't heard anything.

“This is a very big concern to me because he's not the only one. There's also another lady. And she had to move in the second week, she had move to her son because she's also on oxygen. So, and I just feel it's not fair.

“Public Works came about a year ago and they told us that they are going to put in meters, but we are going be connected to BCM,” she said.

World.title: Stronger consequences needed for criminals – former gangster
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Former gang member Ayoob Toffie has said visible policing can help reduce crime, but it’s not enough.

He said communities become frustrated when suspects are released on bail and later return to commit more crimes.

Toffie said stronger sentences are needed to deter people from crime.

“The police visibility is always there. It makes it difficult for any criminal to move around and do his things. However, it doesn't mean that it is going to stop. I think it would minimize it, but at the very same time, the community are tired of situations where cases are not being prosecuted, guys going out on bail.

“It’s a wicked cycle that keeps on repeating itself. For me, I were sentenced to a double life plus 16 years and I spent 21 years in prison. At the time when I was sentenced, there was no legal directive for any lifer to ever go out. And that pushed me to a point of thinking very deeply if I really want to continue with the crime or not. And because of the deterrence, because of this sentence that was played before me without any legal directive, it forced me to understand that my life is over."

Toffie said gangs are operating across different communities, with their influence extending beyond individual neighbourhoods.

He said their main aim is to control communities through fear, leaving residents afraid to move around freely, especially at night.

Toffie said while visible policing is good, it is not enough to deter criminals from committing crime.

“You'll find that there are gangs, gangsters, a group of gangs that is in Reiger Park, that's got the same gang in Nigel. And you've got the same game or a different gang in Westbury that has got the same gang in El Dorado Park.

“And so, it goes from one to the other, but the entire modus operandi of them all is control. It is to control and to bring fear to our communities. And that is what cannot be allowed because nobody can live in a community where they're fearful, they can't go at night. Our elderly, they can't walk around after five o'clock, six o' clock. Nobody can walk at that time because the control is now in the hands of the gangsters," Toffie said.

World.title: ‘There are gang ecosystems’ - Cape Crime Crisis Coalition
World.content:
CAPE TOWN - The country’s criminal justice system is failing to protect communities.

That's the view of Cape Crime Crisis Coalition’s Llewellyn Macmaster.

He argued that poverty, unemployment, drugs and extortion are fertile ground,

for organised crime and gangs to thrive.

“We must start with the failure of the state in protecting the whole criminal justice system at the moment is broken, I think, and that contributes heavily to the failure. The other factor that we always mention is that the socio-economic conditions.

“They are drivers of gangsterism and organized crime and the drug, illicit drug trade. In our discussions, I mean, even the first submission that we made to Professor Cachalia when he met with us soon after his appointment was that you've got to look at gangs differently.

Macmaster believes gang violence does not need a one-size-fits-all approach.

“It's no longer just the street gangs of yesteryear. These are gang ecosystems. They have established alternative governance and economies in our communities. And with a high unemployment and poverty that's ravaging our communities, these organized criminals find a way to assert themselves in communities.

“And of course, when you add the whole issue of extortion, I think an easy way for elements to sort of put pressure on communities, on shebeens or taverns or informal businesses. I think that is what drives this. People have the sense, I think, that they can get away with it because the police are not successful. Yes, there are successes and every time acknowledge that, but clearly it is not enough,” he said.

World.title: Snow and very cold weather in some parts of SA
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The South African Weather Service is warning of disruptive snow and severe weather across several provinces as a cold front hits.

Snow is already reported in high-lying parts of the Western Cape.

The Weather Service warns the snowfall is likely to spread to parts of the Eastern Cape where it could close roads and temporarily cut off some communities.

Damaging winds and waves are also expected along the KwaZulu-Natal coast, while thunderstorms could affect parts of Gauteng and neighbouring provinces.

A cold front and cut-off low are bringing very cold conditions.

Residents and motorists are urged to take precautions as the weather system moves inland.

Heavy snowfall has trapped multiple vehicles and forced the closure of three Eastern Cape mountain passes: Barkly, Penhoek, and Boesmanshoek.

Weather forecaster Tokelo Chiloane said amaging winds and waves are also expected along the KZN coast with the snow already falling in the province, while thunderstorms could affect parts of Gauteng and neighbouring provinces.

World.title: Ruto: Broad-based government has accelerated delivery of development plans
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during a broad-based government meeting in Naivasha on August 10, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has said the formation of the broad-based government has accelerated the implementation of development programmes that were contained in the competing political manifestos ahead of the 2022 General Election.

Speaking during a broad-based government meeting in Naivasha, Ruto said the Kenya Kwanza and Azimio political formations had campaigned on different approaches but shared several areas of convergence in their development plans.

He said the broad-based arrangement had therefore brought together ideas and priorities from both sides of the political divide, creating an opportunity for faster implementation.

“The meeting is consequential because we bring a hybrid of ideas, we converge the plan that was in Azimio broadly carried by ODM and converge with the Kenya Kwanza,” Ruto said.

According to the President, the result has been an acceleration in the implementation of the government’s development agenda over the past two years.

“That is why in the last two years the programme of implementing what we wanted for Kenya has picked the pace, there has been acceleration for the delivery of our plan since we became a broad-based government,” he said.

Ruto said the challenge facing his administration after winning the election was not simply having a manifesto but possessing the political courage to implement commitments made to Kenyans.

“The challenge was if we had the courage to implement the manifesto and commitment we made to the people of Kenya,” he said.

He cited several areas in which he said the government had made progress, including agriculture, education and healthcare.

On agriculture, Ruto said the administration had worked on fertilizer subsidies, farmer registration, dealing with cartels, improving prices and opening new markets.

“We have done well on agriculture, fertilizer subsidy, registering farmers, dealing with cartel, improving prices, opening new markets and farmers and pastoralists will be our witness,” he said.

He also pointed to developments in education, including efforts to address teacher shortages, changes to funding models and the construction of classrooms.

“We have improved our education space, all the challenges that were there including teachers shortage, funding models, classrooms construction we can proudly face the nation and say we have done what was required of us,” Ruto said.

On healthcare, the President said his administration had made progress in expanding health coverage.

“On health care coverage we have also done enough,” he said.

Ruto also praised members of his Kenya Kwanza team for supporting difficult policy decisions, recalling debates surrounding housing, healthcare and education.

He said leaders should not expect to remain popular while implementing major reforms.

“I told you then it was not necessary being popular all the time,” he said.

The President said the Naivasha meeting would focus not only on reviewing the government’s record but also on determining what could be achieved in the coming year and beyond.

“We want to agree together on not only what we have achieved but what is achievable and we can do together in the coming one year and by God's grace in the next five years and into the future,” he said.

World.title: Charlene Ruto's Koito lights up Kilgoris
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto’s daughter, Charlene Ruto, is engaged to Tanzanian entrepreneur Isaiah Yunge.

The drums rolled, traditional songs filled the air and dancers swayed in colourful rhythm as Kilgoris was transformed into a spectacular theatre of love, culture, wealth and political power.

At the expansive Intonna Heritage Farm in Naserian Village, President William Ruto’s daughter, Charlene Chelagat Ruto, took a major traditional step towards marriage as the First Family hosted her Koito ak Chaik—a colourful Kalenjin engagement and farewell ceremony.

For hours, the skies above Kilgoris were punctuated by helicopters ferrying distinguished guests to the President’s family property, while luxury vehicles streamed through the gates carrying politicians, government officials, business personalities, relatives and friends.

On the ground, the mood was unmistakably festive. Traditional songs echoed across the expansive farm as dancers moved to the rhythm, colourful attire transformed the venue into a sea of elegance and culture, and guests embraced the joy of a ceremony that combined an ancient African tradition with the unmistakable grandeur of Kenya’s First Family.

It was romance wrapped in tradition—and tradition presented on a spectacular scale.

The guest list read almost like a roll call of Kenya’s political establishment. Leaving the Narok delegation was Governor Patrick Ole Ntutu, who joined Kilgoris MP Julius Sunkuli and former Narok Governor Samuel Tunai in celebrating the First Family on the special occasion.

The ceremony also brought together elected leaders from across Narok County, creating an impressive gathering of the county’s political establishment at the heart of Trans Mara.

From governors and Senators to MPs, the event brought together leaders from across the country. Top government officials and senior executives too came dressed for the ceremony
