He says he was held from August 1 to August 7 without the police taking any formal statement from him; that on the night of August 3, Ministry officers, NSA agents, and a police unit compelled him to surrender his phones and passwords; that he was accused that same night of being connected to a drug cartel and receiving payments from it; and that when told to go home the next day, he refused, unwilling to leave custody without assurance of his safety. He says he was eventually released on August 7 still without his phones, was handed a suspension letter the same day citing disruption of the inmate interview, and points out — pointedly — that if such an infraction occurred, the Ministry has its own disciplinary board, raising the question of why the matter was routed through the police at all.

The Ministry’s statement, dated after Kolako’s, never mentions the six days in custody, the confiscated phones, the cartel accusation, or the suspension letter’s specific wording. Its account of “money allegedly being provided to him” through an outside contact reads, against Kolako’s statement, like a paraphrase of the same cartel allegation he says was leveled at him directly on August 3 — except the Ministry frames it as an open investigative question rather than something already put to him as an accusation days earlier.

Two different appeals to legitimacy

The rhetorical strategies are as different as the accounts themselves. The Ministry leans on institutional language — need-to-know principles, chains of authorization, the presumption against guilt before findings are concluded — to argue that what looks irregular from outside was, in fact, procedure. Kolako leans on personal biography: nine years as a teacher, three as a transit conductor, twelve in law enforcement, a salary that never topped $224 a month, and what he describes as an unblemished record he says he has refused to trade for money. He closes not with a request for due process in the abstract, but with a direct, public appeal — naming the Attorney General, the heads of the NSA, the Ministry of National Defense, and the police, and even invoking the U.S. Embassy — asking that drug-case detainees be moved to a secure facility abroad so the investigation cannot be compromised from within. He also names four individuals he asks the public to remember as the investigation proceeds, a move that reads less like a defense and more like a warning.

What the contrast reveals

Neither statement is a neutral document — one is an institution defending a decision it has already made, the other is a man defending a record he says has never been in question. But the specific, checkable claims in Kolako’s account — who he called, what time the suspension letter arrived, how long he was held, when his phones were taken and by whom — give reporters concrete threads to pull that the Ministry’s more abstract statement does not offer. Whether Colonel Roosevelt Varney and Assistant Minister Gabriel Fayiah Ndupellar confirm they were uninformed of the operation, whether police records show a formal statement was ever taken from Kolako during his custody, and what the suspension letter actually says about the alleged disruption are all now matters of record that could be verified rather than argued. Until they are, the public is left with two accounts of the same afternoon that cannot both be complete.

World.title: What Trump’s New Order Means for Liberia — and Why Liberia’s Own Law Looks Nothing Like America’s
World.content:
What Trump’s New Order Means for Liberia — and Why Liberia’s Own Law Looks Nothing Like America’s

Washington is fighting over whether being born on American soil should be enough to make you American. Monrovia settled that question generations ago and settled it the opposite way. The two debates rarely touch — until an executive order like this one lands, and Liberians realize how differently their own country answers the same question.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia – The story behind this summer’s executive orders begins with a defeat. Trump’s original January 2025 order sought to end birthright citizenship outright for children born in the U.S. to undocumented or temporary- visa parents — a direct challenge to more than a century of settled interpretation of the 14th Amendment. The Supreme Court rejected it on June 30, 2026, ruling 6-3 in Trump v. Barbara that birthright citizenship remains a constitutional guarantee the president cannot unwind by executive action alone.

Rather than drop the fight, the administration narrowed it. The first of the two new orders carves out specific, smaller exclusions from automatic citizenship — children born to employees of foreign governments, such as embassy or consulate staff, and children whose parents are members of designated foreign terrorist organizations or are found to have engaged in fraud to obtain citizenship. The second, the “Ending Birth Tourism” order, is broader in practical reach: it directs the Secretaries of State and Homeland Security to deny visas, revoke travel authorization, and impose permanent entry bans on any foreign national a consular or border officer determines is traveling to the U.S. primarily to give birth. Neither order has been finally tested in court, and legal challenges are expected, but as of this writing both remain in effect.



Where Liberia Fits

Liberia does not appear by name in either order, and there is no evidence in U.S. government data or reporting that Liberia is a significant source country for birth tourism — the countries named repeatedly in coverage of the new policy are China, Russia, Nigeria, and parts of Latin America, including Cuba. But the absence of Liberia’s name from that list is not the same as immunity from the policy’s reach. Liberia has never been part of the U.S. Visa Waiver Program, the roughly 40-country list, dominated by Europe and wealthy Asia-Pacific nations, whose citizens can travel to the U.S. without a visa. Liberians applying for a B-1/B-2 visitor visa now do so under a system in which the consular officer reviewing that application has explicit new authority to deny it, or revoke it later, based on a judgment about the traveler’s intent to give birth in the United States. For the ordinary Liberian traveler — a business visitor, a student’s parent, a relative attending a graduation — the practical change is a wider door for discretion at the visa window, not a new restriction that names Liberia specifically.



The Wider African Picture

The birth tourism order is, in scale, a modest addition to a far larger tightening of U.S. immigration policy toward Africa that was already well underway before it was signed. In December 2025, a separate proclamation placed Nigeria under a near-total visa freeze effective January 1, 2026, blocking new tourist, business, and student visas for Nigerian applicants — a country that had been receiving an average of roughly 128,000 U.S. immigrant and nonimmigrant visas a year, among the highest of any African nation. Existing visa and green card holders were left largely unaffected, but the freeze effectively cut off new legal travel from the continent’s most populous country. Nigeria is not alone: of the 39 countries currently under some form of U.S. travel restriction, 26 are African, and 12 of those are in West Africa, Liberia’s own subregion. Liberia itself has not been placed under a Nigeria-style freeze, but the pattern across the region gives the new birth tourism order an added weight for African readers: it arrives as one more layer in a broader American posture that has grown steadily more restrictive toward the continent over the past year, not as an isolated policy confined to its own narrow purpose.

Liberia’s Own Birthright Rule Is Already Stricter Than America’s Old One

Here is where the comparison becomes genuinely striking rather than merely topical: Liberia never had anything resembling the American tradition Trump has spent two years trying to unwind. Under the Liberian Constitution, a person is a citizen at birth only if they are of Negro descent and born to Liberian citizen parents. Liberia has never granted automatic citizenship simply for being born on Liberian soil, regardless of a parent’s status — there is no Liberian equivalent of the unconditional jus soli the U.S. 14th Amendment has guaranteed for a century and a half. A child born in Monrovia to two foreign nationals gains no automatic claim to Liberian citizenship at all, a position considerably more restrictive, on its face, than even Trump’s rejected 2025 order, which targeted only children of undocumented or temporary-visa parents rather than all foreign nationals categorically.

Liberia is not alone in this approach, but the company it keeps is notable. Analyses comparing citizenship regimes worldwide, including research drawing on the Global Citizenship Observatory’s dataset of national citizenship laws, group Liberia with countries like Israel and Haiti as nations that apply race- or ancestry-based criteria rather than granting citizenship automatically based on birthplace alone. A Pew Research Center analysis found that roughly 32 countries worldwide, most of them in the Western Hemisphere, have birthright citizenship laws substantially like the traditional American model, while around 50 others have more limited variations. Liberia’s model — ancestry and racial descent, not geography — sits outside both groups, closer to the narrower, identity-based citizenship regimes found in parts of Europe, the Gulf, and East Asia than to its own regional neighbors in the Americas that share the U.S. approach.

The Dual Citizenship Reversal

For decades, Liberia compounded that restrictiveness with an outright ban on dual citizenship, forcing members of its own diaspora to formally choose between Liberian nationality and whatever citizenship they acquired abroad. That changed in July 2022, when the Legislature passed, and President Weah signed, an amendment to the 1973 Aliens and Nationality Law repealing the dual citizenship ban and, separately, granting Liberian women the same right as men to pass citizenship to their children — a gender inequity that had persisted in Liberian law for decades.

The 2022 reform did not simply throw the doors open, however. Dual citizenship under the amended law is available to people born outside Liberia if a parent was a Liberian citizen at the time of that person’s birth — an extension of the same ancestry-based logic that governs citizenship at birth, not a break from it. Foreign nationals of Black African ancestry may apply for Liberian citizenship after two years of residence; non-African applicants remain ineligible under current law regardless of how long they have lived in the country. And dual citizens face specific limits once naturalized or reclaimed: they are barred from serving as Minister of Finance and Development Planning, Minister of Defense, or Executive Director of the Central Bank of Liberia, an acknowledgment that Liberia’s own lawmakers were not fully comfortable extending dual nationality into the government’s most sensitive financial and security posts.

A Global Outlier, Either Way

Set side by side, the two systems make an uncomfortable kind of sense together. The United States built its citizenship law on the presumption that geography confers belonging — born here, American, full stop — and has spent the past two years fighting in court over how much of that presumption an administration can chip away by decree. Liberia built its citizenship law on the opposite presumption entirely: that belonging flows through ancestry and race, not geography, and that even reversing a strict ban on dual nationality required careful boundaries around who qualifies and what offices they can hold once they do. Liberians reading about Trump’s birth tourism order and the legal fight behind it are not encountering a foreign concept so much as an inverted mirror of their own country’s much older and, in some respects, considerably stricter rules. Whether that makes the American debate easier or harder to relate to may depend less on the policy details than on which side of the ancestry-versus-geography divide feels more familiar to begin with.

World.title: Liberia: Debt Court Begins Contempt Process Against Finance Minister, LEC MD Over US$415K ELTEL Judgment
World.content:
Contempt proceedings have been initiated at the Debt Court of Montserrado County against the management of the Liberia Electricity Corporation and the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning over alleged non-compliance with a final judgment of US$415,327.08 in favor of ELTEL Network Liberia.

By Victoria G Wesseh

The proceedings were triggered by a Bill of Information filed by ELTEL, asking the court to compel enforcement of its February 4, 2026 payment order.

According to court records, on July 7, 2026, the Debt Court issued show-cause summonses ordering LEC Managing Director Mohammed M. Sheriff and other senior LEC executives to appear before the court to explain why the judgment remains unsatisfied.

In its latest filing, argued last week, ELTEL is also asking the court to extend the show-cause action to include Finance and Development Planning Minister Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, on grounds that the Ministry is the fiscal agent for payment of judgments against state-owned enterprises.

The court has not yet made any finding of contempt against Minister Ngafuan or MD Sheriff. A show-cause summons is not a conviction – it is an order to appear and explain.

Why ELTEL Filed For Contempt

According to ELTEL’s petition, LEC acknowledged liability for the debt on February 3, 2026, and on February 4, 2026, the court entered judgment for US$415,327.08. The court said the sum comprises an arbitral award of US$364,322.00 plus statutory interest, attorney’s fees and court costs.

ELTEL alleges the amount has not been paid more than five months later.

Counsel for ELTEL further alleged in court that the matter was referred to the Executive Mansion and that on July 3, 2026, President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. directed the Ministry of Finance to intervene to satisfy the judgment. That alleged directive has not been independently verified by this paper, and no public response from the Ministry on that specific allegation is on the court record as of press time.

On that basis, ELTEL is praying the court to find willful disobedience and to impose contempt sanctions.

Sanctions under Liberian law for civil contempt may include a fine, an order for coercive imprisonment until the contempt is purged by payment, or other enforcement orders. Such sanctions are discretionary and are imposed only after due process.

The Debt Court is expected to decide whether to grant a final enforcement ultimatum – such as a 72-hour order for the US$415,327.08 to be transferred to the court’s escrow account, or set a full contempt hearing date where Minister Ngafuan and MD Sheriff would be required to appear personally or through counsel to show cause.

Both officials remain entitled to the presumption of compliance until the court rules otherwise, and to present their defense.

The case file shows the underlying dispute stems from a 2016 contract for low-voltage materials that ELTEL alleges it supplied to LEC. The original suit was filed in June 2024 through Attorney-in-Fact Hans Armstrong.

World.title: In Loving Memory of Hon. Sylvester Mondubue “Greg” Grigsby October 15, 1950 – August 9, 2025
World.content:
One year later, from his wife and daughters One year ago today, we said goodbye to our husband and father, Sylvester Mondubue “Greg” Grigsby. The world knew him as a statesman – a diplomat, a Minister of State, a proud son of Sinoe County who gave more than forty years of his life to the service of Liberia. We knew him as the man who came home.

The one who carried cash in his pocket just so he could tip an Uber driver. The one who loved game shows and corrected the history in our television shows. The one whose laugh you could hear from the next room and never mistake for anyone else’s. For fifty-one years, he was a husband. For all of our lives, he was our father. He crossed oceans and boarded late trains for us. He washed dishes, organized closets, and cooked corned beef and rice when one of us was unwell. He played monopoly with his grandchildren. He believed in showing up to show his love, and he showed up.

World.title: Liberian Mining Superintendents at ArcelorMittal Complete Advanced Drill & Blast Training in Brazil
World.content:
ArcelorMittal Liberia (AML) has reaffirmed its long-term commitment to developing Liberian professionals into world-class mining leaders following the successful completion of an advanced international Drill & Blast training program by five of its senior Liberian mining superintendents in Brazil.

According to a release, the specialized technical program was held at ArcelorMittal’s Serra Azul Mine in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, where mining professionals from various ArcelorMittal operations around the world gathered to exchange knowledge and strengthen expertise in modern mining techniques, operational excellence, environmental stewardship, and safety management.

The training exposed participants to internationally recognized best practices in drill and blast engineering, including blast design optimization, fragmentation control, ground vibration monitoring, powder factor management, explosives performance, environmental impact mitigation, and community safety. Participants also received practical, field-based instruction on improving productivity while ensuring responsible and sustainable mining practices.

The Liberian delegation consisted of five experienced operational leaders from AML’s Mines Department including Hamilton S.S. Kamara – Superintendent, ROM & Stockpile Management, Solo B. Gbayor – Superintendent, Mines, Ferrison Saye Andrews – Superintendent, Production, Theresa Mamie Nuah Koah – Superintendent, Pit and Toney Bazee Kamara – Superintendent, Drill & Blast.

Their participation reflects ArcelorMittal Liberia’s broader strategy of continuously investing in Liberian professionals by providing access to international technical training, leadership development, and global knowledge-sharing opportunities.

Building World-Class Liberian Mining Leaders

For more than a decade, ArcelorMittal Liberia has consistently prioritized the training and professional development of Liberian employees as part of its commitment to local capacity building. Through scholarships, vocational education, graduate development programs, international exchanges, technical certifications, leadership courses, and specialized overseas training, the company continues to prepare Liberians to occupy increasingly strategic positions across its operations.

The Brazil program represents another milestone in AML’s long-term vision of creating a highly skilled Liberian workforce capable of managing complex mining operations that meet international standards.

Rather than relying indefinitely on expatriate expertise, the company continues to build a pipeline of competent Liberian engineers, geologists, mine planners, production supervisors, and operational managers who can lead modern mining activities safely, efficiently, and responsibly.

This investment is particularly significant as Liberia’s mining industry continues to expand and demands a new generation of technically competent local professionals capable of leading large-scale industrial operations.

Preparing Liberia for the Future of Mining

Speaking following the completion of the program, AML General Manager Selmah Jallah emphasized that exposure to global mining operations is essential for developing the next generation of Liberian mining professionals.

“Liberia’s growing position as a key mining destination requires highly skilled professionals who can operate responsibly while protecting the environment,” Selmah said.

“International development opportunities are essential in preparing Liberian employees for future leadership roles as our mining sector increasingly relies on local talent and expertise.”

She noted that world-class mining is no longer defined solely by production volumes but also by operational safety, environmental responsibility, technological innovation, and strong leadership.

According to Selmah, every international training opportunity strengthens Liberia’s own mining capacity by allowing Liberian professionals to bring home globally tested knowledge and practical experience that can be applied across AML’s operations.

She further commended the five superintendents for their professionalism, discipline, and commitment throughout the program while encouraging all employees to continue demonstrating accountability, integrity, and compliance with company policies.

“Leadership is earned through consistent performance, professionalism, and continuous learning,” she added.

A Culture of Continuous Learning

The training also highlights AML’s philosophy that learning does not end with technical competence but continues throughout an employee’s career.

Production Superintendent Ferrison Saye Andrews described the Brazil program as another important milestone in his professional journey.

Andrews previously benefited from the AML Mineral Development Agreement (MDA) Scholarship Program in 2022, which enabled him to obtain a master’s degree before returning to Liberia to continue contributing to the company’s mining operations.

He said the opportunity to learn alongside mining professionals from different countries broadened his understanding of modern mining techniques and reinforced the importance of continuous professional development.

Similarly, Mines Superintendent Solo B. Gbayor described representing Liberia among mining experts from across the global ArcelorMittal Group as both an honor and an invaluable learning experience.

He noted that interacting with international specialists exposed the Liberian delegation to innovative operational approaches that will help improve safety, efficiency, and productivity within AML’s mines.

The other members of the delegation echoed similar sentiments, expressing appreciation to the company’s management for investing in their careers and providing opportunities to gain practical knowledge from one of the world’s leading mining organizations.

Investing in Liberian Talent

The Brazil exchange forms part of ArcelorMittal Liberia’s broader human capital development agenda, which continues to prioritize Liberians for technical and leadership advancement.

Over the years, the company has sponsored numerous employees for master’s degree programs, specialized mining certifications, engineering training, equipment operation courses, vocational education, leadership development initiatives, and international technical exchanges across multiple countries.

These investments have steadily increased the number of Liberians occupying senior operational and management positions within the company.

By transferring global technical expertise to local professionals, AML is helping develop a workforce capable of managing increasingly sophisticated mining operations while supporting Liberia’s long-term economic development.

As the company continues implementing major expansion projects, the demand for highly skilled Liberian professionals will continue to grow. Programs such as the Brazil Drill & Blast training demonstrate AML’s determination to ensure that Liberians are not merely participants in the country’s mining industry but are equipped to become internationally competitive professionals and world-class mining leaders.

The successful completion of the advanced Drill & Blast program therefore represents more than an individual achievement for the five superintendents. It reflects ArcelorMittal Liberia’s enduring commitment to empowering Liberian talent, strengthening national capacity, and creating a future where Liberians lead every aspect of modern mining—from the pit to the boardroom.

World.title: Chongwe receives ballot papers
World.content:
Distribution of ballot papers in Chongwe District has commenced ahead of Thursday’s 2026 General Elections.

The exercise is being conducted in Chongwe West and Chongwe East constituencies under the supervision of election officials and in the presence of election stakeholders.

Chongwe District Electoral Officer (DEO), Damson Mukwato earlier briefed election agents ahead of the verification of the ballot papers for the forthcoming elections.

Mr Mukwato said the verification process is being conducted in the spirit of promoting transparency, accountability and confidence among all election stakeholders.

He urged election agents to actively participate in the verification exercise and ensure that they adhere to established electoral procedures throughout the process.

” Strict adherence to electoral procedures is important in ensuring that the verification exercise is conducted smoothly and transparently,” he said.

He further called on all stakeholders to cooperate with election officials to ensure a credible and peaceful electoral process as the country prepares to hold the 2026 General Elections.

World.title: Government reaffirms commitment to empowering the girl child
World.content:
Government has reaffirmed its commitment to empowering the girl child.

Senga Hill District Commissioner Elizabeth Goma says government through various interventions in the education sector among them the keeping girls in school initiative, is empowering the girl child.

The District Commissioner said this when she officiated at the 2026 Keeping Girls in School (KGS) Academic Symposium in Senga Hill District.

Ms Goma observed that many girls enrolled under the Keeping Girls in School programme continue to face social and academic challenges arising from vulnerable backgrounds, which often affect their academic performance.

She said the annual symposium forms part of the Case Management System (CMS) interventions designed to improve learning outcomes by creating a platform where implementing schools can exchange best practices on academic achievement.

“The symposium seeks to promote academic excellence among Keeping Girls in School implementing schools while contributing to the development of quality human capital for national development,” she said.

She noted that the programme also provides an opportunity for professionals from various sectors to mentor girls and inspire them to pursue ambitious career paths, especially that beneficiaries of the KGS programme have access to scholarships for tertiary education upon successful completion of secondary school.

Speaking earlier, Senga Hill District Education Board Secretary Charity Lungu described the symposium as an important platform that connects learners with civic leaders and stakeholders who provide mentorship and guidance.

Ms Lungu said although many girls face numerous obstacles in life, education remains the most effective tool for overcoming those challenges.

“Girls should remain focused on their education because there is a time for schooling and a time for marriage, and education helps address many challenges girls face,” she said.

She further encouraged the learners to remember the four important stages represented by a girl’s attire showcased at the event.

“The four types of uniform a girl child can wear are the school uniform, the graduation gown, the wedding dress and the maternity dress. Each has its rightful time,” she said.

Ms Lungu disclosed that Senga Hill became a Keeping Girls in School implementing district in 2025 and currently has 1,297 beneficiaries.

She added that the district has distributed 10 bicycles to beneficiaries, received 2,283 packs of disposable sanitary towels and benefited from education grants amounting to K718,400 in 2025 and K680,000 in 2026 to support 850 learners.

“We are grateful for this support, which continues to transform the lives of vulnerable girls through education,” she said.

Meanwhile, A Grade 12 pupil at Senga Hill Boarding Secondary School, Violet Namwila, expressed gratitude to the government and its partners for investing in the education of the girl child.

“The commitment to empowering girls through education is making a lasting difference in our lives. Your guidance and encouragement have inspired us to dream bigger, work harder and become the leaders of tomorrow,” she said.

Ms Namwila urged fellow beneficiaries to remain focused, confident and determined to achieve their academic and career aspirations by putting into practice the lessons learnt during the symposium.

The symposium, was held at Senga Hill Boarding Secondary School under the theme “Empowering Girls – Creating Leaders for Tomorrow,” .

The symposium brought together government officials, education stakeholders, professionals and beneficiaries of the Keeping Girls in School programme to promote academic excellence, mentorship and career development.

World.title: Malawian, Zambian Die in Vubwi Gold Mining Collapse
World.content:
A Malawian national and a Zambian have died after the earth collapsed on them while conducting illegal gold mining at Chithumba Mining Area in Vubwi District.

The two, identified as 29-year-old Sapilo Lafele, a Malawian national from Kanjawa Village in Chief Kalolo Namitete, Malawi, and 32-year-old Philimon Tembo of Nthawena Village in Chief Mazimawe, Kasenengwa District, died after being buried underground in a seven-metre-deep pit.

Eastern Province Police Commanding Officer Robertson Mweemba confirmed the incident to the media, saying police received a report of sudden and unnatural death from Matthews Banda, aged 41, of Zalila Village in Chief Pembamoyo, Vubwi District, at about 04:30 hours today.

Mr Mweemba said the incident occurred yesterday at around 20:00 hours at Chithumba Mining Area.

He said preliminary investigations indicate that the two illegal miners entered the seven-metre-deep pit at around 19:30 hours to conduct gold mining activities.

“Whilst the duo was still underground, the earth above them collapsed, burying them instantly,” Mr Mweemba said.

He said police officers rushed to the scene after being informed and found other illegal miners attempting to retrieve the trapped miners.

Mr Mweemba said the two bodies were eventually retrieved at around 06:30 hours and inspected by police officers.

He said Lafele sustained a depressed head injury and cuts on the right leg, while Tembo sustained a bleeding nose and cuts on both legs.

Mr Mweemba said police have not suspected any foul play and the relatives have since been advised to proceed with burial.

Mr Mweemba has since warned people against engaging in illegal mining activities, particularly entering unsafe mine pits, saying such activities pose a serious danger to life.

World.title: Former MMD Chairman Backs HH
World.content:
Former MMD National Chairman and Information Minister STAN KRISTAFOR has endorsed President HAKAINDE HICHILEMA and the UPND ahead of the 2026 General Elections.

Mr. KRISTAFOR, who also served as Member of Parliament for Kitwe, says he is campaigning for President HICHILEMA because he believes the UPND has demonstrated its capacity to govern the country.

He says there is currently no credible opposition offering a viable alternative to the UPND, claiming that the Patriotic Front—PF—is virtually finished.

The former MMD National Chairman has cited the defection of former PF members, including MILES SAMPA, to the UPND as evidence of growing support for President HICHILEMA.

Mr. KRISTAFOR has challenged opposition leaders BRIAN MUNDUBILE and MAKEBI ZULU to explain how they intend to create jobs and develop the country if elected.

He says President HICHILEMA’s experience in business and economics makes him a competent leader capable of steering the country forward.

Mr. KRISTAFOR has also called on Zambians to maintain peace before, during and after the elections.

He has urged all political players to respect the outcome of the polls and support whoever is elected to govern the country.

Mr. KRISTAFOR says political differences should not be allowed to degenerate into violence or conflict.

World.title: Govt Releases K21.1 Billion in July
World.content:
Government released 21.1 billion Kwacha in July towards public services, food security, support for farmers and vulnerable households, free education and infrastructure development.

The latest release brings total Treasury disbursements between January and July 2026 to 152.05 billion Kwacha.

Secretary to the Treasury FELIX NKULUKUSA says the releases are aimed at ensuring that public resources translate into tangible benefits for citizens.

Of the July allocation, 6.3 billion Kwacha went towards transfers, subsidies and social benefits, while 5.9 billion Kwacha was allocated to the public service wage bill and related obligations.

A further 4.3 billion Kwacha was used for domestic and external debt service and the dismantling of domestic arrears, while 3.4 billion Kwacha supported government programmes and general operations.

The remaining 1.2 billion Kwacha was directed towards capital expenditure.

Food security remains a key priority, with the Food Reserve Agency receiving 2.7 billion Kwacha in July.

The Farmer Input Support Programme received 660 million Kwacha, bringing total FISP releases for the year to 6.4 billion Kwacha.

Government also released 564.2 million Kwacha for the Social Cash Transfer Programme, bringing cumulative releases for the programme this year to 2.3 billion Kwacha.

In the education sector, schools received 841.4 million Kwacha in grants to support the implementation of the free education programme, bringing total grants released to schools this year to 2.4 billion Kwacha.

Grant-aided institutions, including hospitals and universities, received 709.3 million Kwacha, while the Public Service Pension Fund was allocated 507.3 million Kwacha towards pension obligations.

On infrastructure, 1.2 billion Kwacha was released for capital projects, including 592 million Kwacha for roads, 243.3 million Kwacha for water infrastructure, 188.9 million Kwacha for the rehabilitation of National Assembly buildings, 101.3 million Kwacha for education infrastructure and 50 million Kwacha for mini-hospital projects.

Mr. NKULUKUSA says continued debt servicing and the dismantling of domestic arrears are critical to maintaining fiscal credibility and creating room for investment and economic growth.

He says Government remains optimistic about the country’s economic outlook but will continue to exercise prudence in managing public resources.

Mr. NKULUKUSA says the focus in the second half of the year will be on converting available resources into stronger public services, productive infrastructure, economic opportunities and improved livelihoods.

He says Government will also prioritise expenditure and protect key programmes amid pressure on fuel prices arising from geopolitical developments affecting global petroleum supplies.

This is according to a statement released by Mr. NKULUKUSA.

World.title: VJ Urges Voters to Turn Out in Numbers
World.content:
Veteran politician VERNON MWAANGA has urged registered voters to turn out in large numbers and exercise their right to vote in Thursday’s General Election.

Dr. MWAANGA has reminded voters that they have a constitutional right to elect their preferred President, Members of Parliament, Mayors and local councillors.

He says the election campaigns, which end on Wednesday, August 12, have largely been peaceful.

Dr. MWAANGA has expressed confidence that the counting of votes and declaration of results will also be conducted in an orderly and peaceful manner.

He says Zambia has a proud record of conducting peaceful elections and has urged citizens to uphold this tradition during the current and future elections.

Dr. MWAANGA was speaking in a statement made available to ZNBC News in Lusaka.

World.title: FQM Financing Deal to Boost Zambian Suppliers – MWABA
World.content:
The Association of Mine Suppliers and Contractors has welcomed First Quantum Minerals (FQM)’s initiative to support the growth of Zambian-owned companies in the mining sector.

Association President COSTA MWABA says an agreement between FQM and leading commercial banks will give local suppliers access to affordable financing, enabling them to expand their businesses and compete more effectively with foreign firms.

Last week, FQM signed a Memorandum of Understanding with ZANACO, First National Bank (FNB), ABSA, Stanbic and Inde Credit to develop and deliver financing solutions for Zambian-owned companies.

Mr. MWABA says the arrangement will allow participating banks to assess the risk of Zambian suppliers against FQM’s credit rating, which could help reduce borrowing costs and make financing more accessible.

He says the initiative will also enable local companies to grow by addressing challenges suppliers face in securing financing to fulfil orders.

FQM spent about 2 billion US dollars on goods and services last year, highlighting the potential market for Zambian-owned businesses within the mining supply chain.

Mr. MWABA says the financing arrangement will further help local suppliers and contractors meet the compliance requirements set by FQM.

He says increased participation of Zambian-owned companies in the mining value chain will contribute to job creation, increased tax revenues and improved skills development.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 10, 2026
World.content:
Nigeria Army Rescues 33 Kidnapped Victims in Zamfara

The Nigerian army has said that it has rescued 33 people who were kidnapped by armed men while travelling through Zamfara state in the northwest. Troops and police responded to the abduction in Tsafe. They intercepted the kidnappers as they moved the hostages, forcing the gunmen to flee into nearby bushes. All 33 victims were rescued without casualties. Security forces are tracking the abductors. The rescue comes amid a recent series of successful operations, with more than 300 kidnapped people reportedly freed in separate incidents. Ransom kidnappings continue to be a major security and political problem in northern Nigeria as the country prepares for the 2027 elections.

DR Congo Hands 15 Prisoners to M23 in Peace Deal Move



Democratic Republic of Congo authorities have released 15 prisoners and handed them over to the AFC/M23 rebel movement in the first known prisoner transfer under a 2025 peace deal. The deal is aimed at ending fighting in eastern Congo. The transfer, facilitated by the International Committee of the Red Cross and with Uganda's assistance, follows months of stalled negotiations over a larger exchange involving nearly 500 detainees. The ICRC described the operation as a potential step towards further releases and a "glimmer of hope" for families affected by the conflict. However, fighting between government forces and M23 has continued despite the peace agreement.

Ivorian Drum Looted by France Goes on Display at Home

Côte d'Ivoire has welcomed home the Djidji Ayokwe, a sacred "talking drum" looted by French colonial troops in 1916. It was returned to the country earlier this year. More than three metres long and weighing 430kg, the drum was used by the Ebrie community to send messages, warn of danger and summon villagers. It was paraded through Abidjan before being taken to its home village of Adjame, where traditional leaders and residents held ceremonies to mark its return. The drum is expected to go on display at the Museum of Civilisations in Abidjan as France faces growing pressure to return African artefacts taken during the colonial era.

Nigeria Holds Mass Wedding for 1,500 Couples

Around 1,500 couples have married in a two-day mass wedding organised by Kano State Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf in northern Nigeria to support low-income families and promote social stability. Each bride received a 200,000-naira dowry, business support and household items. Couples underwent screening and counselling before the ceremony. Among those married was a widower who lost his wife and six children in an attack earlier this year. The initiative comes as northern Nigeria continues to face widespread insecurity, including attacks and kidnappings by armed groups.

Africa's UN Secretary-General Bid Struggles for Support

Close 

The United Nations is set to name António Guterres's successor in October, whose second five-year term ends on 31 December. Africa's two candidates, former Senegalese president Macky Sall and Ugandan diplomat Olara Otunnu, are struggling to gain support in the first Security Council vote. Analysts said that Africa's chances are further weakened by the informal regional rotation system, which favours Latin America and the Caribbean this year. Neither African candidate has received backing from the African Union. Three women are also in the race, with UN Trade and Development chief Rebeca Grynspan emerging as the early frontrunner after receiving the most support in the first straw poll.

World.title: South Africa: Ramaphosa Calls on Men to Fight GBV - South African News Briefs - August 10, 2026
World.content:
Ramaphosa Urges Men to Stand Against GBV

President Cyril Ramaphosa has called on men and boys to take a stronger stand against gender-based violence, reports EWN. He said that they must reject violence against women and girls. Speaking at the Women’s Day commemoration at the Union Buildings, he also highlighted women’s achievements in education. He called for more women to enter science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields.

11 Killed in Three Cape Town Mass Shootings

Eleven people have been killed in three separate mass shootings in Cape Town, reports EWN. Three men were killed in Khayelitsha, and five people were killed in Langa. Three others died in a shooting at the Barcelona informal settlement in Gugulethu, where two additional people were wounded. Police have reinforced deployments in the affected communities, but no arrests have been made. The motives remain under investigation.

Malema Faces Prosecution Over 'Rapist' Remark

Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) leader Julius Malema is set to face criminal prosecution for crimen injuria after allegedly calling former Bergview College principal Jaco Pieterse a "rapist", reports EWN. The case stems from allegations that a seven-year-old girl, publicly known as Cwecwe, was raped at Bergview College in Matatiele, Eastern Cape, in October 2024. The NPA initially declined to prosecute anyone over the alleged rape, citing a lack of concrete evidence. However, it has now decided to prosecute Malema following a complaint pursued by AfriForum’s private prosecution unit. The case has been referred to the Johannesburg Magistrates Court.
