World.title: Discovering Mexico: Puebla
World.content:
Listen to this article

Puebla is for you if you like: Colonial history, sweeping mountains, racing while holding tortillas

Mexico’s fourth-largest city, Puebla, has more going on beneath its colonial facades than most visitors realize. Its historic center, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, holds 2,619 monuments — more than any other city in the Americas — plus the tallest cathedral bell towers in the country. The city’s well-preserved architecture has also made it a go-to filming location, standing in for 18th- and 19th-century Mexico and Spain in productions including “Frida” and “Man on Fire.”

All of this is before you get out into the wider state, where sweeping mountain ranges, active volcanoes and enormous cacti dot the landscape. The state is one of the last stops in southern Mexico before the jungle claims the country. We’ve collected some of our best pieces from the last few years, to help you experience one of Mexico’s most genuine — and stunning — regions.

Puebla’s capital — also, conveniently, called Puebla — is filled with the sort of magic that only Mexico’s oldest cities can really offer. Many of the nation’s most definining moments and people have filled these streets (and the tunnels underneath them).

Puebla’s identity is tied up in origin stories, although some more verifiable than others. Its early name, Puebla de los Ángeles, traces to a 1531 account of a bishop’s vision guiding Spanish settlers to the site. Its signature dish, mole poblano, is said to have been improvised by nuns at the Convent of Santa Rosa in 1680 when an archbishop arrived unannounced and the kitchen had little to offer but chilis, chocolate, nuts and stale bread. And on Nov. 18, 1910, the Serdán family home became the site of the first armed clash of the Mexican Revolution, two days before Francisco Madero formally launched the uprising; the bullet-scarred house is now a museum.

While its days of defining Mexico’s future are probably behind it, Puebla remains a fascinating destination for anyone who wants to understand how the modern country truly came to be.

While Oaxaca, Sonora and Yucatán often vie for the title of Mexico’s gastronomic heart, it’s really Puebla that deserves the credit for much of the nation’s great cuisine.

Puebla’s culinary reputation rests on three dishes with stories as rich as their flavors. Mole poblano, which rumour claims is a single flash of nun-driven inspiration, remains the most famous of Mexico’s 300-plus regional moles. Chiles en nogada, with its patriotic red, white and green color scheme, traces back to a 1821 feast honoring independence figure Agustín de Iturbide. Tacos árabes, born from Middle Eastern shawarma techniques brought by 1930s immigrants, is the progenitor of the iconic pastor.

The state is quite a bit more than just colonial architecture and great food, though. Just outside Tehuacán, Puebla’s second-largest city, sits a landscape that looks like it belongs on another planet.

The Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Biosphere sprawls across 145,255 hectares of protected desert, home to more than 2,500 species of cacti — tall and candle-thin, round as beach balls, or shaped like something out of a sci-fi set. A day inside it turns into a full sensory tour of the region: 2,000-year-old salt flats still worked by hand at Zapotitlán Salinas, a lunch built around cactus flowers and hibiscus water (with insects on offer for the adventurous) and a pottery workshop in Los Reyes Metzontla where clay deposits — leftovers from an ancient sea — get shaped into earthy, hand-thrown crockery.

In a small Puebla town two hours north of the city, an entire industry is built on Christmas spirit. Chignahuapan produces an estimated 70 million hand-blown ornaments a year, and inside the country’s largest esfera factory, the process starts with nothing more than a glowing-hot glass tube and a steady breath. From there, silver coatings, hand-mixed paint and careful dabs of glitter transform each piece into something ready for the tree — some ornaments even take a year to master.

Step inside the traditional workshop where trompos, Nativity scenes and piñata-shaped baubles come to life, one painstaking layer at a time.

In the days before Day of the Dead, the Puebla town of Huaquechula holds a tradition unlike anywhere else: the trueque, an ancient barter market where locals swap goods — peanuts, sugar cane, homemade bread — for everything needed to build their altars. Families trade for marigolds and cockscomb flowers, while vendors carry stacks of pan de muerto in its many forms, from bone-topped loaves to body-shaped muertitos dusted in red sugar.

Beyond the market, the town runs on hospitality: cooks prepare meals for hundreds of festival participants around the clock, and visitors are waved into strangers’ homes to see their altars up close. Huaquechula offers a rare, local variation on Mexico’s most iconic holiday — equal parts market day, family reunion and open-door celebration of the dead.

Our glimpse into Puebla ends on a unique note. The annual Carrera de la Tortilla, a 5-km race through Tehuacán that retraces the daily walk local women make to market, tortillas and all. Most runners came from Santa María Coapan, the self-proclaimed “Tortilla Capital” of Mexico, who run decked out in traditional Mixtec dress.

Part sporting event, part tribute to the women who keep the tradition alive, it’s one of Puebla’s more charming annual customs.

Puebla, Where Magic Lives in Every Journey / Sub English

Watch this video on YouTube

How to get there

When it comes to arriving in Puebla, it really only makes sense to arrive from Mexico City.

By air

Puebla International Airport: 45 minutes from the city center, the airport offers connections to almost every major Mexican destination, plus Newark, Houston and Los Angeles.

Mexico City Benito Juarez (AICM): The big one. About 2 hours (traffic permitting) from central Puebal. Available from everywhere in Mexico, and almost every major global airport besides.

Felipe Ángeles International Airport (AIFA): The eternally troubled AIFA is finally beginning to come into it’s own. 2.5 hours away, it offers similar domestic connectivity to AICM and flights in from Colombia, Venezuela, the Dominican Republic and Cuba.

By road

Mexico City: 135km (83 miles) somewhere between 90 minutes and 3 hours, depending on when you travel. National holidays often lead to enormous tailbacks, but tackling the drive early on a weekday often means you can get there in less than two hours.

World.title: Ohuira Bay communities weigh federal plan for Sinaloa ammonia plant
World.content:
TOPOLOBAMPO, Mexico — When federal officials finally unveiled a plan last week to address the 12-year conflict over a nearly completed ammonia plant beside Ohuira Bay, Indigenous Yoreme activist, rural sociologist and law student Melina Maldonado did not feel relieved.

She felt crushed.

After six days of roundtable discussions, she had begun to feel hopeful; it seemed they were really taking in new information and seeing a different side to the debate. The proposal led her to believe otherwise.

“They didn’t listen to our reasons for saying no,” Maldonado said. “They listened for a way to make it a yes.”

The federal proposal promises environmental safeguards, community monitoring and public investment around the German-backed GPO-Proman plant in northern Sinaloa state. But it leaves the project’s operation largely intact — and that has exposed the fundamental divide at the heart of the conflict: The government is offering ways to make the plant safer, while the communities closest to the bay are still adamant that it should not operate at all.

Those communities must now take the proposal into their own assemblies and, using their traditional Indigenous consensus-based governance model, decide whether to accept it. Until then, the blockade outside the gate to the plant — now in its 72nd day — remains in place.

A proposal, not an agreement

The plan emerged after six days of talks involving federal and state officials, representatives of GPO-Proman and members of the ¡Aquí No! (Not Here!) collective, which is led by Yoreme-Mayo communities surrounding Ohuira Bay and has become the principal force opposing the plant.

Federal officials presented the proposal as a path toward resolving a conflict that has become one of Mexico’s longest-running and most contentious environmental battles. But movement leaders emphasized that no agreement has been reached and that they do not have the authority to accept the plan on behalf of their communities.

The proposal must first be explained and discussed in assemblies in Ohuira, Paredones, Lázaro Cárdenas and Topolobampo. These communities surround the Santa María-Topolobampo-Ohuira lagoon system, a Ramsar wetland of international importance, and would bear the plant’s most direct impacts.

Community response to the proposal

“We have to hold our own internal assemblies,” said Claudia Susana Quintero, a Yoreme educator, resident of the village of Ohuira and one of the leaders of ¡Aquí No! “We have to explain it to the community, analyze it and decide how we are going to reach consensus.”

The representatives’ role is to take the proposal home and return with a decision reached collectively — not to accept it on their communities’ behalf.

The US $1.6 billion plant, designed to produce 2,200 metric tons (2,425 tons) of ammonia a day, is reportedly about 88% complete. Opposition began soon after the project was approved in 2014 and has centered on threats to fishing, the lagoon ecosystem, industrial safety and what Yoreme communities describe as a deeply flawed Indigenous consultation.

The current protest began in late May, when residents tried to block the movement of massive absorption towers from the port. Protesters later shifted their encampment to the plant entrance, where they have remained through extreme heat and intense storms.

A project the government considers strategic

President Claudia Sheinbaum has defended the plant as important to Mexico’s goal of achieving greater food sovereignty. Ammonia is a principal raw material in nitrogen fertilizers, and Sheinbaum has said Mexico currently imports nearly all the fertilizer it uses, apart from production by state-owned company Fertinal.

She has also emphasized that the plant is nearly finished, and that it underwent an environmental review and received majority support in the government-led Indigenous consultation — a process the four communities closest to Ohuira Bay continue to dispute.

The Economy Ministry says the GPO plant could reduce Mexico’s fertilizer imports by as much as 70% and keep approximately US $500 million now spent on imports within the Mexican economy.

For the federal government, the plant is part of a broader strategy to reduce dependence on imported agricultural inputs. Opponents say that national goal does not justify concentrating the risks in their communities.

What the government put on the table

The proposal leaves the ammonia plant in place, but would significantly alter how it operates. Among its most significant provisions, the plan calls for GPO-Proman to stop drawing water directly from Ohuira Bay and instead use water discharged through a nearby Federal Electricity Commission canal.

Opponents have long warned that the plant’s authorized system would pull large volumes of seawater from the lagoon and return warmer, saltier water, potentially disrupting fish and shrimp nurseries. Under the new plan, wastewater would instead be carried offshore rather than released back into the lagoon system.

The plan also proposes a new environmental baseline study, continuous water-quality monitoring and an oversight body made up of community members, scientists, government officials and company representatives. Additional measures would address sewage and agricultural runoff already entering the bay, as well as emergency preparedness and civil protection.

Other commitments focus on longstanding community needs, including housing, education, fishing infrastructure and assistance in certifying local shrimp and crab products so they can command higher prices.

Economic development plans in Topolobampo

Federal commissioner Mauricio Rodríguez Alonso, who has led the talks, stressed at a Tuesday news conference that the plan grew out of dialogue among the communities, GPO-Proman and government agencies. He said the company had agreed in principle to its commitments.

Ulises Pinzón, Topolobampo’s municipal representative, said the package could bring meaningful benefits. He was particularly encouraged by provisions giving communities a voice over future petrochemical development.

That is especially significant in Topolobampo, which the federal government has designated as an economic development hub where chemical and petrochemical industries are among the priority sectors. The plan would also keep proposed methanol and urea plants and a port terminal on hold unless the communities agree to them.

But Pinzón noted that many of the promises involve responsibilities the government should already be fulfilling, rather than concessions from GPO-Proman itself.

“On paper, honestly, I see an attractive proposal,” he said. “The question is how we can ensure that these commitments are actually fulfilled.”

That distinction — between a promising announcement and a binding, enforceable agreement — is now one of the central questions confronting the communities.

The risk that remains

For opponents of the plant, the most troubling unresolved issue is the danger of a catastrophic ammonia release. The government proposal does include new safeguards: an emergency-response center, joint industrial-risk monitoring, water curtains around pipelines and storage tanks, and a regional civil-protection plan — something Rodríguez acknowledged does not currently exist.

But movement leaders say emergency planning and mitigation cannot eliminate the underlying danger documented in the company’s own risk assessment.

According to that assessment, a five-minute leak could create a high-impact zone extending roughly 15 kilometers (9 miles) from the plant, encompassing Topolobampo and nearby Yoreme communities. A broader impact zone could extend as far as 45 kilometers (28 miles), reaching toward Los Mochis and other surrounding communities.

“That risk is still there, and it is still not clear to us,” Pinzón said. “The first people affected would be those of us who live in Topolobampo.”

Loss of life is not remediable

Company project documents show the plant is designed to store up to 75,000 metric tons (82,670 tons) of anhydrous ammonia near populated communities. Quintero said the proposal may reduce certain environmental impacts, but it cannot eliminate the consequences of a major industrial accident.

“You can remediate many things,” she said. “What you cannot remediate is the loss of life.”

For Maldonado, this is where the government’s proposal misses the point. Her own community, the Yoreme fishing village of Lázaro Cárdenas, looks across the bay at the plant every day.

The communities’ opposition has never been limited to the plant’s effects on water quality or fisheries, she said. It is rooted in the belief that a facility carrying such risks should not operate near people’s homes. She pointed to the company’s brightly colored risk map.

“This is the risk zone the company itself identified,” she said. “And now they are minimizing it or pushing it into the background.”

A decision made under threat

The communities will not consider the proposal in a political vacuum. Several of the movement’s most visible leaders have received threats related to their opposition to the plant and now live under government protection measures.

Four of ¡Aquí No!’s most visible leaders, including Maldonado, Quintero and Ohuira traditional governor Felipe Montaño, have been enrolled in Mexico’s federal protection mechanism for human rights defenders and journalists. Protection measures can include bulletproof vests and government-issued panic buttons intended to summon help in an emergency.

But Quintero said such equipment offers little comfort as the communities prepare to deliver an answer that government officials and project supporters may not want to hear.

“I know my community is going to say no,” she said. “But now the government is putting us in the line of fire against the rest of society that says yes.”

She worries that the plan could recast defenders as obstacles to jobs and economic development, increasing the pressure on people who have already spent years facing intimidation for speaking publicly.

“A bulletproof vest and a panic button are not going to help me much if someone decides to act tomorrow,” Quintero said.

The experience, she added, has gradually consumed the rest of their identities.

“We are no longer mothers, daughters or sisters,” she said. “We are nothing more than defenders.”

From shock to strategy

By Thursday evening, the mood inside the movement had begun to shift.

Enrique Ayala, a longtime activist staying at the blockade, said movement leaders spent six hours Thursday with scientists and lawyers analyzing the proposal and plotting their next steps.

“The government proposal is one-sided,” Ayala said. “They are pushing ahead with their project.”

But after years of being ignored, Ayala sees the government’s willingness to sit down with them as progress.

“We have to get up, keep going and make proposals of our own,” he said. “After 12 years when they paid us no attention, now we have them sitting at the table.”

And despite the government’s apparent intention to move the plant toward operation, Ayala said the movement has not abandoned its original goal.

“We still believe we can get the company to leave,” he said. “Sometimes you have to dream.”

Tracy L. Barnett is a Guadalajara-based freelance writer and the founder of The Esperanza Project.

World.title: From the archive: A guide to Mexican nicknames and how they’re given
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in February 2025 — is a perfect example, offering humorous insight into the fine art of giving nicknames in Mexico.

If you’ve spent much time among Mexicans, you’ve probably realized something. They love to give each other — and consistently use — nicknames.

I’m not just talking about diminutives of names, though these are also popular. Guillermo, for example, is Memo for short, the same way Bob is a diminutive of Robert.

How nicknames work in Mexico

There’s Alex for both Alejandro and Alejandra, Chio for Rocío, Lalo for Eduardo, Lola for Dolores and Chava for Salvador. There’s also short versions of double names, like Mafer for María Fernanda, Majo for María José and my favorite, Lucifer for Lucía Fernanda, a name most people do not give their kids. And of course, the classic “-ito” and “-ita” can go at the end of many names. So sometimes people call me Sarita, and my partner Juanito. Careful with using these, though, as they’re often infantilizing, and as you very likely know, some people do not like being infantilized.

So you get the idea: most names here have a shortened version. But Mexicans don’t stop there!

My nicknames

I’ll admit that this makes me very happy. As a kid, I never had a nickname, and I was jealous that I didn’t. Thinking back, it’s probably better; it wouldn’t have necessarily been a nice one, as I was both a crybaby and a showoff. Come to think of it, I might still be both of those things. Thankfully, I don’t currently have any nicknames related to either of those characteristics. Yet.

I do have some other fun ones though. “Sirena polar” — polar mermaid — might be the most creative, given to me by a friend of my ex-husband who was amazed that I insisted on swimming in ice-cold water after a hike. For reasons unknown to me, this same friend also often called me “cara de nutria”: otter face. Maybe because otters swim in cold water, too? Another friend, not quite as creative, simply calls me “mi gringa favorita.” I’d be more flattered if I weren’t one of the only gringos she knows.

The futility of protesting against your nickname

Many nicknames are purposefully funny, and sometimes shocking. And from what I can tell, people don’t seem to be insulted by them. Sometimes I wonder if they actually are bothered but know that trying to fight back against the Mexican urge to make fun of everything is futile.

So when you get a name like “El Frijol” because you’re very dark-skinned, you just go along with it, I guess?

In the particular case of another acquaintance, the guy was tall and good-looking. He was married, but seemed to have no shortage of women interested in him, or of self-esteem.

I always wanted to ask him if the nickname bothered him, but we were never close, so the opportunity was lost. But I did get to ask my ex-husband, who his friends had nicknamed “el bello camello” — the beautiful camel — supposedly because they thought he looked Arab.

The new generation of nicknames

Could this be one of those cultural things that’s dying out with more socially conscious and sensitive younger generations? I don’t think it is, as my daughter, age 11, has several nicknames herself. At school, her friends sometimes call her Plana, which means flat. It’s a synonym of her name, Lisa, which means “smooth” in Spanish and is often featured on hair conditioner bottles. And in her Scout troop, every kid has a nickname, each one the name of a bird. She’ll also respond to “Mona,” which is kind of nice. “Mona” is more of a Spanish-from-Spain word for “pretty,” but in this case, of course it’s about the Mona Lisa.

So perhaps the tradition will continue?

Don’t take yourself too seriously

After several years of watching the issue of how people address them being taken very, very seriously north of Mexico, I’ll admit that I find the ability to joke around with silly nicknames refreshing. Like all humor, though, it’s very culturally specific; there are plenty of unspoken rules regarding when it’s funny and good-humored and when it’s not.

It’s not that I want the freedom to be gratuitously mean, which is something very different. But I do think that it’s always worth it to not take ourselves so seriously all the time, something most of us can agree makes us generally unlikable.

So if you get a nickname here, try to go with it. Because people don’t get nicknames when they’re not being included in a group. Even if it’s not one you’d have chosen for yourself, it’s a signal that you are part of a community; people know you.

They might be making fun, but it’s affectionate fun. Try to take it that way.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: US suspends avocado certs, fracking studies continue and Peru rift ends
World.content:
Listen to this article

President Claudia Sheinbaum’s daily press conferences set much of the week’s agenda, moving from children’s social media use to a government transparency decree, a high-profile murder, fracking policy and a diplomatic breakthrough with Peru. Economic data told a mixed story too, with a strengthening peso set against a sharp drop in Pemex profit and a battered Sinaloa economy.

Security developments also kept pace, including the arrest of a former Guerrero governor on Ayotzinapa-related charges, a jump in U.S. rewards tied to CJNG’s new leadership, and a fresh U.S. suspension of avocado certifications in Michoacán. On the public health and safety front, a UNAM cheating scandal, a UNESCO deadline to protect the vaquita and a cyclosporiasis scare linked to Riviera Maya travel all drew attention.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Economy: Peso strengthens and avocado trade swings

Mexico’s currency extended a 10-day rally to reach its strongest level since February, helped by the Bank of Mexico holding its benchmark rate at 6.5% and a weaker US dollar following a soft American jobs report. The gains came even as Pemex reported a 70% annual drop in second-quarter net profit, which the state oil company attributed to higher financial costs, tax obligations and an unfavorable exchange rate. Economic disparities varied widely by region, with Sinaloa’s economy posting the worst quarterly contraction of any Mexican state, a result economists linked to the ongoing cartel conflict in the region.

Tourism data added to the mixed picture: Tourism GDP fell 0.8% quarter-over-quarter in the first three months of the year, according to INEGI, driven by a 5.9% quarterly drop in spending by foreign visitors, even as domestic tourism consumption rose 0.5%.

Mexico’s avocado trade also had a volatile week. New data showed exports to the U.S. jumped 35% in the first quarter compared to the previous year, according to Sader. Days later, however, the United States suspended avocado export certifications in Michoacán, citing an unspecified “threat against U.S. interests” — the third such suspension in just over four years. Michoacán’s governor deployed additional state security operatives and the Defense Ministry sent more than 1,500 soldiers to the region in response.

Energy: Government edges toward fracking while banning it in Mexico’s top basin

A government expert committee tasked with assessing “sustainable fracking” recommended prohibiting hydraulic fracturing in the Tampico-Misantla basin, Mexico’s largest-potential shale region, citing environmental, social and biodiversity concerns. Sheinbaum said her government would respect that recommendation, which she reaffirmed at Friday’s mañanera.

However, the committee recommended continued evaluation of two other northern basins. Reuters reported that pilot projects in Coahuila and Tamaulipas could begin as soon as next month if approved, as Mexico looks to reduce its reliance on natural gas imports from the United States.

Security: Pressure builds on cartels and past officials

U.S. authorities raised the reward for CJNG’s new leader, Juan Carlos Valencia González, to $25 million following the February death of cartel founder “El Mencho,” as part of more than $100 million in reward offers and new visa restrictions. Domestically, federal agents dismantled four illicit fuel processing centers in San Luis Potosí, Hidalgo and Morelos, seizing roughly 1 million liters of fuel. In Sinaloa, Sheinbaum acknowledged the murder of content creator César Gastélum, the ninth social media personality killed in the state since 2024. And in a case tied to one of Mexico’s most notorious unsolved crimes, federal authorities arrested former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre on charges of concealing video evidence related to the 2014 disappearance of 43 Ayotzinapa students; Sheinbaum said the arrest was not politically motivated.

Public health, environment and education

Sheinbaum laid the cornerstone for a new IMSS hospital in Oaxaca, part of a three-facility “Health City” complex the government frames as a step toward its planned Universal Health Service. And after the U.K. reported dozens of cyclosporiasis cases among travelers, Mexico stepped up health inspections at Riviera Maya hotels, while officials said the country has not been identified as the outbreak’s source.

Officials at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) confirmed that nearly 60,000 applicants must retake its entrance exam after widespread cheating undermined its first-ever online exam.

Separately, UNESCO gave Mexico until February to show concrete action to protect the critically endangered vaquita porpoise, of which only seven to 10 are believed to remain.

Diplomacy and governance

Sheinbaum signed a decree aimed at strengthening federal government transparency, which officials said would compel departments to disclose more information following the 2024 elimination of the INAI watchdog agency.

On the diplomatic front, Sheinbaum announced that Mexico and Peru would restore relations severed since November, after former Peruvian Prime Minister Bettsy Chávez was granted safe passage from asylum in Mexico’s Lima embassy.

Looking ahead

The coming weeks will test several threads left open this week: whether Mexican and U.S. officials can resolve the security concerns behind the avocado certification suspension, whether President Sheinbaum’s panel of experts finds acceptable conditions in northern Mexico to move fracking pilot projects forward, and how UNAM’s rescheduled in-person exams — set for mid-to-late August — play out after the cheating controversy. Mexico also faces UNESCO’s February deadline on vaquita protections and continued scrutiny of Sinaloa’s cartel-driven economic slowdown.

World.title: Copasul’s US$198 Million Soybean Plant Bets on Mato Grosso do Sul
World.content:
Brazil · Agribusiness

Key Facts R$1.013 billion — Copasul builds its biggest project ever.

— Copasul builds its biggest project ever. 115 hectares — Site along BR-163 highway.

— Site along BR-163 highway. 3,000 tonnes — Daily soybean crushing capacity.

— Daily soybean crushing capacity. Meal and oil — Main products from the new plant.

— Main products from the new plant. 16.7 million tonnes — State soybean crop in 2025/26 (SIGA/Aprosoja-MS).

— State soybean crop in 2025/26 (SIGA/Aprosoja-MS). Energized substation — Infrastructure progress confirmed in March 2026.

— Infrastructure progress confirmed in March 2026. Record national crop — Brazil at 180.568 million tonnes (CONAB).

Copasul’s largest investment ever brings a 3,000-tonne-per-day crusher to BR-163, boosting local processing capacity.

The Mato Grosso do Sul soybean plant is about to get a serious upgrade. Copasul, a farming cooperative in the state, is building its largest project ever: a R$1.013 billion (US$198.3 million) soybean processing facility on 115 hectares along the BR-163 highway. The plant will crush 3,000 tonnes of soybeans per day into meal and vegetable oil. That makes it a cornerstone for the region’s fast-moving agribusiness sector.

The plant’s main substation was energized in March 2026, a key step before commercial operations begin. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The scale of the Mato Grosso do Sul soybean plant

The new facility sits right on BR-163, a key road linking Mato Grosso do Sul to export ports. It covers 115 hectares, which is roughly 160 football pitches.

The R$1.013 billion (US$198.3 million) price tag is the biggest investment in Copasul’s 40-year history. The cooperative’s leadership has called this a turning point for its members.

When running at full capacity, the plant will process 3,000 tonnes of soybeans each day. That translates to about 1 million tonnes a year, depending on operating days.

Output will focus on soybean meal for animal feed and vegetable oil for food and industrial uses. These products command higher prices in the market than raw grain.

Construction is well underway. In March 2026, Copasul reported that the main electrical substation was energized, a big step for the industrial complex.

But the cooperative has not given a definitive start-up date for commercial operations. It is still finishing secondary systems and testing equipment.

The timing could not be better. Mato Grosso do Sul produced 16.7 million tonnes of soybeans in the 2025/26 crop, with around 80% already sold, according to SIGA and Aprosoja-MS, as reported by Campo Grande News.

That is a huge supply base for the new crusher, ensuring a steady flow of raw material from day one.

The plant will also include a rail spur and truck unloading bays to handle the heavy inbound flow. This setup keeps the operation smooth and reduces waiting times for farmers.

Why local processing matters

For years, Mato Grosso do Sul has shipped most of its soybean as raw grain. That means lower returns for farmers because they depend on distant buyers.

Processing locally adds value, keeps more money in the state, and creates jobs. It also shortens the distance between farm and factory.

The new plant will help change that dynamic. Instead of sending beans to other states or ports, Copasul can turn them into meal and oil right at home.

This gives farmers more options when selling their crops and reduces their exposure to volatile freight costs. That is a practical shield against market swings.

It also supports Brazil’s broader push toward higher-value agribusiness. National soybean output hit a record 180.568 million tonnes in 2025/26, up 5.3% from the previous year, per CONAB.

Exports also grew, to 116.3 million tonnes. But processing capacity is the next frontier for capturing more revenue within the country.

For you, if you live in or invest in Latin America, this is a sign of where the region is heading. Agribusiness is no longer just about growing commodities.

It is about building infrastructure to process them and capture more of the global market.

Impact on logistics and the local economy

BR-163 is strategic. It runs from Mato Grosso do Sul up through Mato Grosso and toward the Amazon ports, giving access to international buyers.

The new plant adds to the corridor’s importance, pulling in soybeans from surrounding farms and pushing out processed products to markets.

The plant will also generate tax revenue for the state and municipality. Construction work alone has likely brought hundreds of jobs to the area, and permanent roles will follow once operations begin.

Copasul has not released full annual output figures or employment numbers. But a project of this scale typically creates hundreds of direct and indirect jobs.

That is a big boost for a region where agriculture is the main economic driver. Local suppliers of packaging, fuel, and services will also benefit from the activity.

The cooperative is also betting on the long term. Brazil is set for its third straight record soybean harvest in 2026/27, according to early projections.

That means a steady supply of raw material for years to come. It also gives the cooperative confidence to invest in expansion beyond the initial build.

Challenges and what’s next

Getting the plant online is not without hurdles. Energy costs, logistics bottlenecks, and international price swings all play a role in profitability.

But the energized substation shows that Copasul is pushing forward despite those challenges. The cooperative has already overcome land, permitting, and construction delays.

The state’s soybean farmers have another concern: tight margins. With input costs climbing, as noted in a recent feed food industry report, processing locally can help farmers capture more value from each tonne.

Copasul will also face competition from other crushing plants in Brazil. But its location on BR-163 and its cooperative model, where farmers share in the profits, give it a distinctive edge over rivals.

Watch for the official commissioning date in the coming months. Once the plant starts up, it will be a game-changer for Mato Grosso do Sul’s agribusiness sector.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Mato Grosso do Sul soybean plant? It is a new soybean processing facility built by Copasul cooperative along BR-163. It will crush up to 3,000 tonnes of soybeans per day into meal and vegetable oil, representing a R$1.013 billion (US$198.3 million) investment. Why is the new plant important for Mato Grosso do Sul? The state produces 16.7 million tonnes of soybeans but lacks factory capacity. This plant adds local processing, meaning farmers can sell closer to home and the region keeps more of the value chain. When will the plant start operations? No official start-up date has been announced. In March 2026, the main electrical substation was energized, showing progress, but the cooperative has not confirmed when commercial operations will begin. How does this affect soybean prices for farmers? Local processing reduces transport costs and gives farmers more buyers, which can support better prices. It also adds demand for the record 2025/26 crop, where 80% was already sold.

World.title: Brazil Northeast Governor Races Heat Up After Bahia Debate
World.content:
Brazil · Elections

Key Facts Debate date — Bahia’s first 2026 governor debate aired Sunday 9 August on Band Bahia.

— Bahia’s first 2026 governor debate aired Sunday 9 August on Band Bahia. Three candidates — ACM Neto, Jerônimo Rodrigues, and Ronaldo Mansur took part.

— ACM Neto, Jerônimo Rodrigues, and Ronaldo Mansur took part. Close poll — A Quaest April survey put Neto at 41% and Rodrigues at 37%, a technical tie.

— A Quaest April survey put Neto at 41% and Rodrigues at 37%, a technical tie. Key themes — Health, education, security, and the environment dominated exchanges.

— Health, education, security, and the environment dominated exchanges. Pernambuco race — João Campos (PSB) faces incumbent Raquel Lyra (PSD) in a rematch.

— João Campos (PSB) faces incumbent Raquel Lyra (PSD) in a rematch. Regional stakes — The northeast is Brazil’s electoral battleground, with millions of votes at play.

— The northeast is Brazil’s electoral battleground, with millions of votes at play. Center shift — Analysts say the region’s voters are moving toward centrist candidates.

ACM Neto and Jerônimo Rodrigues clashed in Bahia’s first 2026 debate, while Pernambuco’s João Campos and Raquel Lyra gear up for a tight rematch.

The Bahia governor debate set the tone for Brazil’s northeast races, where outcomes could tip the 2026 presidential balance. On Sunday, ACM Neto and Jerônimo Rodrigues faced off in their first televised debate, showing how health, education, and security are the battleground issues for millions. For anyone in or watching Latin America, this region’s political direction signals Brazil’s broader mood before October.

Candidates faced off in Salvador on 9 August, with health and education dominating the exchanges. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What Happened in the Bahia Governor Debate

The Bahia governor debate aired at 20:00 on Band Bahia, with ACM Neto from União Brasil, incumbent Jerônimo Rodrigues from the PT, and Ronaldo Mansur from PSOL on stage. It was the first face-to-face meeting of the campaign season.

The exchanges were sharp. Neto, a former Salvador mayor, attacked Rodrigues over public services and infrastructure.

Rodrigues hit back, defending his record and pointing to federal investment from Lula’s government.

Mansur, the PSOL candidate, used the platform to push left-wing positions on inequality and the environment. He criticised both main rivals, positioning himself as the outsider in the race.

Health and education drew the most fire. Neto claimed hospitals in the interior are understaffed, while Rodrigues touted new clinics and school construction.

Security also came up, with each candidate blaming the other for rising violence in certain regions.

The debate was a preview of the campaign’s core clash. Neto represents the centre-right opposition, Rodrigues the ruling PT coalition, and Mansur the radical left.

Each tried to frame the state’s problems in their own narrative.

Pernambuco: A Rematch With National Echoes

In Pernambuco, the race is a direct rematch between João Campos of the PSB and incumbent Raquel Lyra of the PSD. Campos, the mayor of Recife, lost narrowly to Lyra in 2022, and this time he’s the favourite in early polls.

The two have traded barbs for months. Campos accuses Lyra of ignoring the capital’s needs, while Lyra says Campos is a product of the old political machine.

No debate has been confirmed yet, but both campaigns are preparing for a brutal air war.

Other candidates are registered, including Ivan Moraes from PSOL and Guilherme Fonseca from PSTU. But the real fight is between Campos and Lyra, with the result likely to be decided by a few thousand votes.

Pernambuco’s governor’s seat is a springboard for national politics. Both Campos and Lyra are seen as future presidential hopefuls, especially if they can win the state with a strong margin.

Why the Northeast Matters for Brazil’s Future

The northeast has around 27% of Brazil’s electorate — roughly 42 million voters. It has been a stronghold for the PT for two decades, but the 2026 elections show the region moving toward the centre.

A researcher told Valor International that the northeast ’gravitates toward center’ as voters focus on practical issues like jobs and public services. That trend benefits candidates like Neto and Campos, who mix moderate rhetoric with local appeal.

For investors, the northeast is a major market for infrastructure, agribusiness, and renewable energy. Governor races here determine how those sectors are regulated and taxed, so the outcomes matter beyond politics.

For expats living in Salvador or Recife, the campaigns will shape everyday life — from public transport to healthcare access. The results on polling day will also indicate Brazil’s national direction heading into the 2028 presidential cycle.

What Is at Stake

Brazil elects state governors alongside its president. Governors run health, schools, policing and much of daily life in their states.

The northeast is one of the country’s most closely watched regions at the ballot box. It is populous, and its votes carry real weight nationally.

Bahia and Pernambuco are two of its biggest states. Both races pit well-known local names against each other.

The first round of voting is set for October. The campaign, and debates like this one, will shape the months ahead.

Debates give voters an early read on the candidates. They also test how each contender handles pressure on live television.

For businesses, a state’s leadership shapes taxes, infrastructure and the local investment climate. That makes these races worth watching from abroad.

Turnout in the northeast can swing national results too. That is why party leaders in far-off Brasilia pay close attention.

Expats living in these states feel the outcome directly. Local government touches everything from clinics to road repairs.

Foreign companies with operations in the region also track the vote. A new governor can change priorities on permits and public works.

Campaign Issues That Resonate Beyond Brazil

Health was the top issue in the Bahia governor debate, and it’s a shared concern across the northeast. Public hospitals are often overcrowded, and rural areas lack specialists.

Candidates are promising new equipment and staff, but funding is tight.

Education also took centre stage. Neto proposed technical schools to boost youth employment, while Rodrigues pointed to university expansion under PT governments.

Mansur called for free universal childcare, a costly pledge.

Security is rising up the agenda after recent crime spikes in Salvador and Recife. Voters want visible police presence, but candidates differ on whether to invest in repressive or preventive measures.

The environment emerged as a secondary theme, especially in Bahia’s coastal and farming regions. Mansur pushed for stricter protections, while Neto and Rodrigues balanced green talk with agribusiness support.

Frequently Asked Questions

When was the first Bahia governor debate in 2026? The Bahia governor debate aired on Sunday, 9 August 2026, at 20:00 on Band Bahia. It featured ACM Neto, Jerônimo Rodrigues, and Ronaldo Mansur. Who are the main candidates in the Bahia governor race? The main candidates are ACM Neto (União Brasil), Governor Jerônimo Rodrigues (PT), and Ronaldo Mansur (PSOL). A Quaest April poll showed Neto at 41% and Rodrigues at 37%, a technical tie. Who is running for governor in Pernambuco? The leading candidates are João Campos (PSB), mayor of Recife, and incumbent Raquel Lyra (PSD). Other registered names include Ivan Moraes (PSOL) and Guilherme Fonseca (PSTU). Why are the northeast governor races important? The northeast holds about 27% of Brazil’s electorate and has long been a PT stronghold. Results here will shape national politics and influence policies on infrastructure, agribusiness, and social spending.

World.title: Colombia Gas Import Terminal Lands New Floating LNG Ship
World.content:
Colombia · Energy

Key Facts Early 2027 — Excelerate’s floating gas terminal, the Express, starts service in Colombia.

— Excelerate’s floating gas terminal, the Express, starts service in Colombia. Seven-year charter — Signed with a subsidiary of Frontera Energy.

— Signed with a subsidiary of Frontera Energy. Storage — The Express vessel holds about 150,900 cubic metres of gas.

— The Express vessel holds about 150,900 cubic metres of gas. Separate plan — Ecopetrol’s own Pacific coast terminal targets first gas in late 2026.

— Ecopetrol’s own Pacific coast terminal targets first gas in late 2026. US$172 million — Estimated cost of Ecopetrol’s Pacific project.

— Estimated cost of Ecopetrol’s Pacific project. The problem — Colombia’s older gas fields are running low, so it now needs imports.

A seven-year charter with Excelerate Energy brings the floating gas terminal Express to Colombia from early 2027, as the country scrambles to replace falling domestic output.

The Colombia gas import terminal is about to double its capacity, and that changes how the country powers itself. Excelerate Energy has signed a seven-year charter to bring its floating unit, the floating gas terminal Express, to Colombia from early 2027. The deal is with a subsidiary of Frontera Energy, and it is built for one purpose: covering a widening shortfall in domestic natural gas. If you live in Colombia, or you have money in Latin American energy, this means imports are no longer a stopgap. They are becoming a permanent feature of the market.

The FSRU Express has a storage capacity of 150,900 cubic metres, larger than the existing Cartagena regasification unit. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Why Colombia Now Needs Imports: Colombia gas import terminal

For decades, Colombia produced all the gas it needed. That era is ending fast.

Output from mature fields, especially in the Llanos and offshore Caribbean, has been declining year after year. The national pipeline system can move gas from production zones to cities like Bogotá and Medellín, but with less supply at the wellhead, the system is tightening.

Utilities and industrial buyers face the real risk of shortages, especially during dry seasons when hydro power flags and gas-fired plants must run harder. The response has been swift.

Colombia already operates one regasification terminal at Cartagena, and it recently returned to full service after maintenance. But one terminal is not enough.

The new Colombia gas import terminal project adds a second floating unit, and Ecopetrol is pushing a third on the Pacific coast. All of this is happening because the geology is no longer cooperating.

Reserves have fallen, and major exploration finds have not kept pace. Imports, once unthinkable, are now a strategic necessity.

The Excelerate and Frontera Deal

Excelerate Energy is a specialist in floating LNG regasification. The floating gas terminal Express is a converted vessel with a storage capacity of 150,900 cubic metres.

It will dock at a Colombian port and convert imported LNG back into gas for the grid. The vessel is currently under a charter elsewhere, and it will finish that job and go through a planned dry dock later in 2026.

After that, it sails to Colombia and begins commercial service in the first quarter of 2027. The charter runs for seven years.

The counterparty is a subsidiary of Frontera Energy, a Canadian company with extensive operations in Colombia. Frontera will use the terminal to bring in gas, either for its own operations or to sell into the market.

Excelerate’s Q2 2026 materials confirm the early 2027 start. The company is positioning the Colombia gas import terminal as a core part of its Latin American growth strategy.

Ecopetrol’s Separate Pacifico Push

Excelerate’s project is not the only game in town. Ecopetrol, the state-controlled oil company, is developing its own floating terminal at Buenaventura on the Pacific coast.

This is the Pacifico project, and it is moving on a faster track. Ecopetrol launched a public tender for LNG supply with deliveries expected in late 2026.

One source says the first cargo arrives in October or November, another says the second semester of 2026. Either way, this terminal comes first.

The Buenaventura infrastructure has an initial capacity of 60 GBTUDs, or 60 million cubic feet per day. It is scalable to 180 million cubic feet per day.

The total investment is estimated between US$150 million and US$172 million. Financing comes from the Financiera de Desarrollo Nacional and BTG Pactual, each contributing US$65 million, and the terminal is being built by PIO SAS under contract with Ecopetrol.

Why Colombia Needs Imports Now

Colombia used to produce all the natural gas it needed. But its older fields are running low, and big new discoveries offshore are still years from delivery.

A floating gas terminal is a shortcut. It is a special ship that receives super-cooled gas, warms it back into a usable fuel and feeds it into the pipeline network.

That lets a country add supply in a couple of years instead of the decade a land-based plant can take. It also avoids a large upfront building cost.

For households and factories, the goal is simple: keep gas flowing and prices steady. A shortfall would push up power bills and hurt industry.

Ecopetrol, the state oil company, is working on a separate import plan on the Pacific coast. Together the projects aim to plug the gap from more than one direction.

The seven-year charter also signals this is not a quick patch. Colombia expects to rely on imported gas for years.

What This Means for You

If you are an expat living in Bogotá or Medellín, gas shortages affect your daily life. They push up electricity prices and can force rationing.

With more import terminals online, the risk of blackouts and price spikes drops. For investors, the signal is clear.

Colombia is committing to LNG imports for the long haul. Seven-year charters and state-backed tenders create stable revenue streams.

The companies involved — Excelerate, Frontera, Ecopetrol — are betting billions on this transition. But there are risks.

Imported LNG is more expensive than domestic gas, and that cost gets passed to consumers. Colombia still needs to solve its exploration problem, or it will rely on imports for decades.

For now, the terminal race is on. The Pacific coast terminal, if it hits its 2026 target, will be the first new piece of infrastructure, and the Excelerate unit follows in 2027, reshaping how Colombia powers its economy.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will the Excelerate Colombia gas import terminal start operating? The floating gas terminal Express is expected to begin service in the first quarter of 2027. The vessel finishes its current charter and undergoes dry dock in 2026 before sailing to Colombia. How much will the new terminal cost consumers in Colombia? Specific tariff details are not yet public. Imported LNG is generally more expensive than domestic gas, so household and industrial bills are expected to rise as import volumes grow. Is Ecopetrol’s Buenaventura terminal the same as the Excelerate project? No. They are separate projects. Ecopetrol’s Pacifico terminal at Buenaventura targets late 2026, while Excelerate’s floating gas terminal Express arrives in early 2027. Both aim to cover the same shortfall. Why is Colombia importing gas if it has its own fields? Domestic production has declined as fields mature. New discoveries have not kept pace. Imports are now needed to bridge the gap, especially during dry seasons when gas-fired power plants run more.

The zinc producer reported net revenue of US$908 million for April to June 2026, with adjusted operating earnings of US$286 million and net income of US$98 million. Mining zinc output rose 8% year on year to 79,000 tonnes. That rebound is worth watching, because Nexa is the region’s largest integrated zinc producer, with assets in Peru and Brazil. For investors, the quarter points to firmer zinc prices, better operational stability, and a clearer picture of what Nexa can deliver in the second half.

What Drove the Quarter: Nexa second-quarter results

The revenue jump came from both higher volumes and stronger zinc prices. Nexa’s mining segment produced 79,000 tonnes of zinc in the quarter, up 8% from a year earlier.

That growth was led by the Aripuanã mine in Brazil, which treated 399,000 tonnes of ore and delivered 8,800 tonnes of zinc. The mine also contributed by-product credits from lead, copper, and precious metals, boosting overall profitability.

adjusted operating earnings of US$286 million implies a margin near 31.5%, a solid result for a base metals producer. The company credited better operational performance and cost control.

Net income of US$98 million marks a clear turnaround from the same period last year, when losses weighed on the stock. Revenue of US$908 million translates to about R$4.63 billion at the current exchange rate of US$1 = R$5.1073.

Nexa also benefited from a recovery in zinc prices on global markets. China’s resumption of industrial activity and tighter concentrate supplies supported prices during the quarter.

That helped offset higher energy costs in Peru and Brazil, which had squeezed margins in previous periods. The company managed to keep costs in check despite these pressures.

Aripuanã Keeps Shining

Aripuanã remains the growth engine. The underground mine in Mato Grosso state ramped up steadily during the quarter.

Its ore throughput of 399,000 tonnes shows consistent processing, with grades in line with guidance. This steady performance underscores the mine’s reliability.

The mine’s 8,800 tonnes of zinc in concentrate came with by-product credits from lead, copper, and precious metals. Those credits boost the overall margin, making Aripuanã one of Nexa’s most profitable sites.

Watch for further ramp-up in the second half, as the mine approaches nameplate capacity. That could add more tonnes and further improve unit economics.

Cerro Pasco Plans Change

In Peru, Nexa completed a review of its Cerro Pasco complex. The open-pit life at Atacocha has been extended, while the larger Phase II expansion moves to 2032.

That delays a major capital project, which frees up cash flow in the months ahead. The revised plan lowers near-term spending and aligns output with current market conditions.

The company said the revised plan lowers near-term spending. It also aligns output with current market conditions.

For investors, that means less dilution and a clearer path to free cash flow, though it trims long-term growth potential. The trade-off is a more conservative capital approach.

Why Nexa Matters in Latin America

Nexa is not just a miner; it is a key supplier of zinc to global markets. Its smelters in Peru and Brazil process concentrates into refined metal.

That makes it a critical link in the regional supply chain for construction, autos, and galvanised steel. Zinc is essential for protecting steel from corrosion, which is vital for durable infrastructure.

For anyone living in Latin America, zinc demand tracks infrastructure spending. Higher zinc prices also support mining jobs and tax revenue in Peru and Brazil.

A stronger Nexa means more export revenue and stability for local economies that depend on metal exports. This reinforces the company’s role as a pillar of the regional mining sector.

What Nexa Does

Nexa is one of Latin America’s larger zinc producers, with mines and smelters in Peru and Brazil. Zinc is the metal used to stop steel from rusting.

That ties Nexa’s fortunes to global building and factory demand. When construction picks up, so does the need for galvanized steel.

The company has spent heavily to bring its Aripuana mine in Brazil up to full speed. Getting that operation running smoothly has been a focus for management.

For investors, Nexa offers direct exposure to metals prices. Its shares tend to rise and fall with the zinc market.

Nexa also produces copper, lead and silver as by-products. That mix cushions the company when any single metal weakens.

The miner is listed in both New York and Sao Paulo. That gives foreign investors an easy way to buy in.

Looking Ahead

Nexa’s management sounded confident on the earnings call. They highlighted the margin surge and improved cash generation, part of the message of the Nexa second-quarter results.

But they also noted risks, including ore grade variability and energy costs. These factors could affect profitability if they worsen.

The key question is whether zinc prices hold. If China’s property sector stays weak, prices could slip.

A sustained downturn would pressure Nexa’s revenue.

Still, with Aripuanã ramping and Cerro Pasco costs under control, Nexa looks well placed for the rest of 2026. The company seems ready to capitalise on its operational strengths.

That implies an operating earnings margin of roughly 31.5%, a strong performance for a miner. It shows Nexa is running its operations efficiently, despite cost pressures in Peru and Brazil. How did the Cerro Pasco review affect Nexa’s plans? The review extended the open-pit life at the Atacocha mine and pushed the Phase II expansion to 2032. That delays a large capital project, preserving cash in the months ahead. It also reduces near-term growth but aligns spending with market conditions. World.title: Mexico Unveils First Step of Sheinbaum Anti-Corruption Decree
World.content:
Mexico · Politics

Key Facts Decree signed — Sheinbaum signed the transparency decree on 4 August 2026.

— Sheinbaum signed the transparency decree on 4 August 2026. No new body — This is not a new anti-corruption agency; it is a decree plus a promised package.

— This is not a new anti-corruption agency; it is a decree plus a promised package. Four areas — It expands disclosure in contracts, Pemex and CFE subsidiaries, audits, and state adoption.

— It expands disclosure in contracts, Pemex and CFE subsidiaries, audits, and state adoption. Secrecy limits — Exemptions are restricted mainly to national security and public interest cases.

— Exemptions are restricted mainly to national security and public interest cases. Partial versions — Even when withholding is allowed, partial public versions are preferred over full secrecy.

— Even when withholding is allowed, partial public versions are preferred over full secrecy. September bill — The full anti-corruption reform package goes to Congress in September 2026.

— The full anti-corruption reform package goes to Congress in September 2026. 30 day rule — Extra public-interest data must load into the transparency platform within 30 business days.

A transparency decree signed on 4 August tightens disclosure rules across the federal government. A broader reform package is promised for September, but no new agency exists yet.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum signed an anti-corruption decree on 4 August 2026, aiming to strip federal officials of their discretion over what they disclose. The Sheinbaum anti-corruption decree is the first step of a broader reform package she plans to send to Congress in September, meaning the fight against graft is far from finished.

Sheinbaum signs the transparency decree at the National Palace on 4 August 2026, with officials from the Federal Auditor’s Office present. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the Decree Actually Does: Sheinbaum anti-corruption decree

The decree is not a new anti-corruption agency. It strengthens transparency rules across federal government bodies, as reported by El País and Mexico News Daily.

Its core aim is to remove officials’ discretion over what information becomes public. Specific rules now dictate what must be published, ending the patchwork of selective disclosure.

Disclosure expands in four key areas: public contracts, Pemex and CFE subsidiaries, audits and fiscalisation, and an invitation for states, municipalities, and other public powers to adopt the same standard.

Secrecy exemptions are now limited mainly to national security and public interest cases. Even then, the preference is for partial public versions rather than full withholding.

This is a meaningful shift in how Mexico’s federal government handles information. But it does not replace the constitutional system or create a new watchdog.

One report notes the government wants to ’dismantle the current National Anti-Corruption System’ and rebuild coordination among investigative institutions. That is intent, not a completed legal change.

The decree will be incorporated into the General Transparency Law later, according to sources. That points to an upcoming legislative process, not a done deal.

Within 30 business days, additional public-interest data must be added to the transparency platform. That is a tight timeline for federal agencies to comply.

The September Package: Promises, Not Reality

The bigger reform package is expected to go to Congress in September 2026. Nothing has been submitted yet, and no text is publicly available.

Government officials describe it as a ’reengineering’ of the anti-corruption framework. That could mean merging institutions, but details remain unknown.

No approved 2026 law creating a new anti-corruption body is identified in any source. Anyone expecting a finished agency is jumping ahead.

The September bill will face a tough ride. Congress must debate constitutional changes, and opposition parties will demand transparency in the reform itself.

Sheinbaum has promised zero impunity and defended that policy publicly. Her July defence of anti-corruption efforts in Edomex shows this is a central priority.

But promises are not policy. Until the bill reaches Congress and passes, the current system remains intact, with all its flaws.

The decree is symbolic of intent, yet it has real, immediate effects on disclosure. That makes it a solid first step, not a final solution.

Why This Matters for You

If you live in Mexico or invest here, transparency in federal contracts means you can finally see where public money goes. That reduces risk of hidden costs or corrupt deals affecting your business.

For investors in Pemex or CFE, the new disclosure rules on subsidiaries will expose financial health and governance issues. This shifts how you assess risk in Mexican energy assets.

State and municipal adoption of these standards is voluntary for now. But if they follow, local procurement becomes more predictable for foreign firms looking to win contracts.

The September reform could reshape accountability bodies entirely. Watch for it — it may change how corruption cases are investigated and prosecuted across the country.

Why This Matters to Business

Corruption has long been near the top of the list of worries for companies working in Mexico. Bribery and red tape raise costs and scare off investment.

A decree is a rule the president can sign on her own. A full law needs Congress, so it is harder to pass but also harder to undo later.

That is why the promised September package matters more than the decree itself. Turning a pledge into law is the real test.

For foreign investors, clearer rules and more transparency are welcome. They make it easier to plan and to compete on a level field.

Mexico has cycled through anti-corruption promises before, with mixed results. Investors will watch whether this effort has teeth.

The signal Sheinbaum wants to send is that her government takes the issue seriously. Following through will matter more than the announcement.

Clear anti-graft rules can lower the everyday cost of doing business. Firms spend less time and money navigating opaque processes.

Timeline and What to Watch Next

On 4 August 2026, the decree was signed. Within 30 business days, the transparency platform must incorporate additional data, likely by mid-September.

In September, the government will submit the broader anti-corruption package to Congress. That is when the real fight begins.

The decree already tightens rules on contracts and audits. You can check the federal transparency portal now to see new data appearing.

Watch for congressional debates on the reform package. They will reveal whether the government intends to merge or abolish existing anti-corruption bodies.

No new agency or law exists yet. The only concrete change so far is the decree, with its expanded disclosure rules and limited secrecy exemptions.

Expect a lively autumn in Mexican politics. This reform is a cornerstone of Sheinbaum’s presidency, but its fate lies with Congress.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this a new anti-corruption agency? No. The 4 August decree strengthens transparency rules, but it does not create a new body. A broader reform package, which could include institutional changes, is only promised for September 2026. What does the decree change immediately? It removes officials’ discretion over disclosure, expands public information in four areas, and limits secrecy exemptions. Federal agencies must also add more public-interest data to the transparency platform within 30 business days. When will the full reform arrive? The government says it will send a broader anti-corruption package to Congress in September 2026. No bill text is public yet, so exact changes to the current system are unknown. How does this affect foreign investors? You gain more visibility into public contracts, audits, and Pemex or CFE subsidiaries. That reduces information asymmetry when assessing risk, though state and local adoption remains voluntary.

World.title: Chile Capital Market Reform: Tax Cut Aims to Revive Stocks
World.content:
Key Facts Tax cut — The 10% capital-gains tax on listed shares would be eliminated, with an effective date of January 1, 2027.

— The 10% capital-gains tax on listed shares would be eliminated, with an effective date of January 1, 2027. Congress timeline — The bill is expected in Congress by mid-September 2026, with approval targeted for December.

— The bill is expected in Congress by mid-September 2026, with approval targeted for December. Broader scope — The reform may also remove taxes on bonds, funds, and derivatives, plus internationalise the peso.

— The reform may also remove taxes on bonds, funds, and derivatives, plus internationalise the peso. Market boost — Analysts see the package as bullish for Chilean equities, improving policy certainty and reducing burdens.

— Analysts see the package as bullish for Chilean equities, improving policy certainty and reducing burdens. Peso depth — Measures aim to ease foreign participation and develop the local debt market.

— Measures aim to ease foreign participation and develop the local debt market. Separate reforms — The capital-market bill is distinct from the pension reform, which has its own 2026 milestones.

— The capital-market bill is distinct from the pension reform, which has its own 2026 milestones. Potential inflows — One estimate suggests the reform could channel about US$400 million monthly into local markets.

Chile · Markets

The government plans to scrap the 10% capital-gains tax on listed shares and simplify rules, targeting deeper markets and more investor inflows by 2027.

Chile capital market reform is set to give local stocks a serious lift. The government plans to scrap the 10% capital-gains tax on listed shares, aiming to deepen the market and pull in more money from both local and foreign investors.

Chile Capital Market Reform: Tax Cut Aims to Revive Stocks. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the Reform Changes: Chile capital market reform

The headline change is eliminating the 10% capital-gains tax on shares with stock-exchange presence. One source, citing Garrigues and KPMG, says the effective date is January 1, 2027.

The package goes further. Reports say the government is considering removing capital-gains taxes on bonds, funds, and derivatives too, which would make a wider range of investments more attractive.

Regulation would also get simpler. Creating funds, issuing bonds, and registering securities would involve less red tape, according to a T13 report.

The reform aims to internationalise the Chilean peso, making it easier for foreign investors to participate. It also targets deeper debt-market development, with more transparency and stronger repo-market infrastructure.

These changes could make Chile more competitive as a regional financial hub. They build on the country’s stable institutions and open economy, which already attract global investors.

The goal is to boost market liquidity and financing options for local companies. A deeper market can support more startups and expansions, adding jobs over time.

The government’s plan also includes better electronic trading systems and faster settlement. These upgrades could reduce costs and improve efficiency for everyone involved.

There are talks of easing restrictions on foreign institutional investors. That move could unlock more capital from pension funds and sovereign wealth funds abroad.

Why It Matters for Investors

For anyone living in or invested in Latin America, this is a big deal. Chile has long been a regional safe haven, but its equity market has struggled with low depth and limited financing capacity.

Scrapping the capital-gains tax removes a direct drag on returns. It also signals policy certainty, which tends to boost valuations and attract fresh capital.

One estimate from El Mostrador suggests the reform could channel about 12 million UF per month, or roughly US$400 million, into local markets. That is an analyst projection, not an official government figure.

JP Morgan has already called the broader economic overhaul a positive catalyst for local stocks. Expect the reform to amplify that effect, especially for listed companies with strong domestic exposure.

The removal of taxes on bonds could also make fixed income more appealing. That might draw in yield-seeking investors who were previously put off by taxes.

A more internationalised peso could reduce exchange-rate volatility. That stability helps planners and investors who need predictable cash flows.

With fewer taxes, companies may find it easier to raise capital through public offerings. That could lead to more listings and a richer mix of investment choices.

Investors should also watch for ripple effects on the corporate bond market. Lower taxes could make such bonds more attractive, giving firms another funding route.

What Still Needs to Happen

The bill is not law yet. The government aims to submit it in the first half of September 2026, with congressional dispatch by December.

That is a tight timeline. Congress has already been busy with other reforms, including the pension overhaul, which has its own September milestones like the PGU increase and employer contributions.

The capital-market bill is separate from those pension changes. Mixing them up would be a mistake, as they address different parts of the economy.

If the December target slips, the January 1, 2027 effective date for the tax cut could also move. Watch for exact language in the bill when it lands.

The bill’s details will spell out which securities are covered and any conditions. Analysts will be parsing that text for surprises.

The government may also need to secure cross-party support. A divided Congress could slow progress, but the reform has broad backing from financial groups.

There is also the question of how the tax cut will affect public revenue. The government expects the market boost to offset any short-term loss.

Legal challenges could arise from affected parties, but that is common with major tax overhauls. Still, the idea is to keep the timeline on track through careful drafting.

How to Position Your Portfolio

You might consider adding Chilean equities before the reform passes. The tax cut alone makes listed shares more valuable to both local and foreign investors.

Bonds and funds could also benefit if the tax removal extends to them. The peso’s internationalisation could boost currency stability, which helps all local assets.

Be selective though. Not all companies will benefit equally.

Look for firms with strong earnings, good governance, and exposure to domestic growth. Also, keep an eye on the exact scope of the bill.

If derivatives are included, that opens up hedging opportunities with lower costs.

A deeper market might also mean more initial public offerings. Early investors in well-run companies could see substantial gains.

Diversify across sectors to spread risk. The reform’s impact will vary, so a balanced approach is wise.

Consider consulting a financial adviser who knows Latin American markets. They can help you tailor these ideas to your own risk tolerance and goals.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does the capital gains tax cut take effect? The 10% capital-gains tax on listed shares would end on January 1, 2027. That’s if Congress passes the bill by December 2026 as planned. The government targets submission to Congress in early September 2026. Will the reform affect foreign investors in Chile? Yes. The bill aims to make it easier for foreign investors to participate, partly by internationalising the Chilean peso. Removing capital-gains taxes on shares and other securities could lower your cost of investing in Chilean markets. Is this the same as the pension reform? No. The pension reform has its own rules and timeline, including employer contributions starting in September 2026. This capital market reform is a separate bill focused on taxes and market infrastructure, with a January 1, 2027 tax target. What could delay the reform? Congress has a busy schedule. The December target for passage could slip if debates drag on or if other reforms take priority. If the bill is delayed, the effective date for the tax cut might move too. Watch for official announcements on progress.

World.title: BHP Bets Big on Chile Copper: US$14.7bn Plan
World.content:
Chile · Mining

Key Facts Investment scale — BHP plans US$10.7bn to US$14.7bn in Chile, its largest cycle ever.

— BHP plans US$10.7bn to US$14.7bn in Chile, its largest cycle ever. Main targets — Funds will go to Escondida, Spence, and Cerro Colorado operations.

— Funds will go to Escondida, Spence, and Cerro Colorado operations. Escondida focus — US$7.3bn to US$9.8bn earmarked, including a new concentrator.

— US$7.3bn to US$9.8bn earmarked, including a new concentrator. First approval — Environmental permit secured for early works in July 2026.

— Environmental permit secured for early works in July 2026. Spence projects — Two growth projects sanctioned in June 2026.

— Two growth projects sanctioned in June 2026. Timeline — Spending spreads over a decade, with output stabilising through the 2030s.

— Spending spreads over a decade, with output stabilising through the 2030s. Jobs impact — Cerro Colorado restart could bring up to 3,433 construction workers.

The mining giant is pouring up to US$14.7 billion into its Chilean copper operations. Here is what it means for global supply and your portfolio.

BHP Chile copper investment is the company’s biggest ever in the country, with US$10.7bn to US$14.7bn pledged over about ten years. The money goes to Escondida, Spence, and Cerro Colorado, tied to BHP’s July 2026 update on growth in Chile. For foreign investors, this signals that copper supply from Chile, the world’s top producer, will stay strong. But it also shows rising costs and technical challenges in a country that makes about a quarter of the world’s copper.

Aerial view of the Escondida mine in Chile’s Atacama Desert, where BHP will build a new US$4.4bn to US$5.9bn concentrator. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)
