What happens when Bob Marley, Toots Hibbert, Jimmy Cliff, Peter Tosh, Bunny Wailer, Burning Spear, Marcia Griffiths, Dennis Brown, U-Roy, Gregory Isaacs, Shabba Ranks, Ini Kamoze, Eek-A-Mouse, and others are placed beside the existing recipients?

If the qualifications are sound, they should help us understand the hierarchy. If they cannot, perhaps the problem is not the artistes. Perhaps the problem is the criteria.

That is where Part II begins.

Tomorrow: Jamaica’s Reggae Icon Award – when the same test is applied to the giants

World.title: Two spectacular weeks of agricultural immersion at Tuskegee for Jamaican high school students
World.content:
Cornwall College students (from left) D’Andre Granston, Jeremiah Bent and Samijana Gardner who participated in the Tuskegee summer programme.

TWELVE students and three teachers from a collection of Jamaican high schools were blown away by their recent immersion in agriculture, as part of the Tuskegee University Agri-Trek Summer Programme in Alabama, United States.

The schools included Cornwall College, Maldon High, Knockalva High, Herbert Morrison Technical High, Montego Bay High and Cambridge High, all from St James.

They spent two weeks receiving hands-on learning across agriculture and education, during which they were given a chance to experience the rich history and culture of Tuskegee University and the surrounding Tuskegee area.

The students were effusive in their reflections on the experience which, they all concluded, had positioned them for greater things that would provide them with valuable educational, cultural, and personal development opportunities, bound to redound to the benefit of Jamaica.

In their joint report on the trip, Cornwall’s Jeremiah Bent, Samijani Gardener and D’Andre Granston, and Maldon High’s Deontae Forrester, and Dave Brown described the Tuskegee University Agri-Trek Summer Programme as “an unforgettable experience”, meeting with the 140 participants, Jamaica being the only other country outside the United States.

Through mentors in different fields the students participated in research activities, laboratory exercises, discussions, and poster presentations that helped develop teamwork, communication, and critical thinking skills.

“We learned how technology can be used to collect, analyse, and display geographical information. Others explored biotechnology and learned how scientists can extract DNA from one plant and transfer it to another.

“Students involved in veterinary science learned practical skills such as measuring goat weight, determining body condition scores, and conducting FAMACHA scoring to assess animal health,” read the joint report.

FAMACHA is a method used to assess anaemia risk in livestock by examining the colour of an animal’s eyelid against a five-point scale.

One of the most rewarding aspects of the programme was interacting with students from the various states across the USA, they noted, adding that they proudly shared aspects of Jamaican culture and taught the Americans some Jamaican expressions.

They visited a canine detector facility where they learned how specially trained dogs assist in protecting agriculture by detecting prohibited agricultural products.

The report continued: “We also toured the Atlanta International Airport Plant Inspection Station where we learned about inspections, invasive pests, plant diseases, and regulations that protect the agricultural sector from harmful organisms entering the country.

“One of Jamaica’s main sources of income is within the agricultural field. The inspections and regulations that we have learned can help to better protect our agricultural integrity from invasive pests and diseases from foreign countries.

“Another memorable experience was the trolley tour of Tuskegee University’s historic 5,000-acre campus. We visited museums and learned about the rich history of the university; its founders; and its contribution to agriculture, education, and scientific advancement.”

Maldon High’s science teacher Glenviel Wynn said walking the Tuskegee campus was inspiring as the university’s legacy as a centre for African American education, innovation, and leadership under Booker T Washington is still very present.

“The Tuskegee area itself reflected that same spirit — a strong sense of community, agricultural heritage, and commitment to service. That history reminded me that agriculture and education are not just about production, but about empowering people.

“One of the most impactful parts of the visit was observing Tuskegee’s approach to pedagogy. Lessons were not confined to lectures. Instructors used experiential learning — students learned by doing, troubleshooting, and reflecting.

“This showed me that effective agricultural education must connect theory to practice. I plan to apply this by structuring future lessons with more field-based activities, group problem-solving, and reflection sessions so learners can take ownership of the process.

“The exposure to vertical hydroponic farming showed me how space and water can be used more efficiently. Seeing crops growing in controlled environments without soil made climate-smart agriculture tangible.

“This is especially relevant given the increasing unpredictability of weather here in Jamaica… I now see vertical farming as a viable way to produce vegetables year round, reduce water use, and involve youth in agriculture,” said Wynn.

The experience took them to Auburn University’s aquaculture unit where their small-scale fish production and water-quality management helped students to understand the link between fish, water, and plant systems through integrated approaches.

Wynn said it gave him ideas for diversified, resource-efficient enterprises and improving the system at Maldon High School.

Even at a small scale, aquaculture can improve household nutrition, place less stress on natural aquatic systems, and provide additional income, he noted.

The students were thankful to the Maldon and Cornwall alumni, the Sweet Water Foundation, and the Tuskegee University “for the knowledge, mentorship, hospitality, and the chance to connect with such a powerful legacy”.

World.title: Lionel Messi bids farewell to father who guided his glittering career
World.content:
Argentina's football star Lionel Messi (second left), his wife Antonela Roccuzzo (third right), and relatives, attend the funeral of his father, Jorge Messi, at El Prado cemetery, on the outskirts of Rosario, Santa Fe province, Argentina, on August 9, 2026. Jorge Messi, the father and agent of Lionel Messi, has died aged 68, the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner's childhood club Newell's Old Boys announced on August 8, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

ROSARIO, Argentina (AFP) — Argentina football icon Lionel Messi bid farewell Sunday to his father Jorge, the global star’s emotional anchor and agent since childhood who passed away following a battle with cancer aged 68.

The eight-time Ballon d’Or winner touched down on a private flight from Miami late on Saturday with his wife Antonela Roccuzzo and their children.

A private ceremony with close family and a few Argentina teammates took place at a cemetery in the town of Perez, adjacent to Rosario, later Sunday.

The gates of the town’s El Prado cemetery displayed handwritten messages from fans — “Stay strong, Leo, we love you” and “Stay strong, Messi family” — alongside a large floral wreath.

Messi’s teammates rallied around their captain following the announcement that Jorge Messi had passed away late Friday at a clinic in Rosario.

“It will surely do him good for us to be there,” Boca Juniors midfielder Leandro Paredes told journalists after his team’s match on Saturday.

“I need to speak with a few of my teammates to see if we go now or sometime tomorrow.”

According to media reports midfielder Rodrigo de Paul — a close friend of Messi and his Inter Miami teammate — travelled to Argentina.

After scoring a goal in a 2-1 defeat to Monterrey in Miami on Saturday, De Paul paid tribute by taking off his shirt to reveal Messi’s number 10 jersey.

There was a handful of fans outside the cemetery, including 15-year-old Lucas Blanco, who hung a sign reading “Stay strong, Messi” on the gate.

“He has brought so much joy to this country, now it’s our turn to give a little back and offer him some comfort,” he said.

“We drove 700 kilometres to be here. We wanted to stand by Leo during this time,” said Carlos and Ana, a couple who travelled from Tres Arroyos, a town south of Buenos Aires.

The cause of death was not disclosed, but local media reported that Jorge Messi had been suffering from cancer.

His unusual absence from the World Cup in June had already attracted attention.

Messi’s family asked the media for “humanity” during the tournament amid persistent rumours over Jorge’s health.

After bursting into tears after scoring against Algeria, 39-year-old Messi had admitted to dealing with “a situation outside of sports”.

“I went through a few difficult, complicated days,” he later acknowledged. “But I am grateful to the entire delegation and my teammates, because they stood by me, as always.”

Immediately after the World Cup final defeat against Spain, Messi returned to spend a few days with his family in Rosario.

– Humble beginnings –

A guiding figure throughout his son’s career, Jorge Messi was his first coach who left everything behind to accompany his son to Spain.

A metalworker in Rosario, 340 km north of Buenos Aires, Jorge managed youth teams at the small local club Grandoli.

He was the one who introduced Argentina’s future captain to the game aged four on vacant lots where local kids played.

His life changed course in 2000 when Barcelona invited the young prodigy, then aged 13, to Catalonia to continue treatment for a growth hormone deficiency while playing for the club’s youth teams.

Jorge left behind his job in Argentina, his wife, and his three other children to settle in Spain with Lionel.

“When we arrived in Barcelona, I used to lock myself in my room to cry alone, and my father did the same — either without me seeing him or thinking I didn’t see him. We pretended we were both fine, but we were struggling,” Messi later said.

His father was later the agent who negotiated contracts on his behalf, from Barcelona to Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami.

Messages of sympathy have poured in since Saturday from the football world, including from the clubs Messi played for and the Spanish Football Federation.

The Argentine Football Association (AFA) ordered a minute’s silence before matches and that black armbands be worn at games across all age groups for the week.

World.title: Bravery born of pain
World.content:
HIGGINS...I will do whatever I can to protect the kids of our society

FUELLED by her own childhood experiences with sexual assault and incidents of incest that she’d witnessed, Susan Higgins helped track down Troy Ellis, the man accused of the rape and murder of eight-year-old Talia Thompson in Discovery Bay, St Ann, in 2023.

Just shy of three years later, her actions have earned her national recognition. Higgins is among four Jamaicans slated to receive the Badge of Honour for Gallantry at this year’s national honours and awards ceremony scheduled for October.

Ellis, while receiving treatment at hospital under police guard following Talia’s death in September 2023, reportedly escaped. But Higgins later encountered him on the road and played a key role in getting him back into police custody.

For the 50-year-old, the national recognition is deeply personal.

“I feel happy and blessed to know that I can be a help to the helpless and a voice of the voiceless,” she told the

Jamaica Observer.

“When I opened the paper [last Thursday] and I saw Susan Higgins, mi dear! It was 140 people and fi mi name in there, me seh! No man, me feel good,” she added, erupting in laughter.

Talia was allegedly raped and murdered on September 23, 2023. Ellis, who was reportedly known to the family, was subsequently taken to hospital after allegedly injuring himself.

When Higgins heard that he had escaped from police custody, she said she immediately felt a sense of urgency to do something.

She said she was on her way home and her daughter was with her. When they got to the vicinity of the Firearm Licensing Authority office in Discovery Bay, she noticed a man attempting to conceal his face when the motor vehicle headlights illuminated him.

She said she immediately became suspicious and asked the driver to turn the vehicle around.

When they approached the man, Higgins said she began questioning him about his injury, deliberately remaining calm and acting as though she was simply curious about why he was on the road so late. She recalled Ellis telling her that he had recently been discharged from hospital.

Higgins said she continued to speak with him through the window of the vehicle while it drove slowly beside him, at the same time her daughter was conducting a quick online search. The search, she said, confirmed that the man she was speaking to matched the description of the escapee.

“I told him to pull up his shirt to let me see his wound. I was just playing slick because I wanted to see if he had a gun on him. When I saw that he didn’t have a gun, I asked him where he was going, and he said ‘Portland Road’,” she recalled.

“I said, ‘Do you need a ride?’ And he said, ‘Yes,’ not knowing it was the police me a carry him to. I said, ‘All right, when you reach your destination you tell me.’ During the ride, he was talking so intelligently to me. He didn’t show any sign of [being of] unsound mind, so I talked to him and talked to him until he said, ‘Me a come off here so.’ When he said that, me dumb, deaf, and blind, and stopped talking. I took him straight to Discovery Bay police,” said Higgins.

When they arrived, Higgins said the station’s door was closed, so she instructed her daughter to knock.

A cop came outside and Higgins said the driver immediately announced that they had found the man wanted in connection with Talia’s death. At that point, Higgins said Ellis became aware that he had been identified and attempted to resist.

She said she struggled to restrain him before eventually getting him into the police station, after which his identity was confirmed and he was returned to police custody.

For Higgins, the decision to intervene was not about recognition or praise, it was about doing what she would hope someone else would do if her child was in danger.

“Too many times children are being murdered, raped, left abandoned. As a woman, I didn’t get the love and the care of a parent. I actually grew up in the wild because my parents gave me away to a family, and [a man] attempted to rape me. It made me so aggressive, and I said if anybody ever do this to any pickney, if me catch them, me a go unalive them, but I did my best that night to not do what I wanted to because my little daughter was there and I couldn’t bear to do it,” she told the Sunday Observer.

“So many kids get raped and murdered, and so many of these cases go unanswered. I said, I am going to stand up and be a voice for the voiceless and a help for the helpless,” said Higgins.

“I will do whatever I can to protect the kids of our society,” she said. “I didn’t know the parents or the grandparents of that child, but I feel elated that I can help a mother to get some form of justice,” said Higgins.

“As I go along, I will always try to help somebody. My living will not be in vain,” she declared.

World.title: EU conservative chief demands migrant return hubs in Africa
World.content:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and her right-wing government are among the harshest critics, with Rome introducing border controls for travelers from Spain on Friday and sparking retaliation from Madrid.

Weber echoed proposals made last week by EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner, arguing that countries outside the bloc could be offered closer trade ties, economic collaboration and legal migration opportunities in exchange for accepting the installation of return hubs.

“Migrants who have no right to remain must leave Europe — no ifs, ands or buts!” he wrote, adding that returns must no longer depend on the political will of individual member countries.

Weber also rejected internal border controls within Europe as a long-term solution. “They may be necessary in exceptional situations. But they do not address the root cause of the problem … There can therefore be only one answer: strong, joint European protection of the external border.”

In early June, the European Parliament and European Council announced new EU rules on migrant returns, including removals to countries outside the bloc in return hubs.

Weber also argued that the Ceuta crisis, which left around 100 dead, was the result of unilateral national action and said that the Spanish government’s “political signals” have had “an immediate impact on migration routes.”

World.title: Why Poland’s right-wing split may not save Donald Tusk
World.content:
However, the departure of former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki from PiS complicates the balance of balance of power on the right.

PiS, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, formally ruptured last month, when Morawiecki stormed out, taking 40 MPs with him to form the new Development Plus party, leaving PiS with 147 deputies.

The split between him and party founder and leader Jarosław Kaczyński quickly became acrimonious.

Morawiecki criticized his own government’s decisions on Covid-19 restrictions and its push to tighten Poland’s abortion law, which outraged many women and saw PiS take a long-term hit in public support.

“Although I oppose abortion, I believed the change would lead to catastrophe — a polling collapse. Unfortunately, I was right,” Morawiecki said on the popular YouTube show Rymanowski Live this week.

He is now trying to set up a more moderate center-right party focused on economic growth which is less partisan than PiS. “Today, Poland does not need to get bogged down in ideological disputes,” he said in Monday’s interview. However, he has ruled out ever working with Tusk in the future.

World.title: A new rival is forcing Italy’s Meloni back to her far-right roots
World.content:
While France and other countries tightened border checks, Italy went further and announced it had suspended the EU’s free-movement Schengen agreement with Madrid. Now, in Italian airports, passengers from Spain are asked to join a different line.

Meloni’s office has made clear it has no intention of lifting the controls until at least Aug. 15, escalating the clash with Spain, which retaliated by imposing checks on travelers from Italy.

“We will not back down one millimeter on illegal immigration,” Meloni posted on X while her allies attacked the socialist Spanish government, accusing it of failing to manage migration flows. “Defending our borders, stopping human traffickers, and ensuring effective repatriation will continue to be this government’s policy,” she added.

The clash with Spain is just the latest sign that the Italian leader is doing all she can to secure her core, hard-right electorate in the face of a challenge from the right by Roberto Vannacci, a former general and member of the European Parliament.

With an election expected as early as next spring, Vannacci’s far-right National Future party has been advancing in the polls, overtaking one of Meloni’s coalition partners, the far-right League party, and gaining on another, Forza Italia, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.

For Meloni, who began her political career in the youth wing of Italy’s post-fascist movement, the challenge strikes particularly close to home.

World.title: Israel rejects Trump’s peace plan for Gaza
World.content:
Hamas has said that it would begin disarming, but in recent days an Israeli official said the country still had “serious security concerns.”

The rejection is a blow to peace negotiations the Trump administratoin has been brokering since September. The U.S. president had described the plan, now rejected by Israel, as a “critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government” and giving Israel “the security it deserves.”

Israel appears unlikely to pull back significant forces or make other concessions ahead of legislative elections scheduled for October. Netanyahu faces a tough reelection battle, with his far-right coalition partners urging him to keep up the pressure on Hamas and leave forces in Gaza. Opponents also accuse him of failing to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack when Hamas-led militants attacked Israeli communities, killing about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and taking 251 others hostage. Israel responded with a punishing military offensive that has killed more than 73,000 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.

Netanyahu said on Sunday that he is now in discussions with U.S. officials about how to move forward. “They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us, and we know how to stand up to these things,” he said.

World.title: Russia and Ukraine exchange overnight strikes, WHO confirms warehouse destroyed
World.content:
Another overnight strike on the Zhytomyr region injured three people, Ukrainian emergency services said.

Meanwhile, five people died in a Ukrainian overnight drone attack on the Russian city of Belgorod, the regional crisis centre said on Sunday. Acting governor Alexander Shuvayev said earlier on Sunday that three people were killed and 25 others injured in the “massive terrorist drone attack” by Kyiv. The death toll later rose to five.

Zelenskyy condemned what he described as “ballistic terror” attacks on Odesa, Kharkiv, Pavlohrad, and other regions. “Every such attack on human life serves as a constant reminder – we need more pressure, more sanctions against Russia, and more air defense for Ukraine,” he said.

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director-general of the World Health Organization, said on Sunday that a WHO warehouse in Dnipro in Ukraine was destroyed by a strike on Friday.

The warehouse held humanitarian supplies for frontline health facilities. No casualties were reported, as a WHO staff member and drivers managed to evacuate 130 of approximately 300 pallets and left the area before the attack.

“I cannot say loudly enough: attacks on health care MUST STOP. Otherwise, people are deprived of lifesaving healthcare,” Tedros said.

World.title: Germany battling ‘daily’ hybrid warfare attacks, minister warns
World.content:
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt speaks to the media during a news conference at Leipzig airport on Aug. 5, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images

Last week’s drone incident in Lepizig just the latest example.

Germany is being hit by hybrid warfare attacks from foreign powers on a “daily” basis, the country’s interior minister has warned, after a drone packed with explosives was found at Leipzig Airport earlier this week.

Espionage, sabotage, cyber attacks and covert actions “with the aim of destabilizing Germany or directly harming it” are a “constant reality,” German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told BILD in an interview on Sunday.

Dobrindt suggested on Thursday that a drone incident at Leipzig Airport may have been an attack by a state actor. The minister has stopped short of specifying which foreign powers are behind the hybrid attacks.

World.title: Six Colombian rebels killed in 'message' by President Abelardo de la Espriella's new government
World.content:
Days after Colombia's newly elected President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in, and who had vowed a battle against crime as a major part of his campaign, the leader announced the killings of six members of armed groups by Colombian forces on Sunday.

 

The far-right leader promised a fight against criminal groups that were profiting from drug trafficking as the country experiences its worst wave of violence in the past decade.

In a statement, the far-right leader said the operation was intended to send a clear and forceful message to all criminals in Colombia.

"There is nowhere for them to hide when the State is determined to act. I have given specific instructions to law enforcement agencies to carry out all necessary operations that were held back by the previous administration (of Gustavo Petro)," said De la Espriella.

Sunday's military operations marked the new administration's first actions against illegal groups, which campaigned on a pledge to confront "narcoterrorism without truce".

In a show of force, President Abelardo de la Espriella's swearing-in ceremony was held in the southwestern city of Cali, which is known for its high violence and crime rates.

De la Espriella wants to build mega-prisons similar to the one in El Salvador and increase airstrikes against guerrillas and narco traffickers.

The six killed by Colombian forces on Sunday include four members of a splinter faction of the former FARC guerrilla group, as well as two members of the Gulf Clan, Colombia's main drug cartel, in Antioquia department in the northwest.

Meanwhile, on Saturday, De la Espriella's first day in office was marred by two separate bombings, leaving at least one police officer dead and wounding several people. FARC guerrilla members used explosives to destroy a highway tollbooth near Cali, with two security guards suffering minor injuries, according to Colombia's army.

World.title: Revealed: The best European countries for digital nomads in 2026
World.content:
In 2026, your office could well be wherever your laptop happens to be.

 

A new ranking has revealed the best European countries for digital nomads in 2026, weighing up everything from rent and groceries to Wi-Fi speeds, coworking spaces, safety and visa rules.

LEI register, a global database system, looked closely at 40 countries across the continent using 19 distinct metrics to determine the best location for remote workers.

English proficiency, healthcare and local events were also examined to rank these nations – and Estonia came out on top.

The best European countries for digital nomads

One of three Baltic states, Estonia scooped the first place spot, thanks to affordable living costs, solid infrastructure, and a digital nomad-friendly attitude.

A one-bedroom apartment in an Estonian city centre comes in at an average of €573 per month, while groceries for a month will set residents back around €247.80.

Internet speeds are decent, safety is the highest across all countries, and digital nomad visas last a year and cost €85.

Next in the ranking is Iceland. Despite the fact it’s one of the most expensive destinations – monthly rent is an average of a steep €2,098, while groceries cost €541.62 – it ticks numerous boxes.

It has the highest internet speed of any country, as well as the most coworking spaces and Airbnb availability. It was also found to be very safe and plays host to countless events.

In third place is Portugal, a long-time favourite with digital nomads thanks to its excellent internet speeds, high English proficiency and the availability of visas.

While a one-year digital nomad visa costs €80, rent in the city centre is relatively high, at an average of €919 per month. Nevertheless, the country is so well set up for remote workers when it comes to infrastructure that it remains a favourite choice for many.

Montenegro is fourth in the ranking, in part because it has an extremely affordable visa fee, at just €26 and the visa lasts for up to 730 days – the longest period of all nations included in the study.

Rent here averages €576, while groceries cost around €211.22 every month. It does fall down on healthcare, but Airbnb availability is second on the list, meaning it’s ideal for digital nomads on a modest budget.

Rounding out the top five is Croatia, which offers the second-longest visa period at 540 days.

It also has the third-highest safety rating, as well as the fourth-highest Airbnb availability per capita. City centre rental properties go for an average of €663, and monthly groceries come in at €232.46. While English proficiency here is high and there are plenty of events, internet speeds leave a lot to be desired and are the slowest on the list.

Completing the top ten are Slovenia, Czechia, Spain, Lithuania and Romania. All offer pluses and minuses depending on what a particular digital nomad is hunting for, but all make reliable choices if you’re unsure where to start.

The worst choices in Europe for digital nomads

At the other end of the scale, there are five nations which some digital nomads may wish to avoid, according to the ranking.

Ireland came in dead last, despite the fact it placed fourth for English proficiency, and also has solid offerings in events and coworking spaces.

It falls down in high rent and less than ideal safety and healthcare rankings. Most importantly, though, is its lack of a digital nomad visa, which means it’s not easy to make Ireland your base.

Switzerland is in second-to-last place and it also has no digital nomad visa available. It also has high grocery costs and rent is an average of €1,785, but fast internet, safety levels and high availability of coworking spaces go in its favour.

Following hot on Switzerland’s heels are Belarus and Bosnia and Herzegovina. While they’re both significantly more affordable than the central European nation, neither offers a digital nomad visa.

Belarus is particularly poor when it comes to internet speed and coworking spaces, and while Bosnia and Herzegovina isn’t too pricey, it also offers some of the weakest infrastructure on the list.

Also – perhaps surprisingly – in the bottom five is France. While it remains the most visited country globally by tourists, it’s not an ideal choice for digital nomads.

While it has excellent healthcare and internet speeds, it doesn’t offer a visa for workers, English proficiency is low and its safety index is the absolute worst in the ranking.

World.title: Vintage computer collecting grows as the AI boom reshapes tech
World.content:
Software engineer Josh Dersch estimates he owns more than 200 vintage computers and devices in his Seattle home — part of a growing collector trend that has also spread to Europe.

 

“It’s always been fascinating to me to see the origins of things,” Dersch said. “It’s a fun challenge to debug and repair. You can understand the entire system from top to bottom.”

Dersch is part of a growing community of vintage computer collectors who are preserving the classic machines that helped launch the digital revolution. While Silicon Valley has since moved on to shaping the future of artificial intelligence, these hardware enthusiasts are intent on saving the Atari, Commodore and IBM machines that are ancestors to today’s laptops, wearable devices and smartphones.

Where others see junk, people like Dersch see artifacts of computer history that are worthy of attention and respect. They delight in hearing the beeps and chimes of their childhood and firing up a low-def game of “Pong” or “Space Invaders.”

“The enthusiasm for the history of computers and all the stuff around it is growing,” said Erik Klein, president of the Vintage Computer Federation, which organises an annual festival at the Computer History Museum in Mountain View in the heart of Silicon Valley.

Vintage computer festivals bring collectors together

This year more than 3,500 people attended the two-day Vintage Computer Festival in early August that celebrated the 50th anniversary of Apple, founded in 1976 in nearby Cupertino, Calif. It featured a panel with co-founders Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne reminiscing about the company’s early days as a scrappy start-up led by the late Steve Jobs.

More than a dozen such gatherings have since sprung up in cities across North America, South America and Europe.

Growing interest is reflected in more demand for vintage computers in online marketplaces, Klein said. Rare, iconic computers like the Apple-1 — the company’s first product — can fetch hundreds of thousands of euros.

Collectors exhibited the computer systems that they have painstakingly restored to their original working condition, allowing attendees to play with the computers built long before the internet, social media and AI transformed the world.

Restoring the ‘grandfather of the modern computer’

Dersch drove down from Seattle to showcase the pride of his collection: the Xerox Alto. He spent years restoring what's considered “the grandfather of the modern computer,” which was developed at the pioneering Xerox Palo Alto Research Center in the 1970s.

The Alto was one of the earliest computers to move beyond text on screen and use the mouse and graphical user interface — such as windows, icons and cursors — that became the industry standard. The model famously inspired Jobs and Bill Gates to incorporate the technologies in their early products.

Klein, a Silicon Valley software engineering manager, was a passionate collector until his hobby overwhelmed his home and family life. He had as many as 150 computer systems — complete with accessories, documents and packaging — crammed into his wardrobes and garage.

He said his beloved collection had become an “albatross” and he worried about burdening his family. So he started selling and giving away his machines until he only had a few favourites left at home.

Similar events for collectors spread to Europe

Now Klein channels his passion for vintage computers into organising festivals, repair workshops, swap meets and other events as president of the Vintage Computer Federation.

“So it’s really about evangelising that history and evangelising this hobby of maintaining, collecting and enjoying this vintage technology,” Klein said.

Sellam Ismail is thrilled to see the collector community develop and mature since he organised the first festival in 1997, drawing about 150 hobbyists to a venue east of San Francisco. He ran the events for a decade.

He later co-founded the Vintage Computer Federation, which runs festivals in the US and Canada. He’s helped other groups launch similar festivals in Argentina, Germany and Switzerland.

“The community grew up. More and more people started getting old computers, started collecting them,” said Ismail, who once had a massive collection he stored in a warehouse. “Next year is the 30th anniversary. And I expect this to continue and grow even bigger.”

World.title: MySpace comeback? Owners drop a major hint and here's what we know
World.content:
MySpace, once the most popular social media platform in the world in the mid-2000s, could be returning soon. It comes as many social media users are returning to nostalgic, analog experiences, instead of algorithm-driven ones.

 

The current owners of the platform, Tim and Chris Vanderhook, who also founded Viant Technology, hinted at the potential relaunch in a documentary titled “MySpace”.

“We still own MySpace. We are stewards of the MySpace brand at this point and we are going to relaunch MySpace. We’re just waiting for the right time to do it. And if that one doesn’t work, we’ll do it again,” said the Vanderhook brothers in the documentary.

The platform was founded in 2003 by Tom Anderson and Chris DeWolfe, leading to the iconic “Tom from MySpace” profile, which was every new user’s first friend.

Related Meta launches Muse Code tool amid AI hacking revelations

This potential relaunch follows a previous failed attempt back in 2013, as the company tried to pivot into a niche music discovery dashboard, rather than a fully-fledged social media network.

Back in the 2000s, the platform quickly saw soaring popularity and briefly became the most visited website in the US in 2006, overtaking Yahoo Mail and Google Search in terms of visits.

This was mainly due to users loving its profile customisation options and music integration features. Features like the “Top 8” public ranking of best friends and signature profile soundtracks further contributed to high user engagement.

The platform also effortlessly captured the 2000s “emo” and other alternative subcultures.

However, the platform’s popularity started declining around 2009, mainly due to the rise of Facebook, as it became more difficult to retain advertisers.

A string of ownership and management changes over the years also contributed to declining consumer interest.

Surviving a different market

MySpace could have a key opportunity to capture a wave of younger users, who are currently dealing with rising digital fatigue and are increasingly fascinated by analog devices, simpler social media platforms and early 2000s culture.

Millennial users also still crave MySpace’s authenticity, without the need for endless filters and constant social performance. The brand also still has massive recognition.

However, analysts warn that the platform could still have a tough time relaunching, due to a fundamentally different market compared with the mid-2000s. The current market is highly competitive and overcrowded by giants like Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

As such, trying to compete directly with them could be very challenging and make it considerably more difficult to find advertisers.

The consumer base has also changed fundamentally in the last decade, with users now used to algorithm-driven feeds and content catering to significantly shorter attention spans.

Key markets like the US and EU have also seen rapidly evolving regulatory changes in the last few years, with more scrutiny around digital safety and data privacy.

Previously, MySpace had lost out to Facebook due to the very features that once made it unique — its music and customisation options, which eventually became too loud, cluttered and complicated for users who wanted a cleaner, simpler feed.

As such, the platform will need to find a way to better balance uniqueness with what current users are looking for now, such as clean interfaces and better discoverability, if it is to have a shot at success in today’s market.

World.title: Meloni and Frederiksen reiterate opposition to 'uncontrolled immigration'
World.content:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni published a joint statement with the Danish Premier Mette Frederiksen on Monday, confirming their united front in the fight against “uncontrolled migration”, vowing to "protect" Europe’s Christian cultural heritage.

 

The statement notes that the two are the only female leaders of European governments and, despite coming from different political backgrounds and geographical realities, are united by a shared commitment to defending Europe.

"We do not accept uncontrolled immigration into Europe, and we have promoted a rigorous migration policy, both in our own countries and across Europe," Meloni said in a Facebook post.

"No one can deny the negative impacts of illegal immigration on our societies: rising crime rates, increasing pressure on public services and an erosion of public trust. It is particularly serious when illegal migrants, who have no right to remain in our countries, commit violent crimes, traffic drugs or are responsible for sexual violence," the post reads.

Frederiksen and Meloni have recently emerged as the EU's most vocal advocates for a tougher migration policy, notably since the crisis in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, which saw tens of thousands of irregular migrants crossing the border within hours.

In response, Italy and Denmark led an open letter to the EU institutions, signed by a total of 22 member states, calling for coordinated action to combat illegal migration, strengthen external borders and address so-called "pull factors."

For the two leaders, ordinary citizens have paid too high a price for uncontrolled migration for too long — a tougher approach to migrants who have committed serious crimes, they argue, means greater security and protection for communities.

"So what more can we do? We need to set up repatriation centres in third countries, as well as other innovative solutions outside Europe. We are working hard on this," the post reads, referring to return hubs, an approach Italy has been trialling in Albania and that was recently written into a controversial EU law.

"But this is not enough. Compliance with our laws must go hand in hand with respect for European values. This applies to irregular migrants, but also to the millions of foreign nationals living legally in our countries and across Europe," the statement adds.

For the two prime ministers, the migration issue ultimately comes down to respect for Europe's Christian cultural heritage and shared values, which both vowed to defend.

World.title: Top tips and tricks for travelling internationally with young children
World.content:
Travelling with babies and toddlers can be daunting for parents. Questions about air travel, what to pack and safety are often top of mind, especially on long-distance flights and international trips.

 

“Travelling with kids is a whole new world," said Dr. Shannon Thompson, a paediatrician at Cleveland Clinic Children's, adding that it's important to “enjoy your kiddo on your trip” as much as you can.

Here are some tips and tricks for parents to travel safely with young children – and have fun with them, too.

Look for amenities like cribs and high chairs before you book

Before you decide where to stay, consider your options for baby-proofing.

Check whether items like portable playpens, cribs and high chairs are offered to guests. If you are staying somewhere with stairs, a balcony or a pool, inquire about baby gates; if they are not provided, see if they are available for rent nearby or consider bringing travel-friendly foldable mesh gates.

Pack electrical outlet covers and wipes to clean any dirty surfaces your kiddo might touch.

For babies, safe sleeping is still essential on vacation. Children younger than one should sleep on their back on a flat, firm surface such as a mattress in a bassinet, crib or playpen with nothing more than a fitted sheet, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.

The organisation also recommends babies sleep in the parents' room – but not in the parents' bed – for at least the first six months.

You should also consider how you will get to your lodging: Will you fly in and rent a car or take a taxi, or take public transit from the airport? Will you mostly be driving or walking?

For parents, these factors can determine whether you want to bring a stroller and a car seat, both of which you can gate check for free when you fly, or rely on using a sling or baby carrier.

Plan for snacks and diaper changes on the plane

“Flying with kids is one of those big, intimidating things,” Thompson said. “I think the biggest thing to think about is always safety and then of course their comfort.”

While children under two can fly in their parents’ lap, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency recommends securing them in their own safety seat, such as a car seat certified for use on planes. This requires buying a seat for your child.

For long-haul or international flights, ask the airline if they have bassinets available.

Baby food such as formula, puree pouches and breast milk are not subject to the 100 millilitre rule when passing through security, but only for use during your trip (so you won’t be able to bring excessive amounts) and you might be asked to prove its authenticity.

In addition to snacks, don't forget to carry on diapers, wipes, a portable changing pad and sealable plastic bags for disposal. Bring extra clothes to layer or change in case of accidents or messy spills.

Swallowing and chewing can help with ear pressure, so nursing little ones or giving them a bottle or pacifier can ease discomfort during take-off and landing.

Speak with your pediatrician beforehand if your child is prone to ear infections, and before travelling abroad, ask them what vaccines may be recommended.

Keep kids entertained on and off the plane

For flights with young kids, Christy Slavik, owner of the travel agency Mom Approved Travel, recommends “having little surprises that you can distract them with” – such as sticky mats for travel-sized play doh, suction cup toys and other games that are small and light to pack.

If sightseeing once at your destination, think about ways to make activities more fun and interactive. For art museums, bring notebooks that kids can draw in, or ask them what types of animals they can find in the paintings, Slavik said.

“Kids need a mission. They need games,” she said. “You have to get creative sometimes when you're travelling."

Exposing children to other cultures, foods and languages can also be fun. Some may enjoy picking out snacks at markets, for example, or learning foreign words for their favourite dishes and activities.

There are options for places to stay that are family friendly, with amenities such as pools or games. For those travelling abroad on a budget, many hostels offer private rooms for families so they don’t have to share a dorm-style room with bunk beds. Hotels and hostels provide the opportunity to meet other travellers, including fellow children who can become playmates.

The perks of travelling with extended family

Helping mums actually enjoy their vacation – and relax amid the stress that can come with planning and travelling – is a core goal of Slavik's travel agency.

One way parents can get a break is by planning trips with grandparents or other family members.

This helps with babysitting duties, while also allowing loved ones to have special bonding time with kiddos. Just make sure they also have their own down time and aren't wearing themselves out, Slavik said.

“When you bring grandparents to a vacation, you're giving them the opportunity to experience those moments together,” she said.

World.title: Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy
World.content:
The launch of the Yeni Party in Turkey promises to energise the country's struggling opposition. But while some polls show it leading, it remains vulnerable – already beset by arrests it says are "politically motivated".

Advertising

In a glitzy video, set to pumping music and shared widely across social media, Ozgur Ozel launched the Yeni Party – "New Party" – vowing to usher in a new era in Turkish politics and end President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s long rule.

Ozel founded the New Party after a court removed him from leading the main opposition party, the Republican People’s Party (CHP).

His rival, former party leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu, 77, who lost every election during his decade in charge of the CHP, replaced him.

Many in the country believe Erdogan played a role in the removal of Ozel, as his popularity grew thanks to tireless campaigning.

Riding the wave

The New Party is settings its sights beyond the CHP’s usual supporters.

"It covers the whole political spectrum in Turkish political life," explains Ozel's advisor Ilham Uzel.

"There are critical elements like democratisation, rule of law, secularism and a pro-Western approach, so we maintain these main pillars. But it is not confined to social democracy; we reach out to every section of Turkish society, including Islamists and conservatives, nationalists and liberals. We have Kurdish supporters."

The New Party is riding a wave of excitement. Ninety-one out of 135 CHP parliamentary deputies have defected to its ranks, joined by dozens of mayors and it is swiftly becoming the main opposition in parliament.

Turkey opposition worries that Europe is sacrificing democracy for security

Some polls show the party soaring above 30 percent, leaving Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party behind, while the CHP’s support has collapsed.

The New Party’s broad approach is finding fertile ground. "Even those who still support the governing coalition, the AK Party and MHP, are unhappy with how things are or how politics is practised, especially regarding economic issues. So there is a push towards change," says political commentator Sezin Oney.

"There is a yearning to change things at the grassroots, and the New Party may be the only party that can represent a new way of doing politics. But they have to live up to it, of course."

Corruption charges

Erdogan has remained in power for more than 20 years partly by exploiting divisions within the opposition, which is made up of conservatives, hardline secularists, and both Kurdish and Turkish nationalists.

The New Party has a key advantage over the strongly secular CHP, whose history is linked to past policies targeting Turkey’s large Kurdish minority and religious conservatives.

"CHP is identified with many bad experiences that the Kurds and conservative people had in past decades," said Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

"If you look at what Ozgur Ozel says during his speeches, you may clearly see the Yeni Party doesn’t have the baggage of CHP."

Erdogan has also often exploited the CHP’s history, painting it as anti-religious and hostile to Kurdish minority rights. The New Party faces the tricky task of keeping CHP loyalists on board while reaching new supporters.

But for now, simply staying out of jail may be the most pressing concern for its representatives.

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Several mayors who joined the New Party have been arrested on corruption charges, widely seen as politically motivated. In the past two years, 26 opposition mayors and hundreds of officials have been imprisoned on corruption allegations, compared to two mayors from Erdogan’s AK Party.

"They are cracking down on our party – every other day, mayors are arrested," says Uzgel. "They filed another charge against our leader. Nobody is safe in this authoritarian regime. So Mr Ozel is on the spot, definitely."

Ozel is protected by parliamentary immunity, but Oney warns he may be running out of time.

"Ozgur Ozel might be imprisoned himself once his immunity is removed by a parliamentary vote, that's a possibility. The only immunity he can have is the immunity bestowed upon him by the people. So only public opinion is protecting him. How much can it protect him? We'll see."

With parliament about to break for summer until October, Ozel has a brief window to strengthen his party and rally public support.

World.title: UEFA, CONCACAF and AFC accuse Infantino of 'breach of trust'
World.content:
A few weeks ago, Gianni Infantino looked set for another unopposed term as FIFA president. Now, with an election looming, the beleagured Swiss executive is counting the numbers and could be hanging by a thread.

Gianni Infantino's already perilous position as FIFA president took another blow on Monday, as three continental federations banded together in an apparent attempt to try to force him out.

An "Open Letter to the Football Family" signed by the heads of UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia) appeared to take aim at Infantino – without actually mentioning him by name.

"This is about something more fundamental: the integrity of the game, and the integrity of those elected to lead it. Leadership in football is not a possession. It is not about holding – or demanding – power to be held," the statement read.

"It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it. When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."

FIFA accused of blackmail in exchange for Infantino support To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The letter criticizes Infantino's now scrapped plan to form a subsidiary arm of FIFA in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors. It says that even in withdrawing the plan FIFA "did not acknowledge that the proposal itself was inherently wrong."

It also labels the plan a "fundamental breach of trust" and lambasted Infantino's seemingly unilateral actions in bypassing the executive FIFA Council for his initial proposal and then holding a summit in Morocco with only selected senior figures within the organization.

"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him. There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness," the letter reads.

The statement comes after media reports that UEFA paid off an alleged mistress of Infantino during his time at the European confederation. FIFA in response criticized "unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims" and said that "it is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine FIFA and its President." FIFA have not yet replied to a DW request for comment on the open letter.

What does this change?

Were the national federations of the three confederations to fall in line, there would be easily enough votes to oust Infantino at the presidential election next February. FIFA has 211 voting members and thus a presidential candidate in a two-horse race would require 106 votes next March. UEFA (55 members) AFC (46) and CONCACAF (35) would easily have enough if each confederation's members voted as a bloc.

However, this seems unlikely. While UEFA, who have driven much of the opposition, seem relatively united, the picture in the two other confederations is more mixed. Mexico, one of CONCACAF's most powerful nations and a World Cup 2026 cohost, have backed Infantino while Qatar, who hosted the 2022 World Cup, is one of several Asian nations to have broken ranks.

The South American federation CONMEBOL (10) does not yet have a clear position on Infantino, but one of its most powerful nations, Argentina, have lent Infantino their support. The Oceania federation (11) has also yet to make its position clear.

Perhaps the best news for Infantino was the backing of the African confederation, CAF (54), last week. A statement from the organization's executive committee said that CAF: "unanimously reconfirmed its support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino and thanked him for his support for African Football, over the years."

Is there a candidate to challenge Infantino?

This is the big question. As it stands, no candidate has stepped forward. Infantino won the last presidential election unopposed and looked likely to do so again next March, until a few weeks ago.

Though the clear positioning of several confederations against Infantino suggests that running unopposed again is now unlikely, a candidate that can unite those federations in opposition to the Swiss administrator is the next step.

"There's such an imperative to get a candidate who could unite the whole world of football, not just Europe in this case," UEFA vice president, Laura McAllister, recently told DW.

"It's not as easy as people might think. The right candidate has to also have the right level of support, but if we're talking about the right candidate, then I think that person, that man or woman needs to be somebody who recognizes that we are simply custodians of the sport and that we look after it and hopefully leave it in better health."

What might happen next?

There will no doubt be plenty of backroom talks about finding a candidate and announcing them at the right time. But given that Infantino retains a reasonable amount of support, football's powerbrokers will likely want to ensure whoever they might put up can win. UEFA executives will likely discuss this at the Super Cup (between the winners of last season's Champions League and Europa League) later this week, while other federations will look to do similar.

Looming in early September is the first FIFA tournament since the controversial sell off plan was announced. The U-20 Women's World Cup is being held in Poland, a UEFA member, and it is not yet clear whether European teams will participate in the tournament with Infantino still in charge.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: Ukrainian drone attack kills at least 13 in central Russia
World.content:
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at targets inside Russia, according to Russian officials. The strikes killed more than a dozen in one of Kyiv's deadliest attacks since the Russian invasion began over four years ago.

A Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Nizhnekamsk, located in an energy-rich Tatarstan region of central Russia, killed at least 13 people and wounded 48 more, according to a local press service statement issued Monday.

Over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from the Russian-Ukrainian border, the region has many major oil refineries that Kyiv has targeted in recent strikes as both sides increase long-range attacks on infrastructure.

The United Nations said such attacks have led to a jump in civilian casualties in Russia and Ukraine.

Unspecified industrial and civilian targets had been hit in Monday's strike, Radmir Belyayev, the mayor of Nizhnekamsk, said in a statement on Telegram.

Ukraine's military ⁠said ⁠it struck the Taneco oil refinery overnight, adding that a ⁠fire was recorded at the site.

The Ukrainian strikes on refineries have led to some fuel shortages and reduced Russia's oil-refining capacity.

Russia has also regularly fired missiles, glide bombs and drones hitting civilian areas in Ukraine and causing thousands of civilian casualties, according to the United Nations.

Russia, Ukraine: Deadly drone and missile attacks escalate To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Kyiv: Air campaign aims to bring Putin to negotiating table

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the campaign aims to force Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the more than 4-year-old full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

"We do deliver entirely justified responses, and every Russian strike will be met with our response. Russia's war will be felt more and more at their own home — in Russia," Zelenskyy said late Sunday in a social media post.

Ukraine's air force said Russia fired 126 drones in its overnight attack.

The Russian Defense Ministry said it shot down 456 Ukrainian drones fired overnight. The ministry, however, does not include how many drones or missiles reach their targets or how many were intercepted in the Tatarstan region.

Near the front line in Ukraine, a Russian artillery strike killed five people in a village in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukrainian officials said.

"On August 10, Russian forces carried out a massive artillery strike on the residential area of the village of Bugaivka in the Chuguiv district. Various houses were destroyed as a result of the enemy attack. Five people were killed," the regional prosecutor's office said in a statement on Telegram.

World.title: Thai ex-lawmaker shoots local official dead over loan
World.content:
A former lawmaker confessed to shooting a senior official at a government office over a money dispute, police have said. The incident came just days after Thailand's deadliest shooting in nearly four years.

Thai police arrested a suspected gunman — identified as former lawmaker Chalong Riewraeng — after he allegedly fired shots that killed a local politician on Monday at a government office on the outskirts of Bangkok.

Authorities said the former MP confessed to the shooting.

Surrounded by police, Chalong told reporters he attempted to speak with Thongchai Yenprasert about money.

"I followed him to his car and hit his car's window, saying I want to talk," the suspect said. "He said he will not talk, so I pulled my gun. I did not aim to shoot, but his driver pulled a gun and pointed it at me so I fired."

Thongchai, who was chairman of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organization, died of his wounds, according to Sakon Sukprom, director of Phra Nang Klao hospital.

Thongchai's driver was also shot and successfully underwent surgery, Sakon added.

Nonthaburi Governor Chestha Mosikarat told reporters the suspect and victim were "friends for a long time" and the incident likely stemmed from a misunderstanding.

Police said the motive for the shooting was a "personal issue."

"According to his confession, it was about money that the ... chairman borrowed from him for several years, and he asked for the return of the money several times," regional Police Commander Wattana Yeechin told reporters, adding that the dispute was over several million baht (1 million baht is about €26,220 or $30,300).

Second recent shooting

This comes just days after a 14-year-old's shooting rampage, first at his home and then at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, left nine people dead and over 20 injured. That incident was Thailand's deadliest mass shooting in nearly four years.

Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul had reiterated his intention to tighten gun control laws in the wake of the shooting. The Southeast Asian country's current gun laws do not include mental health screenings and allow people as young as 20 to have guns.

Thailand had around 15 guns per 100 ⁠residents, the highest rate in Southeast Asia ​by a wide margin, according to a 2017 estimate by the Small Arms Survey.

Police used water cannons to disperse the crowd of students marching towards the state assembly in Ranchi in the eastern state of Jharkhand on Monday, reports said.

The sit-in protests in Jharkhand began on July 25.

Students are demanding the cancellation of recruitment examinations citing irregularities Image: ANI Video Grab

Student leader Devendra Nath Mahto has been on an indefinite hunger strike since August 2 is demanding action over alleged irregularities in the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC), Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission Combined Graduate Level (JSSC CGL) and other competitive examinations required to qualify for government jobs.

Meanwhile, authorities on Monday arrested former Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) chairperson L Khiangte in connection with alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations, reports said.

The protest witnessed heavy police deployment across state capital Ranchi Image: ANI Video Grab

Earlier, Chief Minister Hemant Soren has assured the protesting students that his government would take action over alleged exam irregularities and invited them for talks.

World.title: When extreme heat threatens Europe's nuclear power
World.content:
Warm rivers and low water levels are forcing nuclear power plants to reduce output across Europe. Over a year, the losses are minimal, but on critical days the loss of power has consequences for grids and prices.

The state of the Danube is currently showing just how dependent nuclear power plants are on their local conditions. At the power station in Paks, Hungary — which normally produces about 40% of the country's electricity needs — only one of four turbine units is still operating. Due to record-low water levels in the Danube, the country's only nuclear power plant was even briefly at risk of a complete shutdown.

But for the European electricity market, France is of far greater significance. No other country in Europe relies so heavily on nuclear power, and if output in France drops, the country supplies less electricity to its neighbors, and may even become an electricity importer itself.

Reduced power

Over the course of the entire year, heat-related production losses at French power plants are minimal, but during individual weeks of extreme heat, the restrictions can be significant.

A 2023 report by France's official audit office estimated that, between 2000 and 2022, annual losses across all of the country's nuclear reactors due to high water temperatures and low river levels amounted to less than 1% of annual nuclear power production in any given year. Even in the extremely hot summer of 2003, they amounted to only about 1.5%.

But the annual figures obscure short-term fluctuations. In the summer of 2003, French nuclear power plants had to temporarily reduce their output by more than six gigawatts, and the most recent heat waves at the end of June and in mid-July 2026 saw the maximum available capacity was temporarily limited by eight to nine gigawatts. This corresponds to up to one-fifth of the nuclear power capacity normally available to France in the summer.

But eight gigawatts less capacity is not the same as an eight gigawatt overall shortfall. Even without the low water levels, some reactors would not be running at full capacity — either because of lower summer demand, high solar-power production, or bottlenecks in the power grid. According to grid operators, France still had sufficient reserves even during the 2026 heat waves and, on balance, remained an electricity exporter.

Hungary's power options after drought shuts nuclear plant To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other countries feel the impact

Nevertheless, such restrictions are relevant for grid operators and electricity traders. For them, it doesn't matter how much electricity was ultimately produced by nuclear power plants at the end of the year: What is crucial for the stability of the power grids and short-term price surges is whether the power is actually available when it is needed.

And here, experience shows that heat waves increase electricity demand due to air conditioning. Not only that: As this year's heat waves are affecting large parts of Europe, reserves from abroad are also declining.

Rivers getting warmer

Nuclear power plants suffer from low water levels because they must discharge a comparatively large amount of waste heat per kilowatt-hour generated. Only about one-third of the heat generated in a nuclear reactor is converted into electricity; the rest is released into the environment via the cooling system — often into rivers or the sea. But if the river is carrying little water, the waste heat is distributed over a smaller volume of water, and the water temperature rises faster.

Warm water also contains less oxygen, and legal temperature limits are in place to protect fish and other aquatic life. When operators throttle back a reactor in the summer, it is therefore usually not an emergency shutdown for reactor safety, but rather a measure to protect the local river life.

In critical situations, French authorities occasionally grant exemptions from these limits. In such cases, water bodies are monitored more closely, allowing the state-owned power company EdF to produce additional electricity in the short term.

A power plant with cooling towers draws significantly less water from the river and discharges considerably less heat directly into the water than a plant with an open cooling circuit. However, cooling towers do not make a nuclear power plant independent of weather conditions, as the Golfech plant demonstrates.

Located on the Garonne River, which is particularly warm in summer and frequently experiences low water levels, it is one of the most vulnerable sites, despite its cooling towers.

Meanwhile in Chooz on the Meuse River, the reactors had to be throttled back in 2020 despite the cooling towers, to avoid jeopardizing the drinking water supply in Belgium.

The Chooz power plant in France had to be throttled down in 2020 Image: Francois Lo Presti/AFP

Repairs also reduce output

Not every decline in nuclear power production can be explained by the weather. Four years ago, France's reactors generated nearly 82 terawatt-hours less electricity than in 2021. This headline-grabbing crisis was caused less by climate change than by stress corrosion cracking and postponed maintenance work.

But looking ahead, the French audit office expects that climate-related reactor downtime could triple or even quadruple by 2050. Given the low baseline so far, even that would not yet constitute a widespread outage, but it could become critical for individual sites.

With additional cooling towers, deeper water intake structures, and better maintenance planning, France can at least partially counteract this trend. However, making the power plants more heat-resistant costs a lot of money and requires more land.

In its upcoming nuclear power plant modernization program, France intends to take the consequences of climate change into account. Four of the six modern EPR2 reactors initially planned are to be built on the coast, in Penly and Gravelines. Only the third pair of reactors will be built on the Rhone River near Bugey. Cooling towers there are intended to limit the thermal load on the river and water intake.

The Garonne River in France saw extremely low levels in 2022 Image: Valentine Chapuis/AFP

Consequences across Europe

The consequences of French reactor curtailments are evident in the European electricity market. On June 24, capacity was reduced by approximately 4.1 gigawatts due to high river temperatures. As a result, France's electricity exports fell to about three gigawatts, after the country had supplied 10 to 12 gigawatts to its neighbors just the week before.

Combined with higher electricity consumption, low wind power generation, and increased use of gas-fired power plants, this contributed to electricity prices in France and Germany briefly climbing to their highest levels since January 2025.

During the subsequent heat waves in July, the curtailment of reactors was even more extensive, though the impact on other countries was less significant. On July 13, eight reactors with a combined capacity of 6.3 gigawatts were affected, and two were completely taken offline. Nevertheless, France only intermittently exported more than 10 gigawatts and imported affordable solar and wind power from Spain.

The heat-related curtailments of nuclear power plants currently appear to be a manageable problem for the country. Whether this will develop into a Europe-wide shortage in the future will likely depend not least on the development of foreign demand and the reserves of wind and solar power.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: China: Typhoon Dolphin prompts mass evacuation, canceled flights
World.content:
Even as it weakens, Typhoon Dolphin is disrupting life in China. Close to 1,500 flights have been canceled in Shanghai while parts of Beijing are under flood alert.

Heavy rainfall and strong winds prompted flood alerts and more than 1,000 flight cancellations across China on Monday, even as Typhoon Dolphin weakened.

China's National Meteorological Centre (NMC) issued its least severe typhoon alert on Monday morning as the storm lost power after making landfall in China's Zhejiang Province on Sunday.

Despite the weaker storm, the NMC warned that parts of east and central China will continue to receive heavy rainfall. Authorities issued their most severe flash flood alert for parts of eastern and southern Zhejiang on Monday, state news broadcaster CCTV reported.

China's Zhejiang province has faced the worst of Typhoon Dolphin so far Image: AFP

Five districts in Beijing are also under red alerts for heavy rainfall on Monday, with risks of landslides and flooding.

The storm had already forced over 300,000 people in eastern China to preemptively relocate, while bringing heavy rainfall to northern Taiwan over the weekend. In Shanghai, authorities evacuated more than 30,000 people out of high-risk areas. Overall, some one million people have been told to seek shelter.

Social media images showed high speed winds and overturned trucks in Zhejiang on Sunday, where the typhoon made landfall Image: Social Media/REUTERS

Typhoon Dolphin disrupts transport in Shanghai

Shanghai's two main passenger airports, Pudong International Airport and Hongqiao International Airport, canceled 943 flights between them for Monday, the airport authority said in a post online. That's a reduction of capacity by nearly 40%.

On Sunday, the two airports had cancelled nearly 1,500 flights, or about 60% of their scheduled travel, according to state media.

The typhoon has lost some of its strength but China's weather agency still expects days of heavy rainfall Image: cnsphoto/REUTERS

Public transport services in the city were also impacted, with several local trains suspended.

At the same time, Zhejiang province began to resume its transport facilities.

Zhejiang's Ningbo International Airport will resume flights midday on Monday but warned that some of the scheduled travel may still be delayed or canceled as the storm had "not yet completely dissipated."

China is dealing with Typhoon Dolphin just two weeks after Typhoon Noul struck its southern Guangdong province. Last month, Typhoon Maysak killed 11 people and injured over 300 in the central Hubei province.

Extreme weather systems are a common feature in China this time of the year, with typhoons leaving significant displacement, infrastructural damage and loss of lives. Scientists warn that the intensity and frequency of such extreme weather have increased and will continue to rise amid climate change.
